docs.title: source-manager
docs.text:
A desktop GUI for viewing and managing Git repositories, on macOS, Linux and Windows. Built with Qt/QML and libgit2 — one native window, no browser engine, no daemon.

It is a full client rather than a viewer: it stages at line level, rewrites history, resolves conflicts, moves objects over the network, reads pull requests and CI from three forges, and tells you what it did afterwards.

  • :material-rocket-launch: Getting started

    Build it, install it, and find your way around the window.

  • :material-format-list-bulleted: Features

    Every surface, every verb, and why each behaves the way it does.

  • :material-scale-balance: Comparison

    Fourteen other git clients, measured — and where this one is behind.

  • :material-map-marker-path: Roadmap

    What is outstanding, what was declined, and what will never be built.

docs.title: What it does, in one screenful
docs.text: A fleet home Every registered repository's branch, drift, uncommitted work and stopped operations on one page — grouped, and filled by scanning a folder History A branch graph with lanes and ref pills, searchable six ways including the content a commit changed, filterable by author, period, ref and signature Staging File, hunk or individual line — and discard and revert at the same three granularities Rewriting Interactive rebase you plan before anything is written, amend, reword or edit any commit, cherry-pick a commit or a range Conflicts Three-way per hunk, showing what the current choice would actually write, with an external merge tool beside it Transport Fetch, push, pull and clone, off the interface thread, one at a time, with force-with-lease and a plain force behind a third gesture Forges Pull requests, reviews, line comments and CI from GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket, including self-hosted instances Trackers Tickets read and written from GitHub Issues, Jira or Linear — and link rules that need no key at all Insights History metrics, DORA with the definition printed beside every figure, per-person figures with the caveat kept, CI health Keyboard A ⌘K palette and a two-press hint overlay, both fed by one registry every control registers itself with Honesty An operation log that types each write and offers a way back only where one exists — and says plainly when there is not

docs.title: The five things nothing else in the field does
docs.text:
1. Honest undo. Every operation is typed — ref-move, inverse, destructive, remote, none — and a way back is offered only where one can be kept, with file-level backups taken before the writes that destroy content held in no git object. See Undo, backups and the log.
  2. It teaches the command line. The git command you would have typed is printed beside the decision, and the CLI vocabulary is the palette's own search index — so searching stash push finds the button.
  3. Repository insights. History metrics, DORA, team and per-person figures, CI health, each figure carrying the definition that produced it. This is normally a separate SaaS product. See Repository metrics.
  4. The keyboard model. A palette and a two-press, usage-ranked hint overlay, with an audit test that fails the build when a control is reachable by neither route.
  5. A review draft that survives. Write a review over several minutes and it survives the network failing, the app closing and signing out — with the forge's own pending review visible in the diff and marked as unsent.

docs.title: What it deliberately does not do
docs.text:
Absences here are positions rather than backlog, and each is argued rather than asserted:

  • No "Undo everything" button — the reflog records refs, not files, and a button that cannot tell those apart is most confident when it is most wrong.
  • No agentic AI — nothing edits files, runs commands or takes several turns. Generation produces a draft a reader reviews before it is used.
  • No embedded terminal and no Explorer shell extension — both declined with the cost written down. See Closed as decisions.
  • No branch picker that checks out — the breadcrumb's picker narrows the history and people rely on it not moving HEAD.
  • Absent rather than greyed controls: a verb that cannot apply to this repository is not drawn at all.

docs.title: Honesty about what is proven
docs.text:
The project's own documentation draws a line between what is implemented and what has been exercised, and these docs keep it. Three things are proved in shape and never against the real thing:

Unverified surfaces

  • Windows has never been executed. CI proves the tree configures, compiles, links and passes the suite headless under MSVC — and nothing about window chrome, native choosers, high-DPI on a real display, or paths typed with a drive letter.
  • GitLab and Bitbucket are fixture-proved. Their tests pin the URLs built and the JSON mapped onto the documented fields; no live instance has ever answered.
  • The AI providers, x509 signing, both keychain backends and the sparse verbs are implemented and unexercised.

Every page that touches one of those repeats the caveat where the claim is made.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text:
Source-available under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0: free for personal, hobby and other noncommercial use, including reading, modifying and sharing the source. Commercial use requires a paid licence.

Everything a single repository needs to be worked in day to day is free, permanently — staging, committing, history, blame, branching, merging, transport, conflict resolution, stashing, and the interactive rebase. What a licence adds is twenty named features: the forge, the tracker, metrics, stacks, the model, an unlimited fleet and the rest.

Every feature page says at the top which side of that line it is on, and names the feature id its controls carry. See Licensing for the whole table, what stays free, and the six promises a lapsed licence keeps — or Free or paid, page by page for the one-screen version.

docs.text:

Commits made before the licence changed remain under GPLv3, the licence they were published under.

docs.title: What is free, permanently
docs.text:
Everything a single repository needs to be worked in day to day: staging, committing, discarding, history, blame, diffing, branching, merging, transport, conflict resolution, stashing — and the interactive rebase, which is what "worked in day to day" means on any repository with a review culture, and which is the single most conspicuous thing GitKraken charges for.

Named, because "day to day" is doing a lot of work in that sentence:

Free Which is Changes and staging File, hunk and line, staging and discarding alike, plus ignore and delete Reading a diff Unified, split, syntax, word marks, images, binary, folds History, graph and search The walk, the lanes, six search scopes, the filters Blame and file history Including renames and the change heatmap Comparing two refs All three readings Branches Create, rename, delete, check out, upstreams, drift, the table Rewriting history The interactive rebase, amend, reword, edit, cherry-pick, revert, reset Merging and conflicts Unconditionally — the whole Conflicts surface, plus your own merge tool Tags and notes Both kinds of tag, and a commit's note Stash Create, apply, pop and drop Worktrees and submodules The whole lifecycle of each Sparse checkout The cone-mode verbs Remotes and transport Fetch, push, pull, clone, the lease, the credential ladder Git LFS Pointers, fetch, checkout, locks Signing Making one, and the verdict on somebody else's Patches Writing one, a series, and applying one Hooks List, edit, enable, delete Maintenance The .git breakdown and all nine verbs Your editor, terminal and file manager Templated, and discovered on the PATH Ticket link rules #412 and PROJ-88 turned into something to press, with no key at all Settings, themes and the keyboard Every preference, three palettes, the palette and the hints Up to three repositories in the fleet The fourth is what a licence is for

And one row in that table is marked free rather than paid, so the line is visible and one word from moving: rebase-interactive, the interactive rebase.

The list in the app is generated from the same table that does the gating, so it cannot come to disagree with what is actually gated. Moving a feature between the tiers is one word in one row, and that row also carries the words the offer is written from — a feature cannot be gated and left off the page that sells it, nor listed there while being free.

docs.title: Six promises a lapsed licence keeps
docs.text:
These are the invariants that stop a pricing decision becoming data loss, and they are named tests rather than intentions:

  1. A gated control is absent, not greyed. It does not register, does not take a hint key, and does not appear in the palette.
  2. Exactly one discoverable route to what a licence adds — the licence window, reachable from the application menu and by name from the palette. Without it, absent controls would make the paid tier invisible and unsellable: the rule against greying is not a licence to hide the offer.
  3. Never gate an exit from a stopped operation. Continuing or aborting a rebase, a merge, a cherry-pick or a bisect, resolving a conflict, and writing a resolution are free for ever. A trial that lapses overnight must not leave anybody in a detached HEAD with no button. The check refuses those ids ahead of the feature table, rather than relying on them having been left out of it, because the table is the thing most likely to be edited in a hurry.
  4. The entire Conflicts surface is free, unconditionally. A merge run at a command line can drop somebody onto it.
  5. Stash create, apply, pop and drop are free. Stashing is where work goes to be safe.
  6. Downgrading is read-only, never destructive. Forty registered repositories still list and still open; only the forty-first is refused. Nothing deletes an entry to enforce a limit.

docs.title: A gated control is drawn, and pressing it opens the offer
docs.text:
This reverses what the app used to do, and the old rule is worth stating because most of its reasoning survives: an absent control never lies about what this copy can do, and absent-not-greyed is how every other unavailable thing here behaves.

What it costs is that somebody who has not paid sees no evidence the paid tier exists at all — and a feature nobody can see is one nobody asks about, so somebody who would happily pay never finds out what for.

There is a way back: a setting hides the paid features, off by default and offered only on an unlicensed copy. It is stored and honoured on every copy all the same, so a licence that lapses does not silently un-hide what somebody put away.

The distinction the two rules turn on: "may this be shown" and "may this be run" are separate questions, and the second goes on keeping paid commands out of both keyboard routes.

docs.title: How the check works
docs.text:
Offline, and there is no phone-home. An Ed25519 signature over the key's payload, verified with a public key compiled into the binary.

A key is read from an environment variable, then a file in the app's own configuration directory, then the settings — and which of the three answered is published, because "Remove" clears the two the app owns and cannot unset a variable in a way that would survive the next launch. The button is absent for the environment rung and the verb refuses by naming the variable if it is reached anyway.

Coverage is measured against the build, not against the calendar. The price is one payment for the version bought, with bug fixes for a year and none after — so a licence covers any build committed within a year of its issue date, compared against the commit date of the build you are running. Compared against today it would lapse while you were still running the build you paid for. A build whose commit date is unknown (a tarball) is covered: a tarball is not evidence of anything, and refusing there punishes the one reader who cannot check.

Two public keys, and rotation is why. Either is accepted, so retiring a compromised key means shipping a build that drops it and keeps the other — and everything the survivor signed goes on working. With one key that same event would invalidate every licence ever sold.

What rotation does not do

It does not revoke. A leaked key mints licences until a build omitting it reaches the reader, and no client-side check can do better. Rotation bounds the damage in time; it does not undo it.

No obfuscation, no anti-tamper, no phone-home. A check that runs on your own machine is bypassable by anybody who wants to bypass it. The goal is a clear offer and an honest refusal.

docs.title: The check knows nothing about this app
docs.text:
Everything about checking a licence — the key format, the signature, the three places a key may be kept, coverage against the build date, and which features an id is allowed — is its own library, linking Qt Core and libcrypto and not the rest of the application. A file there that reached for a repository, a preference or one of this app's commands would not compile.

That is what makes "it knows nothing about this application" a fact the build enforces rather than a claim in a comment. What a product is — the key prefix, the public keys, the environment variable, the file name, the coverage window, the feature table and the ids that may never be gated — is data, and this app's is nine lines.

Three things stayed with the app because none could be anything else's: the table, because moving a feature between tiers is one word in one row; the ungatable set, because which verbs are a way out of something this app started is a fact about this app; and the fleet cap, which is the one thing the package refuses to model — "how many of the host's own things" can only be answered in some product's own vocabulary.

The library's own test drives it as a different product would, inventing one with its own prefix, variable, file, settings entry, coverage window and two features. That is the only thing that can say the package is reusable.

docs.title: The build with no paid tier on screen
docs.text:
cmake -B build -DSOURCEMANAGER_FREE_ONLY=ON .

Hides the paid features, the switch that would show them, and the licence window — for handing a copy to somebody who should not be offered something they cannot buy.

It is not a second product: the gate, the feature table and the licence check compile in exactly as they do otherwise, and only what is drawn changes. The suite passes in both configurations.

docs.title: Third-party software
docs.text:
The app links Qt, libgit2 and OpenSSL, and ships SQLite inside Qt's SQL driver. Every one of those is dynamically linked, unmodified, and named in the app under About → Third-party notices, with the verbatim licence texts, the copyright lines, and where the corresponding source can be obtained.

That screen is generated rather than written out, so the versions in it are the ones actually loaded rather than the ones this was compiled against — which matters because the project ships against Homebrew's Qt on macOS, aqtinstall's on Windows and the distribution's on Linux. A notice naming "Qt 6.8.0" is a claim about which Qt you are entitled to the source of, and a hardcoded string would be wrong on two platforms out of three.

The texts live in the repository and travel inside the binary, and a test walks the rows against them in both directions — a dependency added without its licence text fails the suite rather than shipping a notice with a hole in it, and a text carried that nothing names is either a dropped dependency whose row survived or weight nobody dares remove.

Each is checked against a phrase from its opening and one from its closing, and the pair is the point: the first catches a document that is not this licence, the second catches one that is and stops early — which no length check can honestly tell from a document that is legitimately short.

Nothing is modified, and the notice says so rather than staying silent — so the day somebody patches a dependency, that test fails and the notice is corrected, which is the only moment anybody would think to.

libgit2's linking exception travels with its GPL rather than beside it: read on its own, the GPLv2 text says the opposite of what applies, and that exception is the whole reason this app can be closed-source at all.

OpenSSL's licence changed at 3.0, so the row reads the loaded major version and, on an older library, names the older licence and points at the project instead of claiming a text this build does not carry.

The build tools — moc, rcc, uic, lrelease — are deliberately absent from the notices: they are GPLv3, which would matter if they were shipped. They are not; they run at build time under The Qt Company's GPL Exception, which exists to permit exactly this, and nothing of theirs is in the binary.

If you redistribute a build

Qt is used under the LGPLv3. Nothing here is statically linked, so it can be relinked against a Qt of your own — and the app says where the libraries are on each platform, because "you may relink" is not much use without saying where they are.

That obligation travels with a redistributed build: keep the notices screen, keep the texts, and do not link Qt statically without a commercial Qt licence.

Before shipping a macOS bundle, tools/verify-macos-bundle.sh reports anything it loads from outside itself — a Homebrew libgit2 that macdeployqt did not copy in works on the machine that built it and on no other.

docs.title: The git GUI field, and where this one sits
docs.text:
A survey of fourteen git clients — the ones people actually use — against this one.

Read the dating before the ratings

The field was compiled in August 2026 from vendor feature pages, product documentation and current reviews. This app's own column has been revised since and the others have not, so a competitor's twelve months of releases are not in it.

Treat the matrix as "what this app can do", measured honestly, and "what they could do a year ago", measured from their own marketing. Feature sets move, and the paid/free splits move fastest of all.

docs.title: Where it stands
docs.text:
It is in the top tier on the core git surface, and ahead of the field on several things nobody else does.

Measured on what a git client is fundamentally for — reading history, reading a diff, staging precisely, and rewriting history safely — this app sits with Fork, Tower, SmartGit and Magit rather than with the free clients it is priced like. Line-level staging, line-level revert, a previewed rebase plan, per-hunk three-way conflict resolution, a full submodule lifecycle, subtrees, worktrees, a stash editor, and a compare surface that tells two-dot from three-dot are collectively a set that only SmartGit and Magit match — and each of those charges or demands Emacs.

docs.title: Five things that are effectively unique
docs.text:
1. Honest undo. Everyone else either has no undo or sells "Undo everything". This app types every operation and offers a button only where one can be kept, with file-level backups taken before the four writes that destroy content held in no git object. GitButler's per-operation snapshots are the only comparable safety net, and it does not distinguish what is recoverable from what is not. → Undo, backups and the log
  2. Teaching the command line. What you would have typed, printed beside the decision. Sublime Merge shows commands as it runs them; nothing else in the field treats the CLI vocabulary as the search index for its own palette.
  3. Repository insights. History metrics, DORA with the definition printed beside every figure, team and per-person figures with the caveat kept, and CI health. No desktop client in this survey has anything like it; this is normally a separate SaaS product. → Repository metrics
  4. The keyboard model. A palette and a two-press, usage-ranked hint overlay, with an audit test that fails when a control registers in neither route. Only Magit and Lazygit are comparably keyboard-complete, and neither is discoverable the same way.
  5. Forge review depth with a local draft. Reading a proposal, writing a review over minutes, and submitting it in one request — with the draft surviving the network, the app closing, and signing out. Every other client that reviews drafts on the server. → Reviewing a proposal

Plus a set of correctness details the field routinely gets wrong: a virtualised diff that survives a ten-thousand-line hunk, a binary change reported as a kind rather than "no textual changes", a working-tree watcher, transport off the interface thread with one operation at a time, and contrast-verified palettes.

Two smaller ones worth naming because nobody else does them: a commit subject inferred from the changed paths and the log with each inference stating its basis — every competitor's suggestion is a model's, and states nothing — and that inference drawn beside the generated draft rather than instead of it, where everyone else ships one or the other.

docs.title: Where it is behind
docs.text:
Coverage is no longer the question; evidence is, and that is worth naming plainly.

The five gaps an earlier revision of this survey identified — Windows, Git LFS, commit signing, one forge, and no custom-command escape hatch — are closed, along with bisect, git-flow, external merge tools, patch import and format-patch, issue links, graph drag-and-drop, git notes, sparse checkout, shallow clone, a keychain, stacked branches, a second window, image diff modes, and AI.

What is left is short enough to state in one sentence: no Azure DevOps, no non-git VCS, no plugin API, no embedded terminal, no shell integration, no partial clone, no agentic AI — and five of those seven are recorded decisions rather than work outstanding.

The residual weakness is not a feature

Nothing Windows has ever been executed. The CI job proves the tree compiles, links and passes headless under MSVC, and says nothing about window chrome, native menus, file dialogs, high-DPI, or drive letters as a user types them.

GitLab and Bitbucket have never had an answer from a live instance. Their tests pin the shape of the requests and the mapping, which is a real guarantee and not the one a user cares about.

X.509 signing, both keychain backends, the sparse verbs and every AI provider are implemented and unexercised.

A competitor that ships to Windows every week has something this does not, and it is not a feature — it is a decade of people running it. The honest summary is that the capability gap is closed and the proving gap is now the whole of the remaining distance.

docs.title: The one-paragraph version
docs.text: On feature coverage this app now leads the field it was compared against, and it keeps the five things nothing else does: honest undo that distinguishes what can be recovered from what cannot, printing the git command you would have typed, repository and DORA metrics that are normally a separate product, a two-press usage-ranked keyboard model with an audit that fails when a control is reachable by neither route, and a review draft that survives the network, the app closing and signing out. Against GitKraken's and GitLens's free tiers it is not close, since both charge for interactive rebase, worktrees, the graph and multi-repo work that is unconditional here. What it does not have is evidence — Fork, Tower and SmartGit have each shipped to real users on three platforms for years, and that is a different kind of claim from a green suite.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The survey's own citations are kept in COMPARISON.md in the repository, which is where this section is derived from.

Two ratings that survey got wrong in its first pass are corrected there and here: Fork and Sourcetree have no AI features. The earlier partial rating for each came from review sites summarising each other rather than from either product, and Sourcetree has an open request for it — which is the opposite of shipping it. That is worth recording rather than quietly editing, because it is the same failure this document warns about elsewhere: a survey is only worth the evidence attached to it, and an aggregator is not evidence.
