docs.title: What the field charges for
docs.text:
Compiled August 2026. Paid/free splits move faster than anything else in this survey — treat the columns as a snapshot rather than a quote.

App Free tier Behind the paywall source-manager Everything one repository needs, day to day, permanently Fleet beyond three, folder import, a second window, forges beyond GitHub, pull requests and reviews, AI, permalinks, stash editing, bisect, stacked branches, recipes and sequences, metrics, subtrees, commit message help, the operation log, other languages GitKraken Public repos only, single profile, single integration, no commercial use Private repositories, interactive rebase, merge conflict editor, worktrees, multiple profiles, multiple integrations, self-hosted/Enterprise, SSO, Workspaces & Launchpad, AI credits, cloud patches Tower None — 30-day trial Everything ($69/user/yr) Fork Unlimited evaluation in practice, licence required for continued use Everything ($59.99 one-time) Sublime Merge Unlimited evaluation, no feature restriction, purchase nags Nothing functional ($99 one-time buys the nag-free licence) SmartGit Full product, non-commercial use only Commercial use; the Distributed Reviews add-on is licensed separately Sourcetree Everything Nothing GitHub Desktop Everything Nothing GitButler Desktop app Cloud/collaboration tiers where offered SourceGit Everything Nothing Git Extensions Everything Nothing TortoiseGit Everything Nothing Lazygit Everything Nothing Magit Everything Nothing GitLens Public and local repositories; inline blame; interactive rebase editor Commit Graph, Worktrees, Visual File History, Launchpad, AI features, Jira integration — all for private repositories

docs.title: The pattern worth noting
docs.text:
GitKraken and GitLens paywall capabilities this app gives away unconditionally — interactive rebase, worktrees, the commit graph, the merge editor, a multi-repo dashboard, pull request management. Against those two free tiers the comparison is not close.

Tower and Fork charge for the whole product. Only Sourcetree, GitHub Desktop and the open-source set are unconditionally free, and every one of those is weaker somewhere significant: no graph, no worktrees, Windows-only, or terminal-only.

docs.title: Where this app's line sits
docs.text:
Not "core is free, teams pay", which is GitKraken's, and not "everything, once", which is Fork's and Sublime Merge's. The line is drawn at one repository, worked in day to day:

  • Free, permanently: staging, committing, discarding, history, blame, diffing, branching, merging, transport, conflict resolution, stashing — and the interactive rebase, which is what "worked in day to day" means on any repository with a review culture, and which is the single most conspicuous thing GitKraken charges for.
  • Paid: the fleet beyond three, everything about other people's proposals, everything that reads a period rather than a moment, and the automation.

Two properties of that line are worth more than where it falls, and both are enforced by named tests rather than intended:

A licence never blocks finishing an operation already in progress. Continuing or aborting a rebase, a merge, a cherry-pick or a bisect, resolving a conflict, and every stash verb are free and cannot be gated — the check refuses those ids ahead of the feature table, rather than relying on them having been left out of it. A trial that lapses overnight must not leave anybody in a detached HEAD with no button.

Downgrading is read-only, never destructive. Forty registered repositories still list and still open when a licence lapses; only the forty-first is refused. Nothing deletes an entry to enforce a limit.

→ Licensing for the full table and how the check works.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
AGENTS.md is the authority, not this section

AGENTS.md is the reference for how the project fits together — the controller layout, the QML shell and its surfaces, the rebase and conflict models, and the conventions and constraints worth knowing before changing anything. Read it first when picking up work.

CLAUDE.md imports it, so coding agents following either convention load the same context.

These pages are an orientation and deliberately do not duplicate it: a second copy of an architecture reference is a second copy to go stale, and this project's own rule is that two spellings of one fact will drift.

  • :material-hammer-wrench: Building

    Dependencies, presets, warnings, and the precompiled header.

  • :material-test-tube: Testing

    One executable per test class, RepositoryMock, the QML suites, and the pipeline.

  • :material-file-tree: Architecture

    The three source layers, the four QML directories, and the two libraries that know nothing about this app.

  • :material-tag-outline: Releasing

    Two versions, a tag that is checked before anything is built, and a draft release.

  • :material-book-open-page-variant: These docs

    Building the site locally, and how it gets to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: The conventions that a change most often breaks
docs.text:
Not a summary of AGENTS.md — these are the handful that a first contribution trips over.

A new file needs a line somewhere. A new .cpp needs a line in its folder's source list; a new .qml needs a line in the resource manifest. Two tests enforce the second, because the QML suites load components by file path from the source tree while the app loads them from the resource — so a component missing from the manifest instantiates in every test and fails the app at startup with no window at all. That has shipped once, with fifty tests green.

Every interactive control declares a command. The design system's button, chip, row, tick and field do it for you; anything else declares its own. An audit test walks the built interface on every surface and fails, by name, on anything interactive that registered neither a palette entry nor a hint key.

A plan function and the operation it guards refuse in the same string. Asserted by a test, because that is the only thing that keeps a confirmation from promising something other than what the button does.

Every write operation has a refusal test: the case where it must decline rather than clobber, asserting nothing on disk changed.

A control that cannot apply is absent, not greyed.

Prose is translated and a git spelling is not. A control's title is prose; its verb is the git spelling and is the palette's search index, so translating it silently stops the palette finding it. Both directions are asserted from the source, because it is a fault in a declaration and is invisible at runtime.

Commits are conventional — feat:, fix:, chore:, refactor:, docs:.

docs.title: Three traps that have each cost an afternoon
docs.text:
QML binds to a property, never to an invokable. An invokable is not a binding dependency, so a binding written over one is evaluated when the component is built and never again. This has cost four separate features; where a controller has both, name the notifying property beside the call, and where the answer is keyed, publish a notifying map and let QML index it.

Never read a derived property inside its own dependency's change handler. Both are marked dirty by one notification and which is evaluated first is whichever was connected first — so a handler on x that reads something computed from x gets the value on its way out.

A part whose input can vanish for a turn needs total accessors. Closing something and hiding the panel that drew it are two property writes, so for one turn the panel is bound to an object that is no longer there.

docs.title: Verify against the pipeline's environment, not your own
docs.text:
A locally green test run is not a green pipeline: CI pins its runner image so the tested Qt cannot change without a commit saying so, and a machine ahead of it will compile things it cannot.

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:ro" ubuntu:26.04
# then the apt line out of ci.yml, configure, build, and ctest

Export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen, or two of the suites abort on the platform plugin and read as code failures.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: An orientation. AGENTS.md is the authority and goes into far more depth; this page is the shape of the thing and the handful of structural decisions that explain the rest.

docs.title: The tree
docs.text:
src/
├── main.cpp            entry point; builds the services and the first window
├── core/               the manager, and state that outlives a repository
├── git/                one controller per git operation, plus the diff parser
├── forge/              pull requests and CI over HTTP, behind a provider seam
├── ai/                 asking a model something, behind its own seam
├── licence/            a licence check, and nothing about this product
└── palette/            a command palette, and nothing about this app

qml/
├── design/             tokens, singletons and primitives. Imports nothing
├── parts/              what the surfaces are built from
├── surfaces/           one file per destination
└── shell/              the window, and the frame around a surface

tests/                  one executable per test class, plus the QML suites

src/ is the single include root, so every local include names its layer, and a test spells it the same way.

The first four folders are a reading aid rather than a link boundary: the backend is one static library filled by a source list per folder, because the manager owns a controller from each and the tests link one target.

docs.title: Two directories are the exception, and the exception is the feature
docs.text:
palette/ and licence/ are each their own library target — the first linking Qt Core and Qml, the second Qt Core and libcrypto, and neither linking the rest of the app. So a file in either that reached for a repository, a preference or one of this app's commands would not compile.

That is what makes "it knows nothing about this application" a fact the build enforces instead of a claim in a comment.

The palette was a sort comparator and a rank table written in a QML file — which is to say logic no C++ test could reach, asserted only through a window somebody had to build. Its vocabulary names no domain: a row is an id, a title, a subtitle, keywords, a group, a note, and two numbers that order an untyped list. It cannot run anything and deliberately never gains the ability: there is no callback on a row, it announces an id, and the host decides what that means.

The licence check carries the key format, the signature, the three places a key may be kept, and coverage against the build date. What a product is — its key prefix, its public keys, its feature table — is data, and this app's is nine lines. Its own test drives it as a different product would, inventing one with its own prefix and features, because that is the only thing that can say the package is reusable.

docs.title: The backend
docs.text:
The controllers are Qt Core only, with no GUI dependency — that is what lets the tests exercise them without a GUI application object. Everything a window needs is built once and handed to a window factory, which creates one manager per window and exposes it to that window's own context.

A manager owns every controller that is about a repository; nine members that are about the reader are shared between windows — the preferences, the fleet, the command counts, the language, the editor template, the keychain, the snapshot store, the command spellings and the version. Two of any of those in one process would be either a divergence or a race, since every one is backed by a file.

Each controller opens its own repository handle per call, through one owning type that closes it on scope exit. Twenty-two controllers used to have a private copy of that open, and underneath them were 357 hand-written frees — one per exit from every function that opened one, so every early return was a leak audited by eye.

docs.title: What joins the general refresh, and what does not
docs.text:
refreshAll() runs after every staged hunk, on every working-tree watcher event, and whenever the window comes back to the foreground. Anything in it is paid at that rate.

So the rule is both halves: an O(history) walk is batched against a time budget and asked for by the surface that draws it. The file history, the reflog, the metrics, the comparison, the commit-message vocabulary and the subtree list are all outside it.

"One commit message per commit and no diff" is a statement about the per-commit cost and not about the total, and it is what let a twenty-thousand-commit walk into the refresh under a comment calling it "the same order of work as the tag list". A tag list is O(refs).

The fleet is deliberately outside it too: summarising it opens every registered repository.

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
Exactly one surface exists at a time. Surfaces are loaded on demand rather than stacked: History and Blame each hold thousands of rows, and there is no reason for the ones you are not looking at to exist.

No surface reaches up into the window. Shared state travels down as properties and back up as signals, which is what lets any surface be instantiated on its own in a test — an id reference into the window would compile fine and break only under test.

The import graph is acyclic and worth keeping so: design imports nothing, parts imports design, surfaces imports both, and shell imports design plus, in three files, the other two. Those three are a widening rather than a cycle, and each is there for a shared element.

Colours come from one place. Not a hex literal and not a computed colour anywhere else — that rule used to be taste and is now load-bearing: forty-five inline colour calls spelled out one palette's ink and accent at some alpha, and every one of them was a component that would have gone on drawing the dark theme after the palette changed.

Do not name a component after a Controls type. An explicit module import beats the implicit same-directory one, so the stock type wins — silently, rendering system chrome. That is why the tick is TickBox and the command type is Command.

docs.title: Two things every control does
docs.text:
It registers itself. The palette and the hint overlay used to be two hand-maintained lists and they drifted — elements got a hint but no palette entry, or neither, and one whole tab strip had nothing at all. Now the design system's button, chip, row, tick and field each declare a command for themselves, so anything built out of them is covered without a thought.

It says what it does. One restyled tooltip, drawn from the title and detail the control already registered. Nothing new is written anywhere, which is the point rather than a convenience: a separate tooltip property would be a third wording of one thing, and the drift between what the palette says and what the pointer says would be invisible, since nobody reads both at once.

Both are structural: one audit test walks the built interface on eight surfaces and fails, by name, on anything interactive that registered neither route; a second fails on any control that is drawn and has nothing to say.

docs.title: The three performance shapes
docs.text:
Every expensive thing here is one of three, and a new one should be one of them too.

Batched against a time budget. A walk runs a batch per turn of the event loop against a millisecond budget rather than a count, because what an item costs varies by orders of magnitude — comparing a field against diffing a large file. A turn always does at least one item, whatever the budget says, or a budget of zero spins for ever making no progress.

Virtualised, with a height known at creation. A list fills its viewport by creating rows until their heights add up to it, and a row whose height is not known when it is created never adds anything up — so slicing a long hunk into smaller pieces made it strictly worse at every size. What virtualisation needs is not smaller rows but rows whose height is arithmetic.

Its corollary: a list's own height must not be bound to what the built rows add up to, or it starts at zero, builds no rows, and stays at zero.

One operation over a set, never N operations. Discarding eight hundred files was eight hundred repository opens, status walks, index writes, snapshots, log rows and full refreshes — none of those costs is per file, and every one is per operation. All four such verbs go through one shared sweep with one budget, one progress row and one Stop that is never gated.

docs.title: The seams
docs.text:
forge/ and ai/ are each a provider interface with a registry, so adding one is a class and one registration line — with the surfaces written against documented field lists rather than against anybody's JSON.

That claim is tested rather than asserted: adding a second forge proved it for every surface and every field list, and falsified it for the transport's write allow-list, which a provider deliberately cannot add a row to. The header says so now. A third forge, shaped differently in three ways, is what actually tested the seam — different paging, no review object at all, and both readings of CI.

The AI seam's claim is narrower and says so: a provider cannot widen what may leave the machine, because the privacy gate reads the URL rather than anything a provider declares.

Every transport is an interface because the tests cannot reach the network, and every implementation must answer on a later turn even when it already holds the answer — or a surface would pass its tests without ever rendering the loading state it spends most of its life in.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
cmake -B build .
cmake --build build

Dependencies and the per-platform install rules are in Installing. This page is what a contributor needs beyond that.

docs.title: Qt 6.2 is the floor, and the Qt 5 fallback is gone
docs.text:
For most of this project's life the root configuration looked for Qt 6, fell back to Qt 5, and set a version variable so that every link line and two conditional blocks could follow. Six QML files carried a sentence explaining what the Qt 5 path would cost them.

All of it is gone, and the argument is not that Qt 5 is old:

Nothing verified it, and one thing made it unverifiable. No build of this project has ever been made with Qt 5 — not on either desk, not in either CI job — and it could not have been: eleven of the QML suites call waitForPolish, which arrived in Qt 6.5, so a Qt 5 configure would have produced a build whose own test suite could not run.

A fallback that no run exercises is not a fallback; it is a set of conditionals that read as safety while guaranteeing nothing. Same fault as a find_program guard that skips in silence.

The floor is 6.2 rather than 6.5, and that gap is deliberate. 6.2 is the oldest Qt 6 LTS and what a long-term distribution ships; the app builds and runs against it. What needs 6.5 is the test suite, which a packager does not run — so raising the floor to 6.5 would refuse to configure on a machine where the product itself works.

Three uses in the QML tree are genuinely version-guarded — the system colour scheme (6.5) and the two native choosers (6.3) — and those guards stay: an unsatisfiable import is fatal to the whole file that writes it, which is why the two choosers sit behind loaders.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text:
-Wall -Wextra (/W4 on MSVC) are on and -Werror deliberately is not.

The compiler's default is close to silent, which is how a /* inside a block comment reached a reader rather than whoever wrote it. Turning the warnings on is one decision; failing the build on them is a second one with a different cost — a toolchain upgrade adds diagnostics, and a build that stops on those is a build that gets the flag removed rather than the code fixed.

They are set once at the root, so the library, the app and every test executable are held to the same standard.

A glob in a block comment

The prose in this codebase is long and quotes patterns, and vendor/** or /sub/*.log inside a /* … */ block opens a nested comment as far as the compiler is concerned — and everything to the next */ is then being read as one comment. Write the prefix and the wildcard as separate quoted pieces, or use // blocks.

docs.title: MSVC needs four flags, and three of them are not preferences
docs.text:
• /utf-8 — MSVC reads source in the machine's ANSI code page, and this tree's comments and labels carry ⌘, ⏎ and ⇧. Without it those are the first thing silently wrong.
  • /permissive- — MSVC's pre-standard lookup accepts templates the other two compilers refuse, which is how a third platform becomes a fork.
  • /bigobj — raises an object file's section limit. It is here rather than after the first failure because that failure is a hard error, not a warning.
  • /W4, and no /WX, for the reason above.

docs.title: The precompiled header
docs.text:
The 129 translation units are half of CI's wall clock, and a precompiled header takes a fifth off it. Measured against a cold build with no compiler cache, at --parallel 2 with four other builds running:

wall user (CPU) sys before 2m45.9s 4m36.2s 49.4s after 2m12.5s 3m25.5s 53.2s −20.1% −25.6% +7.7%

The CPU figure is the one to believe — wall clock on a machine running four other builds is a measurement of the other four as much as of this one. The sys column going up is the honest cost and is what it should be: a ~100 MB file read once per object instead of parsing headers.

Sixteen Qt headers and nothing of this project's own, chosen by how many units include them rather than by taste. Nothing local, deliberately — a precompiled header holding the god header would make an edit to it rebuild every object in the library, which is the cost this is supposed to remove, paid on the edit somebody is actually making.

One for the library and one for the suite. The library's is private: a public one is inherited by everything that links the target, which would put a second, differently-flagged compile under each of the sixty test executables.

The god header cannot be split, and that was checked rather than assumed. The manager includes all 51 controller headers and 44 of the library's 83 units include it, so editing any controller header rebuilds over half the library. The obvious fix — forward-declare the controllers, move the includes into the source — does not work: moc requires the complete type for a property of pointer type, and the generated unit sees only the header. Demonstrated on a three-line file rather than argued from memory.

What is left after the precompiled header is not includes. With nine more headers added, chosen the same way, a cold library build went from 1m07.8s to 1m05.0s — 4%. That is the headroom include hygiene has here; what remains is template instantiation across 83 units.

A unity build was not done, and would not be

It is the larger win and it changes what the compiler sees: concatenated units share a translation unit, so a missing #include in one file is supplied by whichever file happened to be concatenated above it — and the build stays green until somebody reorders the list or compiles that file alone.

A precompiled header cannot do that, since it is a prefix every unit gets whether or not it asked. That asymmetry is the whole reason one of these is here and the other is not.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
CMakePresets.json holds the build configurations — debug / release, each with an -install variant — and is committed because Qt Creator's own build configuration is not: that lives in a gitignored file, is rewritten by the IDE, and carries a kit UUID from the developer's own profile. A preset is the only way for the repository to say how the project is built.

The one thing a committed preset cannot supply is where Qt lives, which is machine-specific. See Installing for the gitignored user-preset that pins it robustly.

docs.title: Packaging: two targets, and the scripts under them
docs.text:
cmake --build build --target dmg   # macOS: a drag-to-install disk image
cmake --build build --target deb   # Linux: a Debian package

Each is declared only on the platform that can run it — a deb target on macOS would be a target that fails when pressed — and neither is in all: packaging takes minutes and is something a person asks for.

Both are a front door and not an implementation. The work is tools/make-deb.sh and tools/make-dmg.sh, and it is there for two reasons: the release pipeline runs them without a build tree of the shape a CMake target needs, and a shell script can be tested — test_debpackage and test_dmgimage run these directly, and ci.yml runs both for real on every push. A target that inlined the steps would be a second implementation, exercised only by whoever happened to use it.

What each produces, and what it deliberately is not, is in Releasing.

docs.title: The disk image, on a Mac
docs.text:
--target dmg stages the built bundle, runs macdeployqt over it to copy Qt in, ad-hoc signs it — not optional on Apple Silicon, where the kernel refuses to run code whose signature does not match its contents — checks with tools/verify-macos-bundle.sh that nothing in it still points at your Homebrew prefix, and lays the window out: the app on the left, an Applications symlink on the right, an arrow between them. It prints the path it wrote.

The window's layout is Finder's, driven by AppleScript, so the first run asks whether your terminal may control Finder. Refusing is not fatal: the image is still built, undecorated, and the script says loudly that it has no layout. That is also what happens on a CI runner, which has no GUI session — so the decoration is the one part of the image CI cannot check, and test_dmgimage's arithmetic plus opening a release candidate on a Mac is what covers it.

It is not notarised. Whoever you send it to right-clicks > Open the first time. To sign it properly, pass a Developer ID Application identity:

./tools/make-dmg.sh --build-dir build --output build/packages \
  --sign "Developer ID Application: … (TEAMID)"

docs.title: The .deb, from a Mac, in a container
docs.text:
--target deb works on macOS too, and does the container run for you:

cmake --build build --target deb    # → build/packages/source-manager_<v>-1_amd64.deb

On a Debian-ish machine that runs tools/make-deb.sh against the build tree already there; on macOS it goes through tools/make-deb-docker.sh, which mounts the checkout read-only, builds inside the container, and runs the same make-deb.sh in there. One name, one implementation, and the difference is the platform's rather than yours.

It is minutes rather than seconds: the whole app is compiled inside an emulated amd64 container. The script says so before it starts.

There are two other doors onto the same thing — the script directly, and compose:

./tools/make-deb-docker.sh --output build/packages
docker compose run --rm deb

All three run one implementation. The toolchain is packaging/deb/Dockerfile, which carries no source at all; the steps are packaging/deb/make-deb-in-container.sh, read out of the read-only mount so it cannot go stale against the tree being built; and what that runs is tools/make-deb.sh, the script the release pipeline runs. tools/make-deb-docker.sh --print-command prints the two docker commands without running them.

The toolchain being an image layer is the difference between a rebuild and a re-install: it used to apt-get install Qt's dev packages inside every run, which under emulation is minutes before the first line compiles.

Three details are load-bearing. The source is :ro because the container runs as root and a writable mount leaves root-owned files in your tree. HOST_UID/HOST_GID are what bring the package back owned by you — through compose on Linux, pass them in (HOST_UID=$(id -u) HOST_GID=$(id -g) docker compose run --rm deb). And:

--platform linux/amd64 is not optional on Apple Silicon

A .deb is built for one architecture and dpkg refuses it on any other. Without the flag you get an arm64 package — right for a Raspberry Pi, useless to everybody on an ordinary PC. The cost is that the build runs under emulation and takes several times longer.

The distribution it is built on decides who can install it. The package depends on the Qt it was linked against, so one built on 26.04 will not install on 24.04 and one built on 24.04 installs on both. ubuntu:26.04 is the default because it is what release.yml builds the published package on: a container run is then a rehearsal of the release rather than an approximation of it, and the floor of both is Ubuntu 26.04.

Nothing on the way to a release compiles against the app's own floor

The app claims Qt 6.2 and every machine that builds it now carries 6.10, so a call newer than the floor compiles everywhere and fails only for somebody on an older Qt. It has happened twice — beginFilterChange() in a proxy, and a closing connection needing a QQuickCloseEvent Qt keeps private before 6.6 — and both were caught by a 24.04 container back when the release was built in one.

What checks it now is a compose service nothing makes you run:

docker compose run --rm floor   # 24.04, Qt 6.4 → build/packages/24.04/

Install the result with apt, never dpkg -i — apt pulls the dependencies in, dpkg only reports that they are missing:

sudo apt install ./build/packages/source-manager_*.deb

docs.title: How old a macOS the build runs on
docs.text:
The cask says depends_on macos: ">= :sequoia", and that is a description of the artifact rather than a policy. The floor is the highest of three numbers, and only one of them is this project's:

  1. Your own deployment target. CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET is not set anywhere here, so the binary is built for whatever SDK the build host has — macOS 15 on the macos-15 runner.
  2. The minimum of the Qt frameworks macdeployqt copies in. Homebrew builds its bottles per macOS version, so a brew install qt on Sequoia gives frameworks built for Sequoia. This is the number that usually decides it, and it is the one people miss: setting a deployment target on your code does nothing about the frameworks sitting next to it in the bundle.
  3. What Qt itself supports. Qt has been dropping macOS versions steadily; check the release notes for the version you are on.

Read what a built bundle actually claims rather than trusting any of the above:

otool -l build/packages/stage/SourceManager.app/Contents/MacOS/SourceManager | grep -A3 LC_BUILD_VERSION
otool -l …/Contents/Frameworks/QtCore.framework/Versions/A/QtCore | grep -A3 LC_BUILD_VERSION

docs.title: Lowering it, and why the obvious route is a dead end
docs.text:
The obvious move is to build on an older runner. It no longer works: macos-14 is deprecated in actions/runner-images, and adopting an image that is being removed buys a lower floor until the day the release stops scheduling. macOS 15 is the oldest image that is not on its way out, which is where the build already is.

So the floor is Homebrew's, and moving it means changing where the dependencies come from — Qt from qt.io (whose macOS packages are universal and target an older macOS), libgit2 and OpenSSL built against the same target rather than taken from brew. That is a real piece of work with its own verification, not a flag, and nobody has done it here.

What has been done is to make the attempt checkable, because the failure is silent:

cmake -B build -DSOURCEMANAGER_MACOS_MIN=13.0
cmake --build build --target dmg

SOURCEMANAGER_MACOS_MIN sets CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET, which governs the app's own binary and nothing else. tools/make-dmg.sh then reads every Mach-O in the finished bundle and reports the highest minimum it finds — the frameworks included — so you can see immediately whether the deployment target achieved anything. --min-macos 13.0 turns that report into a refusal:

the bundle needs macOS 15.0 and --min-macos said 13.0.
Something in it is built for a newer macOS than you are promising — almost always
Homebrew's Qt, libgit2 or libcrypto, which are built per macOS version and do not
follow CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET.

Which is the whole lesson in one message. A bundle nothing can be read out of is reported and not refused: an empty measurement is a parse that failed, not a floor of zero.

docs.title: Intel: a second runner, not a universal binary
docs.text:
An earlier version of this page said Intel meant dropping Homebrew. That is true of building a universal binary on one machine, and it is the wrong way to get there. GitHub offers x64 macOS runners — macos-15-intel and macos-26-intel — and Homebrew on one of those installs x86_64 bottles like any other native machine.

So Intel support is a second job producing a second disk image, not a universal build: the same make-dmg.sh, an artifact named for its architecture, and a cask with on_arm and on_intel blocks carrying a url and digest each. depends_on arch: :arm64 comes out at that point. It is not done here because nobody has asked for it, and it costs a second macOS job's worth of CI on every release.

docs.title: Cross-building: what is and is not possible
docs.text:
From → to Possible? How macOS → Linux .deb yes Docker, above. Not really cross-building: a native Linux build inside a container, emulated for amd64 on Apple Silicon Apple Silicon → Intel macOS not locally Every dependency would need an x86_64 slice and Homebrew's have none. The answer is not to cross-build but to build natively on an macos-15-intel runner — see above Linux → macOS no The SDK cannot be redistributed, codesign and hdiutil are macOS-only, and macdeployqt runs nowhere else. osxcross exists and none of the packaging does anything → Windows no MSVC, and the pipeline is the only place this project has ever built for Windows Linux → other Linux yes The same container trick with a different base image

The short version: macOS builds happen on a Mac and Windows builds happen in CI. Everything else you can do from either.

docs.title: Translations are compiled every build, and extraction is not
docs.text:
The .ts catalogues are source: they carry human translations and a per-message "unfinished" flag a translator clears by hand, so a build that reran extraction would make every compile a working-tree modification and would race two build directories against one file.

cmake --build build --target update_translations

Location comments are switched off, because file-and-line comments move every message in the file whenever a line is inserted above it, and document where a string was rather than anything a translator needs.

Linguist is required, and refusing to configure without it is the icon's lesson applied. The app icon was once assembled behind a guard that skipped in silence, and what it produced was a bundle with no icon and a status line nobody reads. A missing lrelease is the same failure with a worse face — the build succeeds, every test passes, and the app speaks one language for reasons no message anywhere explains.

docs.title: The icon
docs.text:
One generator draws the mark and writes four readings of it: the .iconset of PNGs, the macOS .icns, the Windows .ico, and — from the same PNGs — the six sizes the Linux install rules file into the icon theme.

Both the .icns and the .ico are committed. The first version assembled the .icns at build time with a macOS-only tool wrapped in a guard that skipped in silence, so any build without it produced a bundle with no icon. Writing the container in the generator makes the icon a build input like any other file.

The window icon is a separate thing and is set from the resource: the .icns is what Finder and the Dock show for the application, while the window icon is what a running window carries in the switcher and on every platform with no bundle at all. Setting one and not the other is how an app ends up with an icon everywhere except where you were looking.

Three details differ per platform and each is a reason rather than a taste: the .ico is compiled into the executable, because that is where Explorer reads one from; it has a 48 where the .iconset does not, because Windows picks an entry out of one file while an icon theme scales the nearest size it holds; and its resource id is a bare 1, because the shell shows the lowest-numbered icon resource.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Two command-line flags, off by default, and both draw into the window as well as printing:

  • --trace-timing — every controller refresh, the whole of opening a repository, each navigation, each surface built. They nest, and the lines are indented by depth.
  • --trace-swipe — a line per wheel event with its phase, both deltas, the accumulated travel and whether anything moved.

The panel is not belt and braces. A line on stdout is invisible to an app launched from Finder, can be filtered by a logging rule, and is absent altogether when the build predates the change — and all three read as "the trace does not work", which is indistinguishable from "the thing being traced never happened", which is the question. The panel appears the moment the flag is honoured, so the first is settled before the second is asked.

A flag rather than a setting, because it is a diagnostic somebody runs once rather than a choice about how the app behaves. Off, every entry point returns on a bool and allocates nothing, which is what lets the calls sit in the hot paths — and the switch is writable, so a test can turn it on: the swipe trace shipped switched off on every platform the suite runs on and nothing noticed, because its switch was a platform check no test could reach.

A release build compiles them out entirely.

docs.title: These docs
docs.text: The site is built with MkDocs and Material for MkDocs. The whole project is rooted at docs/: the config is docs/mkdocs.yml, its docs_dir is docs relative to that (so the pages are docs/docs/), and the pinned requirements are inside it.

docs.title: Building it locally
docs.text:
pip install -r docs/docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve -f docs/mkdocs.yml

mkdocs serve watches the tree and reloads, which is what you want while writing. mkdocs build -f docs/mkdocs.yml writes docs/site/ — gitignored, since it is generated. site_dir resolves against the config's own directory, so the output lands beside it whichever directory you invoke the build from.

The dependencies are pinned, for the reason the CI runner images are: a floating version means the toolchain this site is built with changes without a commit saying so, and the first sign of it is a broken build on an unrelated pull request.

docs.title: The build is strict, and that is deliberate
docs.text:
strict: true

A broken internal link is a documentation bug, and the build should say so rather than shipping a 404 nobody notices. It fails on a link to a page that does not exist, a page absent from the navigation, and a reference to a file that is not there.

The cost is that renaming a page breaks the build until every link to it is fixed, which is the point.

docs.title: What goes here, and what does not
docs.text:
Here: what the app does, how it compares, what is coming, and how to build and test it. Written for somebody deciding whether to use it, or using it and wanting to know why something behaves the way it does.

Not here: the architecture reference. AGENTS.md is that, it is the authority, and duplicating it would produce a second copy to go stale — which is this project's own argument about two spellings of one fact, applied to itself. Where a page needs to explain a mechanism it links there instead.

So the architecture page is an orientation: the shape of the tree, the structural decisions that explain the rest, and pointers. If you find yourself transcribing a section of AGENTS.md into it, stop.

docs.title: Three conventions carried over from the app
docs.text:
All three are what makes the rest of the site trustworthy, and each is easy to lose by writing a sentence that reads better without it.

An unverified claim says so where it is made. Not once at the top and not in a footnote — Windows, GitLab, Bitbucket, X.509 signing, the keychain backends, the sparse verbs and every AI provider are implemented and unexercised to some degree, and every page that touches one repeats the caveat. A reader arrives at one page from a search engine and reads that page.

A feature that is absent for a reason states the reason. An absence read as an oversight costs a reader nothing to work around and costs the project its credibility on everything else — so a declined feature says what it would cost and what would unblock it, and a non-goal says what position it is. That is why Closed as decisions and Deliberate non-goals are pages rather than a bullet list.

A feature page says what it costs, on its first line. Every page under features/ opens with a **Licensing — …** line naming Free, Paid, or Free with paid parts, and naming the feature ids its controls carry — the same ids Licensing::catalogue() gates on, so a reader can match a control that is absent to the row that explains it. A new feature page without that line is the drift this convention exists to stop: a page that describes a paid control as though everybody has it is worse than no page, because the reader concludes the app is broken rather than that they have not paid.

The tiers themselves are not restated per page beyond that line. The table in Licensing is written from the app's own catalogue, and a second copy of it in twenty-six places would be twenty-six things to forget when one word moves.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: .github/workflows/docs.yml builds on every push to main that touches docs/ or the workflow itself, and pushes the built site into a second repository, source-manager/docs, which serves it from its main branch at https://source-manager.github.io/docs/.

docs.title: Why two repositories
docs.text:
GitHub Pages cannot be enabled on a private repository below GitHub Pro — it is a paid feature there, and free on a public one. This repository is private, so actions/deploy-pages answered 404 and no setting would have made it stop. The docs repository is public and holds only the build product: nothing is authored there, and anything committed there by hand is overwritten by the next run.

Two things follow from the split, and neither is optional:

  • site_url is the published address, https://source-manager.github.io/docs/. It feeds the canonical links, the sitemap and the social-card metadata, so a wrong one is wrong in three places at once.
  • repo_url and edit_uri stay pointed here, because the "edit this page" link has to reach a file somebody can actually change.

docs.title: The rest of the decisions in it
docs.text:
It builds on a pull request and publishes only from main. A pull request that breaks the strict build should fail there, where it can be fixed before merging — and a job that only ran after merging would report the breakage on somebody else's commit.

Building and publishing are two jobs. The build runs pip and mkdocs; the publish job holds a credential that can write to another repository. Keeping them apart means the credential is never in scope for the step that runs third-party code, and the site travels between them as one tar through the artifact store.

The publish is a real commit, and it deletes. The target's tree is replaced wholesale rather than added to, so a page renamed here stops serving at its old address there. A run whose build output is byte-identical to what is already published commits nothing.

Concurrency is grouped and not cancelled in progress. Cancelling a publish half way is not the same kind of harmless as cancelling a superseded test run.

It is a separate workflow rather than a job on CI. They answer different questions and hold different credentials: CI writes nothing, where this one can write to the docs repository. Adding that to a workflow that builds and runs code would widen what a compromised build step could reach.

docs.title: Setting it up, once
docs.text:
Three things, and the workflow's failure names the first of them.

1. Mint a key pair. It is never used to identify a person, so it is generated with no passphrase and no comment worth keeping:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C 'source-manager docs publish' -f /tmp/docs_deploy_key

2. Install the public half on the docs repository. source-manager/docs → Settings → Deploy keys → Add deploy key. Title it something like source-manager docs publish, paste /tmp/docs_deploy_key.pub, and tick "Allow write access" — without it the push is refused and nothing else is wrong.

3. Install the private half here. source-manager/app → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret, named exactly DOCS_DEPLOY_KEY, holding the whole of /tmp/docs_deploy_key — the -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY----- line, the body, the -----END----- line and the trailing newline. Then delete both files from disk.

Or with the gh CLI, which does all three without the private half touching a browser:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C 'source-manager docs publish' -f /tmp/docs_deploy_key
gh repo deploy-key add /tmp/docs_deploy_key.pub \
  --repo source-manager/docs --title 'source-manager docs publish' --allow-write
gh secret set DOCS_DEPLOY_KEY --repo source-manager/app < /tmp/docs_deploy_key
rm -f /tmp/docs_deploy_key /tmp/docs_deploy_key.pub

Why a deploy key rather than a personal access token. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot reach another repository at all, so something has to be stored, and a deploy key is the narrowest thing GitHub offers: it is registered on one repository, it cannot be widened by editing a scope list, and it does not expire. A fine-grained token with Contents: read and write on that repository would work and is worse on all three counts — it is minted against an account, it can be re-scoped afterwards, and it expires on a date nobody will remember.

There is a second consequence of not using GITHUB_TOKEN, and it is load-bearing: a push made with that token does not start a workflow, and the Pages build on the far side is a workflow. A deploy key's push starts it.

docs.title: Enabling Pages on the docs repository, once
docs.text:
source-manager/docs → Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source → Deploy from a branch, branch main, folder / (root).

That is the other way round from what this repository used to do, and deliberately: the docs repository holds a finished site rather than a build, so there is nothing there for Actions to run. Until the first successful push there is no branch to select, so do this after the workflow has run once.

A custom domain configured there writes a CNAME file into the branch. The publish step reads that file before it replaces the tree and puts it back afterwards, so the domain survives — but it is a decision made over there, and nothing in this repository declares it.

docs.title: Two versions, and they answer different questions
docs.text:
What it is What it answers The release 1.0.0, declared once in project(VERSION) What an installer upgrades from, what a licence is bought against, what to quote in a support request The build The full commit sha, stamped in per build Which code is running — what a bug report needs

Neither is derived from the other, and each is wrong for the other's question. The sha cannot say which release somebody has: there is one per commit and most commits are not releases. The release number cannot identify the code: it is the same string for every build between two releases.

Both are in About, and Copy details carries both.

docs.title: Why the release version is declared rather than described
docs.text:
git describe is the obvious alternative and fails exactly where it matters: a release tarball, an export and a shallow CI clone carry no tags — and "unknown" is not a version a bundle or an MSI will install.

So the number is committed and reviewed like any other source change. Its failure mode is drift from the tag, and that is what makes declaring it safe: a test asserts the two agree whenever HEAD carries a release tag, and skips otherwise, because between releases the declared version legitimately runs ahead of the last tag.

It compares against the tag on HEAD and never a described one: that walks back to the nearest ancestor tag and would compare this build against a release two months old, which is the comparison that must not fail.

One to three dot-separated integers, no suffix

1.0.0-beta is valid semver and is rejected by Apple, Windows and MSI alike, so the test refuses it here rather than letting it surface at packaging time on a platform you may not be sitting at. A field above 65535 is silently truncated by the Windows resource compiler, so that is asserted too.

docs.title: To cut a release
docs.text:
1. Bump project(VERSION).
  2. Commit.
  3. Tag that commit vX.Y.Z.

In that order — the test compares the tag on HEAD against the declared number, so tagging first tags the bump that has not happened yet.

docs.title: And the build version is read per build, not per configure
docs.text:
Three git calls made inline in a CMakeLists would answer once, when the build directory was configured, and go on answering that after every commit — a stamp that is silently a week old is exactly the failure a stamp exists to prevent, and it is invisible. So it runs from a custom target the library depends on.

It costs nothing per build: the header is written through a compare, so an unchanged answer keeps its timestamp and nothing recompiles.

Two facts travel with the sha because it misleads without them. The commit's date, since a hash cannot say how old it is and "does this build have the fix" is what a version is normally consulted for. And whether the tree was modified, because a build from an edited checkout is not that commit — the ordinary state of a working build directory, and the one a bug report must not silently claim otherwise about. Modified is a word beside the number rather than a -dirty suffix on it, because a suffix says the same thing quieter and makes the sha unpasteable into git show or a url.

A source tree that is not a checkout is a state, not a blank: the row reads "not built from a checkout", and nothing is invented in its place.

The Qt and libgit2 versions in About are the ones loaded, not the ones compiled against. They disagree exactly when it matters — two Qt installations, a distribution upgrade under an installed binary, an rpath pointing somewhere unexpected — and an About box is read when something is behaving oddly.

The packaging versions are a different claim

CFBundleVersion and its short-string sibling are still the release version, and the desktop entry's Version=1.0 is the Desktop Entry Specification's own version, which is what that key means in freedesktop's schema. A sweep that "fixed" it would declare this app conformant to a spec revision that does not exist.

docs.title: The release pipeline
docs.text: .github/workflows/release.yml runs on a v* tag. CI asks whether the tree works; this asks whether this thing is shippable, and the difference in failure cost is the whole reason it is a second file: a red CI run is a commit somebody fixes, and a bad release is on other people's machines.

docs.title: It fails before it builds
docs.text: A first job reads the declared version out of the root configuration and refuses a tag that disagrees, in fifteen seconds rather than after three platform builds. The test suite asserts the same thing, and both are worth having: the suite's copy is the one that cannot be forgotten, and this one is the one that answers before the money is spent.

docs.title: Release configuration, and the suite runs against it
docs.text:
CI builds Debug on every push and has never once run the tests against an optimised build — a different program, with different timing, different inlining and different undefined behaviour, and the one people actually get. The release jobs run the suite after building Release.

It also means the diagnostics are compiled out, so a shipped build carries no trace flag and cannot draw a panel of its own timings over somebody's window.

docs.title: Signing is skipped loudly or not at all
docs.text:
A certificate belongs to whoever ships the app and nothing in this repository can hold one, so every signing step is conditional — and the condition is announced three times over: a warning in the log, a section in the job summary, and a sentence in the release notes beside the artifact it applies to.

This project has been bitten twice by a guard that skipped in silence, and an unsigned release is that failure with the worst blast radius available: the reader finds out when Gatekeeper refuses to open it.

Supply any of these as repository secrets to change that:

Secret For MACOS_CERTIFICATE, MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD, MACOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY Developer ID signing MACOS_NOTARY_APPLE_ID, MACOS_NOTARY_PASSWORD, MACOS_NOTARY_TEAM_ID Notarisation and stapling WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE, WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD Authenticode signing

Set SOURCEMANAGER_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID as a repository variable — not a secret, it is public by design — to ship a build that can sign in to GitHub through your own OAuth app.

The obvious spelling of 'skip when there is no certificate' fails silently

A step's own env: block is not in scope for that step's own if: — the condition is evaluated before the environment is applied — so if: env.X != '' naming a secret the step declares is always false and the step silently never runs. Which is to say the obvious spelling fails in exactly the way this file exists to prevent.

The presence check is computed once at job level and the steps read that.

docs.title: The status files exist because the publish job must not guess
docs.text:
Each build job writes whether it signed and whether it notarised beside its artifact, and the notes are composed from those rather than from whether a secret is configured.

Those are different questions and they diverge the moment signing fails for any reason other than an absent certificate — at which point inferring from the secret prints a sentence that is confidently wrong on a page whose entire purpose is telling a reader what they are about to download. A missing status file is an error there and never a default.

docs.title: The notes are a script, not a block of YAML
docs.text:
tools/release-notes.sh is the branchiest thing in the pipeline — signed and notarised, signed and not, neither, twice over for two platforms — and inline it would be logic whose first execution is a real release.

Its test drives it across every combination and asserts the claims rather than the prose, since the wording is meant to be edited and a test pinning it would be deleted rather than read.

docs.title: The release is a draft
docs.text:
Everything up to it is automation and the last step is a judgement: read the notes, check there are four artifacts, publish. A workflow that published outright would turn an accidental tag into a public release.

workflow_dispatch runs the whole thing and publishes nothing, because a release pipeline whose first execution is a real release is one nobody has ever tested — and the publish job is gated on the tag rather than merely on the event, so a dry run cannot reach it by another door. Worth doing once before the first real tag.

docs.title: Three repositories, and what each holds
docs.text:
source-manager/app is the source and is private. source-manager/dist is public and holds nothing but releases. source-manager/homebrew-tap is public and holds the cask.

The split exists for one reason: a private repository's release assets answer 404 without a token, so nothing — not a browser, not brew — can fetch them. Publishing to dist makes the binaries downloadable without publishing a line of source.

Crossing that boundary needs a token the workflow is not given. GITHUB_TOKEN is scoped to the repository it runs in and no permissions: block widens it, so RELEASE_TOKEN — a fine-grained PAT with contents: write on dist, homebrew-tap and apt — is the one required secret in the pipeline. It is checked by name in its own step, because every other secret here is optional and skipped loudly, and this one being absent means there is no release at all.

docs.title: The cask is bumped by a second workflow
docs.text:
Homebrew cask (cask.yml) is a button pressed after the draft is published, and that ordering is the point rather than an inconvenience: a draft release's assets are not downloadable. A cask bumped in the same run as the draft is wrong for as long as the draft sits there, and the failure lands on whoever installs in that window as a 404 or a checksum error — neither of which says "the maintainer has not pressed publish yet".

So the workflow proves the difference rather than assuming it. It fetches the .dmg the way a reader's brew will — anonymously, over the public URL — and stops if that does not answer. It digests what it downloaded rather than copying a line out of the SHA256SUMS.txt a different machine produced three jobs earlier, since the digest a cask carries has to describe the bytes a reader actually receives. The edit itself is tools/bump-cask.sh, which is tested (test_bumpcask) for the reason every other release script is: this is the only thing that runs it, and a cask whose version moved and whose digest did not tells a reader their download is corrupt.

docs.title: The artifacts
docs.text:
macOS    SourceManager-<version>-macOS.dmg           self-contained
Windows  SourceManager-<version>-Windows-x64.zip     self-contained
Linux    source-manager_<version>-1_amd64.deb        needs Qt and libgit2
Linux    SourceManager-<version>-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz needs Qt and libgit2

Two of them are built by scripts this pipeline does not own. tools/make-dmg.sh and tools/make-deb.sh are what the dmg and deb CMake targets run on somebody's own machine, and what ci.yml runs on every push — the .deb built, installed with apt and started, the disk image built unsigned and mounted. So by the time a tag reaches the release job, everything except the certificate has already been exercised. What is left here is the half that can live nowhere else: the signing identity, and the notarisation.

Three things about the macOS job are load-bearing and were wrong first:

  • The install destination is a cache variable set at configure time, which is why the packaging script copies the bundle out of the build tree instead: installing would replace whatever is in the reader's ~/Applications when the same script is run on a person's own Mac.
  • macdeployqt rewrites load commands and therefore invalidates the ad-hoc signature, so the script re-signs before the bundle verifier runs — which checks the signature as its last step and would otherwise fail every run for a reason that is neither a fault nor the one it is looking for.
  • The disk image is what is notarised and stapled, rather than the app, so the ticket travels with the thing the reader downloads and Gatekeeper can check it offline on first launch.

Neither Linux artifact is self-contained, and both say so wherever they appear. The .deb links the distribution's Qt and libgit2 and declares them, so apt resolves what it needs and refuses the package on a distribution that cannot satisfy it — a refusal from the package manager rather than an app that starts and fails. The tarball is the same tree without that metadata, for distributions that are not dpkg ones. An AppImage is what would make either self-contained and is deliberately not attempted: building one means third-party binaries downloaded at release time, and the first execution of that path would be a real release.

The dependency list of the .deb is discovered for the half that can be discovered — dpkg-shlibdeps reads the binary's own load commands — and declared by hand for the half that cannot: a QML module is a plugin found by name at run time and appears in nothing. That declaration is packaging/deb/qml-modules, and test_debpackage fails on an import under qml/ that is missing from it, because the package it would otherwise produce installs cleanly, starts, and draws a blank panel.

That job also builds on the older LTS where CI pins the newer image, and the reasons are opposite: there the newest Qt is wanted so the pipeline and the desk agree and the whole suite can run, here the oldest supported LTS is wanted so the binary starts on the widest range of machines. The cost is that its Qt predates waitForPolish, so the QML suites are excluded there by name — a shorter test list nobody notices is how a release comes to be built from an untested tree, and those suites have already run on the newer image on the commit being tagged.

docs.title: Releasing from your own Mac, without CI
docs.text:
Nothing about the pipeline is load-bearing for publishing — gh release create against source-manager/dist is the whole of it, and every piece the workflow uses is a script in tools/ you can run yourself. The sequence is:

cmake --build build --target dmg          # the disk image, on your Mac
cmake --build build --target deb          # the .deb, in a container, also on your Mac
./tools/changelog.sh v1.2.3 > changelog.md
./tools/checksums.sh <the artifacts> > SHA256SUMS.txt
./tools/release-notes.sh 1.2.3 macos-status.txt windows-status.txt changelog.md SHA256SUMS.txt > notes.md
gh release create v1.2.3 --repo source-manager/dist --target main --draft \
  --title "Source Manager 1.2.3" --notes-file notes.md <the artifacts> SHA256SUMS.txt
./tools/bump-cask.sh …/homebrew-tap/Casks/source-manager.rb 1.2.3 <the dmg's digest>

What you give up by not using CI, in the order it will bite:

  • Windows. There is no way to produce that artifact on a Mac, and tools/release-notes.sh requires a Windows status file and prints the zip in its table regardless. A hand-made release is therefore macOS and Linux only, and the notes will name a download that is not attached unless you edit them. That is the one real obstacle: everything else on this list is a check you are choosing to skip, and this one publishes something untrue.
  • The tag check. release.yml refuses a tag that disagrees with project(VERSION) before it builds anything. By hand, the version in the filename, in the notes and in the cask are three strings you are typing.
  • The test run. The pipeline builds and tests in Release configuration, which no local workflow does; ci.yml is Debug.
  • The Linux build's distribution. The container gives you that back, provided you use the same base image the pipeline pins.

So it is a fair thing to do for a build you are handing to a few people, and a poor way to cut a real release. The middle road is what the split already allows: let CI build and publish the draft, and use the local targets for the copies you hand over directly.

The token is the same either way. gh needs to be authenticated against an account with write access to source-manager/dist, which for a hand-made release is just your own login; RELEASE_TOKEN exists because a workflow has no login of its own.

docs.title: What it does not do yet
docs.text:
No AppImage, no Flatpak and no .rpm, so neither Linux artifact is self-contained and only Debian-family distributions get a package; and no Windows installer, only a zip of the deployed tree. Each is its own piece of work — see the job comments for why none was bolted on untested.

There is also no .pkg on macOS. It would need a Developer ID Installer certificate, which is a different certificate from the Application one the pipeline handles, and what it buys over a drag-to-install disk image is the ability to run scripts at install time — which this app does not need.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure

On a machine with no display — a container, a remote shell, CI — go through Qt's offscreen platform plugin, which needs no X or Wayland server and no xvfb:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen ctest --output-on-failure

Without it, two of the suites abort on the platform plugin and read as code failures rather than as an environment problem.

docs.title: The shape of the suite
docs.text:
Each test class is its own executable, registered under the same name. A new C++ test needs one line in the test list and derives from RepositoryMock when it needs a real repository on disk; a new tst_*.qml needs no build change at all, because the runner discovers them.

Two entry-point rules: use the project's own test main rather than Qt's, because it holds the libgit2 initialisation; and the backend is built as one static library shared by the app and the test executables, which is what lets the whole suite run without a GUI application object — the controllers are Qt Core only, and a file needing QtGui belongs with the app rather than the library.

tests/README.md in the repository has the fixture's helpers and what each suite covers.

docs.title: What a package is not done without
docs.text:
1. A clean build, no new warnings.
  2. The whole suite green, not just your test.
  3. A new controller → a test class deriving from the fixture.
  4. A new .qml → a line in the resource manifest.
  5. Every write operation has a refusal test: the case where it must decline rather than clobber, asserting nothing on disk changed.
  6. AGENTS.md updated — a short section explaining why, not what.

docs.title: No test may open a socket
docs.text:
Two consequences, both solved in-tree:

  • Transport tests use file:// remotes. The fixture makes a second repository on disk, and push/fetch/pull against a local bare repository exercises every code path except TLS and the credential callback — which is the right trade for a suite that must never depend on the network or on who happens to be signed in on the machine running it.
  • Forge and AI tests use a replaying transport with hand-written fixtures from the documented schemas. No fixture may carry a credential, asserted by reading the file's own bytes back.

docs.title: Things that make a test pass for the wrong reason
docs.text:
This is the part worth reading before writing one here, because every entry cost somebody a day.

A test that waits for a race to fall its way is a flake, and one shipped. A walk at a budget of zero — one commit per turn — then a wait for the first result, then a cancel. But the wait spends its first poll processing events for a millisecond, which is long enough for all twenty turns on a quick machine and not on a slow one: it observed a finished search as often as a running one, and failed on its own guard in a container having passed on the host. Where a test needs to catch a batched walk while it runs, hook the signal the walk emits rather than timing it.

A probe with an invisible window measures nothing, and says so with a zero. Two rounds of a pointer-delivery diagnosis were spent on a probe whose window was never shown: nothing is hit-tested there, every count came back 0, and 0 was read as "an item under the pointer consumed it". Any probe of pointer delivery needs a control case that must succeed, or a zero cannot be told from a broken harness.

Run a new guard against the fault before believing it. A fixture test spelling its needles as literals asserted that a file did not contain strings the file therefore contained, and passed. A check for a glyph written as UTF-8 bytes inside a UTF-16 literal matched nothing and passed against the reintroduced fault.

A test that calls the function passes on every day the button is missing. Five features have shipped reachable from nothing — a verb, two dialogs and five invokables — and each read as done. Assert through the route: a test that called the clone verb would have passed on every day its dialog could not be opened. That class is now closed by a test that reads the source for declarations and the whole tree for calls, with no allow-list, because an allow-list is a list of verbs somebody decided not to think about.

A fixture that cannot show the difference asserts nothing. A drag-and-drop feature shipped because every drop target is another row and the fixture had one commit, so the only thing a test could assert was that a drag starts — which it did, throughout. And a latch test needed a history three places deep, because with one entry the second navigation fails for having nowhere to go and the assertion passes with the latch deleted.

Assert the property that would fail, not the one that happens to. A cap test measured on the text went on passing against a one-line fixture and stopped meaning anything the moment a message was long enough to matter. A panel-height test passed on the bug because the panel is capped and a dozen unwrapped entries still add up past the cap — the width was the assertion.

docs.title: The QML suites share one process
docs.text:
Every tst_*.qml runs in one process, against one engine, one manager and one command registry. A suite is never alone with its own state, and that is not an implementation detail: it is why the suite was, for a while, a coin flip — failing about one run in three, only under load, always in the same file, and always in a rotating subset of the assertions that count hint labels.

Two of the four causes were shared files (a settings path and a fixture directory, both fixed per machine, so two runners read and wrote each other's) and two were deferred work read as though it had happened (a destroy that is deferred, so a shell survived into the next file with its commands still registered; and layout, so an item existed before it had a size).

The rules for a new QML test:

  • Build with the temporary-object form, never the plain one. The runner destroys what it hands you after cleanup whether the test passed or not — and the leak that mattered was the one a failing assertion caused.
  • Wait for the teardown rather than assuming it. Skipping those turns does not merely miscount: a second shell built over the remains of the first crashes inside the delegate model's incubator.
  • Poll anything the layout decides — a width, a visibility, or a count that depends on either.
  • A count taken from the command registry describes the process, not your component. Scope it where you can.
  • Anything that reads or walks navigation must reset it in init(), since a place and its history live on the manager and outlive a shell.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml configures, builds and runs the whole suite on every push and pull request, on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Linux is the baseline and must be green: every dependency arrives from apt in one command and the suite runs headless. macOS is the platform the app is developed on, and it gets a job of its own for the one reason CI exists — the two differ in the compiler, in the Qt build and in every one of the install rules, and only a build says which has drifted.

Windows is the one job whose result is the only evidence there is. A green run says the tree configures, compiles, links and passes the suite headless under MSVC, and nothing else. Do not read it as "Windows works."

Three decisions in it are worth keeping:

The runner image is pinned, not latest. The image decides which Qt the distribution packages supply, so latest means the Qt this project is tested against changes without a commit saying so.

The pin moved, and what it was pinning turned out not to be testable. The older image carries Qt 6.4, waitForPolish arrived in 6.5, and eleven QML suites call it ninety-two times — so on the pinned image a third of the suite died with "waitForPolish is not defined" and the pipeline was measuring the other two thirds. Writing ninety-two workarounds around a standard piece of the test framework to preserve a version nobody develops against is the wrong way round. The cost is stated in the workflow: that image is labelled preview, and the way back is the older LTS plus a Qt from aqtinstall, never the older LTS alone.

A build failure hides every test result behind it. The compile error that pin caught was the only thing the pipeline could report, and the two genuine test failures underneath it were found only after it was fixed.

docs.title: It runs at the runner's width
docs.text:
This ran serially for a long time on the argument that the QML suite was one test and most of the wall clock, so parallelism bought only seconds. The premise was right — 78 s of a 113 s suite in one entry — and the conclusion drawn from it was the wrong way round: an indivisible entry that dominates the wall clock is a reason to divide it, not a reason to stop measuring.

Each tst_*.qml is one entry now, and the test phase went from 113 s to 22 s at four cores.

Two findings came out of the measurement:

  • The monolithic run was superlinear. The same 34 suites cost 78 s together and 62 s one at a time, because they share one engine and one registry and what accumulates across them costs more than the process startup that replaces it — so sharding cut total CPU before any parallelism was applied.
  • The wall clock is now one suite. At 4, 8 and 12 way it sits at ~22 s either way, because the slowest suite alone takes 21 s. More parallelism buys nothing from here.

The load objection was the real half of the old argument and is answered rather than dropped: what made a suite fail one run in three was shared state, and both causes are per-process now. What is left is CPU contention, which makes a wait slower rather than wrong.

docs.title: And a warning about measuring anything here
docs.text:
Over three consecutive runs on a shared machine, two suites rose monotonically with the load — a 69% run-to-run spread within one suite, larger than any plausible optimisation to it.

Nothing under about a halving can be shown to have worked on a machine that is not idle, and a change landed on an unmeasurable claim is churn plus a rebase conflict for whoever owns the file. One optimisation was tried, measured, found to be inside the spread, and reverted for exactly that reason.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Twenty-six pages, grouped by what you are trying to do. Every one of them says why a thing behaves the way it does where the behaviour is surprising, because most of the surprising behaviour here is a decision rather than an accident.

docs.title: Working in one repository
docs.text:
• :material-source-repository-multiple: The fleet

    Every registered repository on one page — branch, drift, dirt, stopped operations. Groups, folder scanning, and three ways to remove one.

  • :material-file-edit-outline: Changes and staging

    Stage and discard at file, hunk or line level. Ignore rules. What a verb over a set of eight hundred files costs.

  • :material-message-text-outline: Writing a commit message

    Templates, co-authors, recall, and a subject inferred from the staged paths and the log — each inference stating its basis.

  • :material-file-compare: Reading a diff

    Unified or split, syntax highlighted, word-level marks, image and binary modes, and a ten-thousand-line hunk that does not stall.

  • :material-graph-outline: History, graph and search

    Lanes that mean something, six search scopes, filters that compose, blame, file history, and a change heatmap.

docs.title: Changing what is there
docs.text:
• :material-source-branch: Branches

    Create, rename, delete, check out. Upstreams, drift both ways, tidy-up signals, and stacked branches git records nothing about.

  • :material-call-split: Splitting a branch

    Cut one branch into a stack of smaller ones — a commit, a file, a hunk or a few lines at a time — without rewriting it.

  • :material-content-cut: Taking pieces out of a proposal

    "Take the API change out into its own." Three modes, exact complements, and a retarget where the forge allows one.

  • :material-history: Rewriting history

    A rebase you plan before anything is written, amend, reword or edit any commit, cherry-pick, revert and reset.

  • :material-call-merge: Merging and conflicts

    Merge with the analysis reported, three-way resolution per hunk, and your own merge tool beside it.

  • :material-tag-outline: Tags and notes

    A name and some text about a commit, neither of which rewrites it — and what a note costs you if you expect it to travel.

    Where the bytes are, what is reclaimable, and nine verbs — two of which lose something and say what.

docs.title: Free or paid, page by page
docs.text:
Every page below says at the top which it is, and names the feature id its controls carry. The whole table, and the six promises a lapsed licence keeps, are on Licensing.

Page Changes and staging, Reading a diff, Rewriting history, Merging and conflicts, Tags and notes, Remotes and transport, Git LFS, Signing, Patches, What the git directory is made of, Settings Free The fleet, Writing a commit message, History, graph and search, Branches, Stash, worktrees, submodules, subtrees, Automation and external tools, Undo, backups and the log Free, with paid parts Splitting a branch, Taking pieces out of a proposal, Bisect, Pull requests and CI, Reviewing a proposal, The tracker, Asking a model, Repository metrics Paid

Two things hold whatever the licence says, and they are tests rather than intentions: every way out of a stopped operation is free — continue or abort a rebase, a merge or a cherry-pick, end a bisect, resolve a conflict, stash — and downgrading is read-only: forty registered repositories still list and still open, and only the forty-first is refused.

docs.title: The two rules that explain most of it
docs.text:
Operations are entered from the object they act on. Never from a separate menu of verbs. Rebase from a commit, ignore from a file, bisect from the commit where the thing still worked, a proposal from a branch row.

Refuse rather than clobber. A write checks its preconditions, names the paths, declines, and writes nothing — because a half-applied operation is worse than a refused one. And the sentence the refusal prints is the same string the confirmation showed, so what a dialog promises cannot drift from what the button does.

A corollary worth knowing before you go looking for a missing button: a control that cannot apply is absent, not greyed.

docs.title: Asking a model
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. This page is ai. You still supply the key or the local model. What a licence adds

Bring-your-own-key and local models only. No vendor credits, no account, nothing this project resells. Two consequences run through everything below: the app has to be useful with no key at all, so local models are the default path and were written first; and a key that does exist is kept the way the git credential ladder keeps one.

This reverses a documented position, and the argument is worth reading

The project once recorded that no commit subject would be generated from a diff, because "describing what a change does is the one part of a message not derivable from what changed, and a plausible sentence there would be the most confident lie the app could tell".

Every clause of that is still true. What it did not credit is the safeguard: the reader reviews the sentence before it is committed. A generated subject lands in the box a press away from being changed, marked as generated and naming the model that wrote it, beside a Commit button nobody presses by accident. A lie somebody reads and declines is a draft.

So the line moved rather than went. What stays refused is anything written without a reader in front of it — nothing is generated on a refresh, on a timer, or as a side effect of reading, and no generated string is committed, pushed or applied by the same press that produced it.

docs.title: Four providers
docs.text:
