Local? Needs a key? Ollama on this machine no LM Studio on this machine no OpenAI hosted yes Anthropic hosted yes

The local pair are the default and were written first, so the offline path is the one that gets exercised rather than the fallback nobody runs.

Ollama goes through its own API rather than its compatibility one, which costs a class and buys three things the shim flattens: which model actually answered, which models have been pulled rather than which could be, and a 404 that means a missing model rather than a missing path — the commonest first failure anybody meets here.

Anthropic is the one that proves the seam. Three things there are not the OpenAI shape at all: system is a top-level field rather than a message with a role (sent as a message it is silently demoted to a user turn, which is the failure that looks like the model ignoring its instructions); max_tokens is required; and the reply's content is a list of blocks, of which only the text ones are joined.

Adding a provider is a class and one registration line — and where that claim is narrower than the forge seam's is stated: a provider cannot widen what may leave the machine, because the gate reads the URL rather than anything a provider declares.

docs.title: The privacy gate
docs.text:
A hosted model means somebody's private diff leaves the machine, so configuring a key is not consent to send this repository.

Two answers, and the repository's wins:

  • A global default, and it is the one setting in this app that starts off. Everywhere else the argument is that a thing somebody has to switch on is a thing for people who already know it is there; here what is being defaulted is whether your private diff leaves your machine, and there is no reading of "sensible default" that answers yes to that on your behalf.
  • A per-repository answer in that repository's own .git/config, which is not cloned, so a consent cannot arrive with somebody else's branch. Three values and never two — absent, yes and no — because a repository that has said no must not be overruled by the global saying yes.

A request to a non-local host is refused before it is made, and that is enforced in the transport rather than in the controller that decides — a decision taken in a controller is one a caller can be written around, and the claim being made is that no request is made, which only the thing that opens sockets can promise. A test drives every verb with the gate shut and requires the request log to come back empty.

What counts as this machine is loopback and nothing else. A LAN address is another machine: "it only went to the box under my desk" is not a promise that check is in a position to make. And a URL carrying userinfo is never local whatever its host, because http://127.0.0.1@evil/ is the one shape that gets this question answered wrongly.

The endpoint decides, never the provider's "I am local" flag: somebody who has repointed Ollama at a machine on their network is sending a diff off this one.

It is deliberately not a list of allowed hosts: the endpoints are typed by you — a private Ollama on another machine on the LAN is an ordinary thing to point this at — so a literal allow-list would be either wrong for that reader or so wide as to say nothing.

docs.title: What may be sent, and how much
docs.text:
Every prompt carries a piece of a repository and none of it can be handed over whole: a diff has no upper bound, and what leaves the machine should be the smallest thing that answers the question.

So everything is bounded and says so in the material itself, not merely beside it — the model is that string's reader, and one handed half a diff with nothing saying so will describe the half it got as though it were the change. You are told too: the answer carries whether the material was cut short, because a message written from part of a change reads exactly like one written from all of it.

The ceiling is deliberately not configurable: raising it is choosing to send more of a repository somewhere.

docs.title: Nothing is asked for automatically
docs.text:
Not on a refresh, not on a timer, not as a side effect of reading, and not because a surface was built. The model list is bought by opening the setup dialog rather than by arriving anywhere.

That is a property of the callers rather than of any type, so it is asserted rather than described: a test drives every refresh path there is and requires the request log empty.

docs.title: Three switches, and one deliberate exception
docs.text:
• The feature switch. Off, every AI control is absent — off the screen, and therefore out of the palette and off the hint keys too. The app is exactly what it was before any of this existed.
  • Configured. With no provider chosen the controls stay drawn, and pressing one opens the setup dialog. That is the exception, and it follows the external-tools line: absent-not-greyed is for what this repository cannot do, not for what the app has not been told yet. A control missing for a reason you could settle in ten seconds is a feature you never discover; one that explains itself when pressed is not. It stays enabled for the same reason — a disabled control cannot explain why it is disabled.
  • The remote gate, above.

docs.title: Twelve verbs
docs.text:
Each offered beside the thing it drafts, and none of them replacing a field:

Verb Where A commit message, and the @ai placeholder The commit box A reworded commit message A commit's menu Grouping the working tree into several commits Changes An explanation of one commit A commit's menu A changelog since a commit A commit's menu A summary of what happened over a period History A proposal's title and description The propose dialog A branch name The new-branch dialog A stash description The stash box A commit message for a split part Splitting a branch A free-form question, with saved prompts Changes and History A conflict resolution, per hunk Conflicts

@ai is the best shape in the field, and is why the commit verb takes a hint: you write the half that carries intent, mark where the machine should fill in, and the two are blended rather than one replacing the other. Without the placeholder the hint is empty — passing the box's contents there would quietly turn every generation into a rewrite of whatever was in it.

The changelog is the one verb the old refusal never covered. It summarises what people wrote rather than inventing intent, and its prompt says so: use only what the messages say, infer nothing they do not.

The activity summary is its sibling and is a different question. A changelog is asked of two commits and is written for somebody else, so it leaves out what a reader of release notes would not want. "What happened this week" is asked of a clock and is written for the person who was there, so nothing is left out for being unremarkable. Three consequences: it reads HEAD's own history rather than the list on screen and says so (answering a period from a list narrowed to one author would answer a different question quietly); a commit outside the window is skipped and never a reason to stop, since the ordering is topological as well as by time; and merges are left out, both sides being reached on their own.

The composer proposes and performs nothing. What it proposes is several commits, so you have to be able to disagree with the grouping before any of them exists. Each group is committed on its own press, and anything not committed stays exactly where it was.

Prompt presets encode a repository's message convention — Conventional Commits, Gitmoji, or plain prose — with this repository's own vocabulary woven in from what has already been read out of the log and any commitlint config. A log with no scopes is told to use none, because inventing one is the app deciding how somebody else's log reads.

docs.title: Every generated string says so, and names what wrote it
docs.text:
This is the house rule that an inferred thing names its evidence, and it matters more here than anywhere else in the app: what makes generation defensible is that a reader reviews it, and a reader cannot review what they do not know is a draft.

The model travels with the answer rather than being read off the controller when it is drawn — a label taken from the settings page goes wrong the moment somebody changes the drop-down while an answer is on screen. And it names the model that answered, which is not always the one asked for: LM Studio serves whatever is loaded and reports it back.

docs.title: Nothing in the AI layer writes to a repository
docs.text:
Not one verb. Text is generated into a slot and a surface hands it to the controller that owns the write, which is why the AI reword inherits the rebase's refusals, its published-commit warning and its sentence about how many commits get new hashes. A second write path here would be a second answer to what rewording means, and it would be the one with no refusals in it.

That is also what makes the record honest: the operation log records only what writes, and those rows are the ones the controllers that performed the write already record, in their own words. Generating text that lands in a box for review is not a repository operation.

No git command is printed for any of these. Git has no verb for asking a model, and an invented one is a command somebody pastes.

docs.title: Four states, and a slot
docs.text:
Idle, asking, ready, failed — and every refusal lands in the panel rather than only in the toast, which the first version got wrong: "no repository is open" went to the toast alone, leaving the panel drawing nothing at all, indistinguishable from a control nobody had pressed.

Requests carry an epoch, bumped by a cancel and by the repository changing. The forge layer needs one so a stale list does not land on the wrong repository; here it is worse, because a description of one project's diff landing in another project's commit box is a box somebody presses Commit on.

Cancelling keeps what has already been answered and settles what was in flight as idle rather than failed — you stopped it, and reporting your own press back to you as an error is not news.

docs.title: What is not built
docs.text:
• No streaming. A single complete answer, with an asking state while it is in flight. Streaming would cost a second shape on the transport, on the replay and on every surface that draws a partial answer, and what it buys is watching a sentence appear rather than waiting a moment — worth less here than in a chat client, because none of these answers is long and every one of them is reviewed before it is used.
  • No agentic anything. Nothing runs a command, edits a file, or takes more than one turn. The one verb whose output is code is offered as a side to be chosen. See Deliberate non-goals.
  • No auto-resolving "mechanical" conflicts. The failure mode is silent by construction — see Merging and conflicts.

Fixture-proved and never live-proved

There is no model to reach from the test suite — the sandbox denies egress and CI never should — so what is pinned is the shape: the URL built, the body sent, the JSON mapped onto the answer, the errors told apart, and what the gate refuses.

It cannot say that a real Ollama answers what its documentation says it does, and it cannot say that any of these models writes a good commit message.

Every recording is written by hand from a documented schema, so no fixture can carry a key — asserted by a test that reads the fixture file's own bytes back. That test failed against itself the first time, because the needle was a literal the file therefore contained.

docs.title: Automation and external tools
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. Hooks, your editor, your terminal and your file manager are free. Sequences of your own are custom-actions and the workflow recipes are git-flow. What a licence adds

Four things that are about running something: sequences of the app's own verbs, git-flow as editable recipes, the hooks git would run, and your editor, terminal and file manager.

docs.title: Named sequences
docs.text: "Check out main, pull, check out prod, pull, rebase onto main, check out main" — six things somebody types every week, under a name, run with one press.

docs.title: A step is a verb this app already has, and never a command line
docs.text:
That is the decision the whole feature is shaped by, and three things follow:

  1. Every refusal is a controller's own — a dirty working tree, a diverged history, a branch that does not exist — in the words you would have seen pressing the button.
  2. Nothing new can execute. This grows no way to run a program, unlike the custom command, whose whole subject is running one.
  3. The editor offers a real list rather than asking you to remember git's spelling.

What is given up is everything git can do that this app has no verb for, and the honest answer to that is the vocabulary getting longer one verb at a time rather than a text field that runs whatever is in it.

The vocabulary is published, with each verb's fields, so the editor draws a drop-down and then the arguments for whatever was picked. A verb the list does not hold is dropped on load and on save, so a hand-edited file naming rm -rf gets a step dropped rather than a sequence that runs it.

docs.title: It stops, and says which step and why
docs.text:
The interesting question is not what happens when a sequence works. It stops where it stopped: the refusal is reported with its position — "step 3 of 6, check out prod" — the log holds the steps that did run, and nothing after the failure is attempted.

There is no "continue on failure", per step or otherwise, because a sequence that carried on past a refused checkout would do the rest of its work on the wrong branch.

A merge or a rebase that stopped is not a step that ran. Both report success for a conflicted result — the index is written and the Conflicts surface finishes it — and that is a state for somebody to settle rather than something to run four more writes on top of.

A clean stop is different, and getting that wrong made --no-ff unusable: this app's merge also stops on a clean normal merge, waiting to be committed. "A merge that stopped is not a step that ran" was right about conflicts and was applied to every stop, so a --no-ff step — the whole of what git-flow is — reported "stopped on conflicts" every time. A conflicted stop still ends the sequence in the same words; a clean stop is a merge waiting to be committed, and the step after it commits one.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
Resolved %current-branch Per step, as it runs %default-branch Per step %starting-branch Once, when the run starts %<your-key> From what you type when you press Run

Per step is the point: a sequence moves HEAD, so "check out main, pull, check out %current-branch" would otherwise come back to where it began.

%starting-branch is the exception that proves it, and is what makes a finish sequence possible at all: "check out the trunk, merge the branch I was on, delete it" cannot be written with %current-branch, because after the first step that is the trunk — so the second would merge it into itself and the third would delete it.

A sequence can ask for one value, which is the smallest thing that makes "start a feature called X" writable: without it a sequence can only ever do fixed things, and a branch name baked into a recipe is a recipe for one branch. It is not a widening of the rule above — what arrives is a value landing in a field a verb already had. A missing value is refused before the first step rather than resolving to an empty string: half of feature/ is a branch nobody meant to make, and a sequence that found out on step three would have moved HEAD twice already.

docs.title: Global, and kept in JSON
docs.text: Not per repository: that sequence is the same errand in every checkout you have. It is JSON beside the settings rather than in them, written through on every edit, and nothing recorded can carry a credential — a step is a verb id and arguments that are refs, remotes and messages.

docs.title: Three routes
docs.text:
• Manage → Actions makes and edits them, beside the list.
  • Actions ▾ on the top bar runs one from wherever you are, saying which step it is on.
  • Each sequence is its own palette entry under its own name, because a name is how one is found and a single "Run an action…" entry would put the thing you typed three letters of one level further away.

Sequences that ask for a value are left out of the palette route rather than offered and refused: the palette is built in the shell, which has no field to type a branch name into, so the entry could only ever run with nothing.

docs.title: Workflow recipes
docs.text:
git-flow's six errands as ordinary sequences — feature, release and hotfix, start and finish.

There is no git-flow controller. A workflow is an opinion, and one held in a controller is one the app imposes — on branch names it guessed, in an order it chose, with no way for anybody to disagree. Adding a recipe makes an ordinary sequence instead: it lands in the same file as everything else, renamable, editable, deletable, and adaptable the first time somebody's trunk is not called what this app assumed.

docs.title: How to use one
docs.text:
1. On Manage → Actions, open Add a recipe and pick one.
  2. It lands as an ordinary editable action: rename it, reorder the steps, change a branch name. Nothing about it is special afterwards.
  3. Run it from Actions ▾, from anywhere.

The trunk is %default-branch so a recipe travels between repositories; develop is a literal, because it is git-flow's own name for a branch this app has no way to discover — and an editable copy is exactly what a project that calls it something else needs.

Adding one twice makes two rather than refusing, unlike creating a sequence by name: a second copy to adapt is the ordinary reason to press it again.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Manage → Hooks. A hook is an executable file in one directory with a name git looks for, and every refusal here follows from that: nothing about a hook is in a commit, in the index or in any reflog.

Where the hooks are is a question, not a constant. core.hooksPath moves the directory, and a repository that sets it runs nothing from .git/hooks — so a list hard-coded to that path was confidently showing hooks that could not fire and hiding the ones that would. It is read first, and resolved against the working tree when relative.

That is also what makes this right inside a linked worktree: hooks live in the common directory and a worktree's .git is a file, so the old reading reported "no hooks" — the one answer that is never true.

The tab says whether the path came from config, because "these are the hooks" and "these are the hooks because config says so" are different things to be told, and it prints the resolved directory in full.

The executable bit is what git looks at, so it is what "enabled" means. A file's presence, its name and its permissions are three separate facts and the list carries all three:

  • .sample is not a state — it is a different filename, one git never looks for, and the samples are what git init leaves behind. So a sample is something to install from.
  • An inactive hook is a real hook git will not run. The old list drew any file it found as installed, which is the worst way round: a pre-commit git silently skips looks exactly like one guarding every commit. The count line is "%1 of %2 run" rather than the list's length.

One asymmetry in the write path is deliberate. A hook created here is made executable, because a file git will not run is not what somebody who has just written one meant by "save". An existing hook's bit is left exactly as it was: enabling is its own verb, and saving an edit to a hook you deliberately switched off must not switch it back on behind you.

Nothing is read that cannot be edited. A hook may be a compiled program or a megabyte of generated shell, and a program loaded into a text editor is a program destroyed by the first save. The refusal names the file and its path, so it can be edited where it is — and the editor draws that sentence instead of the box, since an editor beside "this could not be read" is an invitation to press Save.

An unknown name is listed but never created. A file in the directory is shown whatever it is called, marked "not a hook git runs", because it is there and hiding it would be the old column's fault in the other direction; it may be edited, too, since something put it there. Creating one is refused — a new file git will never look at is not a hook.

Deleting is the one thing here that nothing can undo, so it asks, and the dialog offers switching it off instead — which is what most people asking to delete a hook actually want. Its Delete is deliberately not the primary. A sample is never deleted at all.

On Windows, 'enabled' means the file is there

NTFS has no executable bit, and Qt answers the question there from the file's extension — so a hook called pre-commit reads as not executable however it was written, and every row on a Windows checkout would have said "will not run" about hooks git runs perfectly well.

Switching one off then has no mechanism and is refused by name rather than reporting success having changed nothing: renaming it is a name git does not look for, and deleting a hook to "disable" it would be a destructive act behind a reversible-sounding word. Switching one on is refused too, for the opposite reason: it is already true.

Sharing a hook is not something this offers, and the editor says so: a hook is in no commit, so it is not pushed and nobody else gets it. Doing it means committing one somewhere and pointing core.hooksPath at that directory, which is a decision about a repository rather than a verb this app can perform.

docs.title: Your editor, terminal and file manager
docs.text: Open ▾, on the workspace bar and on every fleet card.

docs.title: It works before you have configured anything
docs.text:
The first version gated every route on a command being set, which meant no button, no menu row and no palette entry out of the box — a feature whose only way in was a settings page you would visit if you already knew it was there.

With nothing stored, the first of a small candidate list present on the PATH is taken. Discovered rather than shipped as a constant, because a default naming a program nobody has is worse than none — the button would be there and pressing it would say code could not be started — and the settings row says which one was found and that it was found rather than chosen.

Every candidate takes a path as an ordinary argument, which is the whole test for being on the list: a terminal editor started detached with no terminal around it opens nothing and reports success.

The extra directories a windowed process does not inherit are searched too — ~/.local/bin, /usr/local/bin, /snap/bin, Nix's profiles — because a Homebrew editor is invisible to an app launched from the Dock. Flatpak is out of reach and the code says so: its exports are named by application id, so matching them would mean a second list of app ids for the same programs.

docs.title: They are command templates, not program names
docs.text:
code %1, wezterm start --cwd %1 — because the interesting cases here are all arguments: a new window, a folder opened as a workspace, a shell started somewhere. A field that took only a program would have to grow a second for its arguments and a third for their order.

%1 may appear anywhere or not at all — a terminal that takes its directory from the one it was started in wants no placeholder — and the path is passed as the process's working directory either way.

It is not a shell, and that ceiling is why a stored command is safe to run

No pipes, no &&, no redirection, no substitution, no globbing. The settings file is a text file, and a template that reached a shell would be one line of somebody else's editing away from arbitrary execution the next time the app started.

The path is substituted after the split, inside whichever argument holds it, so a folder called my repo, one with a quote in it, or one called --upload-pack=… is one argument and cannot become two. Anything that genuinely needs a shell goes in a script and the script is named here.

A command naming a program that is not here is kept and reported. One can be installed tomorrow, and refusing to store the line would be this app deciding what may exist then — so the row prints what would run and that it would fail, and the failure names the program and the field to change rather than a bare "could not be started".

docs.title: One button, and the destinations are a list
docs.text:
Editor, Terminal and Open remote were three buttons side by side on the bar and two more on every card — three controls for one question, each appearing and disappearing on its own as a command is set or a remote is added, so the strip changed width under the pointer.

The rows are drawn from one file that both menus use, because two copies had already drifted three ways: the folder row existed on the bar's menu and not on the card's, the forge row read "Open remote" in one and "Open in GitHub" in the other with two palette wordings behind them, and the order differed.

Every label is a whole verb — "Open in editor" rather than "Editor" — because the rows are read in two places and only one of them has a button saying "Open in…" above it.

Showing the folder needs no setting at all: the desktop decides what opens a directory, so this app's part is one url. The label is the platform's proper noun — Finder, File Explorer, or "file manager" elsewhere — because a Mac reader looks for the first and finds nothing under the third. Three names and not two is what the Windows port cost that row: the ternary it replaced is the shape a two-platform project acquires everywhere, right up to the moment a third arrives and the else starts answering for a case nobody chose it for.

docs.title: Where the verbs are
docs.text:
A file has no per-row button — a button per row is a palette entry per row, and the alphabet does not stretch to a file list — so it is a row of the Changes context menu and a button beside a commit's file on History.

Two file lists deliberately do not carry it. A stash's file is a stashed version, so an editor there would open a different file from the one on screen; and a pull request's files are on somebody else's branch, which this checkout may well not have at all.

A commit's file opens as it stands on disk, and the button says so — an editor takes a path, and a commit's copy of a file is an object with no path. Restore is how the commit's version is reached. A path that is not there is refused by name, because an editor handed one creates an empty file, and the commonest way to arrive at one is a row for a file some commit deleted.

On Windows, a .cmd shim is refused rather than wrapped

startDetached runs an executable image, and a .cmd or .bat is a file for the command interpreter — so it fails. That is not an edge: it is how VS Code and several others put themselves on PATH.

The obvious repair is cmd /c, and it is refused: cmd re-parses what it is handed, so &, |, ^ and % in a path would stop being inert, and a folder called a & b is not exotic. This file's whole guarantee is that nothing it holds reaches a shell, and buying one platform's convenience with it would be the worst trade available.

So discovery passes over a shim and falls through to the install directory where Code.exe is, and a typed one is refused by name with the .exe named as what to type instead.

docs.title: A command of your own
docs.text:
A third template, and deliberately not a sequence step: that class's guarantee that every step is one of this app's own verbs is not being traded away for one feature. This is the other thing entirely — an arbitrary program, run once, handed three facts, whose failures are its own.

%1 The repository %2 The branch %3 The picked paths, one argument each

%3 is what makes it a second template rather than a longer first one: a list has to arrive as a list, so it must be an argument of its own and expands to as many as there are — to nothing at all with nothing picked, rather than to an empty string a program would read as an argument meaning "". An argument that merely contains %3 is refused by name, because --file=%3 means one thing with one path and nothing honest with three, and a command whose argument list changed shape with the size of a selection is one that does something different depending on how many rows were lit.

Nothing is discovered here, unlike the two above: nobody can guess what somebody else wants to run. Empty means empty and every route is absent while it is.

It is two settings, because the name is what the control is made of. A button reading "Run", a palette entry reading "Run" and a legend line reading "Run" say nothing about what would happen, and this is the one verb whose subject is a program nobody but its author knows anything about. A command with no name counts as unset.

The button is on Changes' own header rather than the file menu: with nothing picked it is still a perfectly good thing to press — "run my script on this repository" is what most of these are — and a row reached by right-clicking a file would make an empty selection unreachable.

docs.title: Bisect
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. This page is bisect — except End, which is never gated. What a licence adds

A binary search: one commit is known bad, an older one is known good, and testing the middle halves the range every time. Twelve steps over four thousand commits, which is the whole reason git has the feature.

docs.title: How to run one
docs.text:
1. On History, right-click a commit where the thing still worked, and choose Bisect from here. That commit is the good end; the branch you are on seeds the bad end. Both are editable in the dialog.
  2. The app checks out the middle commit and detaches HEAD. Build it, run it, and answer on the operation banner — which is drawn on every surface, so you can walk away and come back: Good, Bad, or Skip for a commit that will not build and so cannot be judged either way.
  3. It narrows until one commit is left and names it. End is always available, never gated, and puts HEAD back.

The gesture is why the commit seeds the good end: somebody reading the graph, recognising a commit as one where the thing still worked, and wanting to search forward from it. The reverse errand is one field away.

docs.title: The search is native and the state is git's
docs.text:
Nothing shells out and nothing needs the git binary — the search is a revwalk and some arithmetic. What it borrows is git's own files: BISECT_START (which is also git's test for whether a bisect is running at all), BISECT_LOG, BISECT_TERMS, BISECT_EXPECTED_REV, and refs/bisect/bad, refs/bisect/good-<sha> and refs/bisect/skip-<sha>.

A private state file beside the rebase's and the merge's would have been easier, and would have made this app the only place a bisect it started exists. Interoperability is the entire point of the choice: a bisect begun in a terminal appears here with its goods and bads intact, one begun here is finished with git bisect good in a terminal, and git bisect log prints both.

The rebase and the merge write their own files because what they record — the plan somebody edited, the ref that was typed — is something git records nowhere. Every fact a bisect holds already has a place in git's layout.

The cost is that git owns these formats: BISECT_LOG's lines are parsed by git bisect replay, so their shape is not this app's to improve. A test writes the files by hand and requires the controller to pick up a search it never started, because a test that only read the properties back would pass just as well against a private format.

docs.title: The next commit is an approximation, and the record says so
docs.text:
The candidates are the commits reachable from the bad one and from none of the good ones, minus the bad commit and anything skipped; the one handed back is the middle of that list in topological order. Git computes a true weight per commit and picks the best split.

The approximation cannot produce a wrong answer, only a slower one — every candidate is a valid thing to test, so whichever is chosen the range still shrinks and the culprit at the end is the same commit — and what it can cost is a step or two on a history with wide parallel branches.

That is why the estimate beside it is a logarithm and the sentence says "roughly", which is the same claim git's own "roughly N steps" makes and is worth no more. The test drives it against a known answer rather than asserting which commit each step lands on, since pinning the sequence would pin the approximation instead of the result.

docs.title: Four states, never three
docs.text:
bisecting Still narrowing found One commit is left, and it is named unresolved Everything left in the range was skipped waiting for a good commit A bad commit with no good one yet, which git allows

unresolved is the one worth having. The culprit is in there and nothing established which; reporting that as found would name a commit on no evidence, which is the one thing a search whose whole output is a name must not do.

The fourth state deliberately does not walk the range: a walk from a bad commit with nothing hidden is a walk of the whole history, which is exactly what must not sit on a refresh path.

docs.title: Skipping is what makes it usable
docs.text: A commit that will not build cannot be judged either way, and without a way past it the search stops dead on the histories it is most needed for. A skipped commit goes into git's own refs/bisect/skip-<sha> and is never offered again.

docs.title: Where the verbs are
docs.text:
Good, Bad and Skip are on the banner and nowhere else, because that is where you will be: building and running the thing you are bisecting, not looking at History. They are absent once the search has an ending — there is nothing left to judge.

End is never gated, the rule every way out on that banner keeps: it works on a bisect this app never started, on one whose state files somebody deleted half of, and after a restart. It is its own button rather than a limb of Abort, whose wording is wrong for a search that has written nothing to abandon.

A bisect is a fifth banner mode rather than a row of its own, because it is not orthogonal to a detached HEAD — it is one, walking commits on no branch of yours. So it ranks above that reading rather than beside it, or the banner would print the less useful of two true things: "HEAD is detached at a1b2c3d" is a fact, and "Bisecting a1b2c3d — 6 revisions left, roughly 3 more tests" is that same fact with the reason and the way out in it. It ranks below the three that write, since a half-finished rebase, merge or pick is work sitting in the index where a search can be picked up again from git's own files whenever you get back to it.

docs.title: What it is in the refresh, and what it costs
docs.text: Nothing running is one file-existence check and no walk at all; something running is a ref glob and one revwalk bounded by the range being searched rather than by the history. That is the distinction the subtree walk failed, and it is why this one is allowed on the general refresh path — where it has to be, because a bisect begun at a prompt has to appear without this app having been told.

docs.title: There is no bisect run
docs.text:
git bisect run <program> executes an arbitrary command line, which is exactly what the action sequences refuse on principle — a step there is one of this app's own verbs so that every refusal is a controller's own — and a settings field whose value is executed is the one thing the external-tools template is careful about even for an editor.

Automating the loop is what a terminal is for; what this offers is the search. It has no printed git command either, since a line there would teach a command this app cannot perform.

docs.title: Two log rows, and never a dozen
docs.text:
A search is a dozen presses of Good and Bad, and a row for each would push every other entry in that repository's log out while saying nothing you come back for. What holds the judgements is BISECT_LOG, which is git's own file.

Both rows offer no way back, and that is honest rather than a gap: a bisect detaches HEAD, and a detach is not a ref move — a mixed reset against a detached HEAD would drag it back and leave the repository detached. The way back is the banner's End, which is on every surface and never gated, which is a better answer than a row somebody has to find.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. Creating, renaming, deleting, checking out, upstreams and the drift are free. Stacks — the recorded base, the chain, the restack and the tree reading — are stacked-branches, and what has been proposed off a branch is forge. What a licence adds

Manage → Branches. Reading branches and writing them are two different jobs and they live apart: the breadcrumb's picker narrows the history to a branch and moves nothing, and this tab is where branches are created, renamed, deleted and checked out.

That split is deliberate rather than an accident of layout — people rely on the picker not moving HEAD, and it says so in as many words.

docs.title: What a row says
docs.text:
Four facts, and they are four rather than one "stale" flag because the ways a branch gets stuck have different people on the hook:

Fact Means ↑3 ↓12 main Ahead of and behind the trunk — what a delete would throw away, and how much of the trunk this has not seen origin/foo Its upstream, and its drift against that merged into main Every commit is already reachable from the trunk upstream gone Config still names a remote-tracking ref that has been pruned away on feature-2 Its recorded stack base, if it has one an age When the tip was last committed to

merged into main is a floor, never a total

It is a reachability test over the commit graph, so it catches an ordinary merge and a fast-forward, and it cannot catch a squash merge or a rebase merge: both rewrite the commits, the original tip is then reachable from nothing, and a thoroughly merged branch reads as unmerged.

Nothing here is called "fully merged", because "fully" is exactly the claim the commit graph cannot support. The tests assert the wrong-looking answer on purpose, so the limitation is on the record rather than waiting to be discovered and "fixed" into a claim.

What can catch those is the forge, and it does — see what has been proposed off a branch.

The trunk is worked out from refs/remotes/<remote>/HEAD first (the server's own answer, and the only source that is right for a trunk called neither main nor master), then a local main, then a local master — and which of those answered is published, because a guess nobody can see is how a surface comes to state something untrue with confidence.

Which commit the trunk is at is a second question, and answering it with the first's answer was a live bug: measured against origin/main, a local main eighty commits ahead is not an ancestor of anything — including itself — so on a repository where git branch --merged main listed two branches, the merged filter came back empty and every row's drift was measured against a commit you had left behind weeks ago.

docs.title: The measurements are asked for, not refreshed
docs.text:
Measuring one branch is an upstream resolution, three ahead/behind counts, a merge base and a descendant test. On a repository with 121 branches and 3000 commits that was 481 ms of a 601 ms refresh — paid on every repository switch, every staged hunk and every working-tree event, for numbers only this tab draws.

So the names, the tips and which branch HEAD is on are read cheaply and always; the four facts are a second pass, asked for when the tab is opened, batched against a time budget. A row carries detailed: false until the pass reaches it, drawn plainly, because no upstream, zero drift and not-merged is exactly what a branch cut this morning looks like.

docs.title: Narrowing the list
docs.text:
Three scope chips — All / Local / Remote — with a count each, remembered as a habit. In all, the locals come first ahead of the alphabet: interleaving origin/main between main and next would bury the eight rows that can be acted on among forty that mostly cannot.

Merged only is a fourth control and deliberately not a fourth scope chip: the three above it are readings of which kind of ref and at most one holds, where this is a question about state and composes with whichever is lit. Grouped with them, "merged" would cancel "local", which is the pairing somebody tidying up wants. It is absent in the remote scope, where the only thing pressing it could do is empty the list.

A name filter lives on the surface rather than in the settings, unlike the scope: a scope is a reading habit worth remembering and a query is three characters you are holding for ten seconds — a list narrowed by a word nothing on screen shows is the one asymmetry that would be a bug.

Sorting — by name or by when the tip last moved — sits behind one control rather than two chips, because that strip already carries three scope chips, a merged chip and a filter field and, at the window's 900px minimum, has to fit all of that beside eight tabs. Alphabetical is the default: it is the only ordering that holds still, so a branch is where it was last time and a row does not move under the pointer because somebody else pushed. An unmeasured row is held at the end by name rather than sorted as its zero, or every row the page has not reached would sit at the bottom and then walk up as the pass landed.

docs.title: A row is three controls, and the rest is a menu
docs.text:
It had five appearing on hover, and the gutter is a fixed width — so on a narrow window what appeared pushed Check out past the right edge, and the verb you were reaching for left the window at the moment you hovered the row it was on.

The menu is opened from the ⋮ and by right-clicking the row — one set of verbs, two ways in, so they cannot come to differ. Two of its rows are routes to surfaces that already existed and could not be reached from here: Compare with current, and Rebase current onto this, both absent on the branch HEAD is on.

docs.title: Checking out
docs.text:
git_checkout_tree and then git_repository_set_head, in that order — the detaching variant leaves the repository detached and orphans the next commit, silently.

What a checkout may destroy is computed before anything is written, as the intersection of what is dirty with what the two trees disagree about. That is git's own rule, and it is why switching branches normally carries work in progress along instead of refusing; it is also the only way the refusal can name the files, which libgit2's "1 conflict prevents checkout" cannot.

With nothing in the way the branch is checked out at once, because a dialog whose answer is already known is a habit rather than a safeguard.

Autostash is its own button rather than a tick, because it is a different operation. Untracked files go into that stash too, unlike git's own autostash: an untracked file the target branch also has is exactly the sort of thing that blocks a checkout, and stashing everything except the blocker would be a joke. Coming back, the stash is applied and then dropped rather than popped — git stash pop reports success after writing conflict markers into the file and dropping the entry, which would leave the only intact copy being the marked-up file you are now staring at.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
Refuses without force where the branch is unmerged, and "merged" here means reachable from HEAD or from the branch's own upstream — a branch that has been pushed is safe to drop even when whatever you are standing on has never seen it.

Deleting the checked-out branch is refused with or without force, because there would be nothing left for HEAD to point at.

The confirmation has three sentences and picks one:

  1. A name and nothing more.
  2. The count, and where the commits go.
  3. Landed but rewritten — the proposal number, and why git cannot see it.

That third one exists because the dialog was telling a false alarm: a squash-merged branch reads as unmerged to git, so it counted four commits and said deleting them would make them reachable from nothing — about work that is already on the trunk under different ids. A false alarm on the one dialog in that list that destroys something is what teaches somebody to press through the real one.

The force is still passed and the confirm is still not the primary, because git's own answer has not changed and the forge reading may be a day old — so the button that makes commits unreachable stays the one the highlight does not lead to. What changed is that the sentence beside it is true.

docs.title: Several rows at once
docs.text:
The same gesture the file lists use — plain click, ⌘-click, shift-click from an anchor — scoped to one kind of row, because a local branch and a remote-tracking ref share almost no verb.

A plain click on a row that is already the whole set lets go of it, which is the only way out of a set now that the strip of bulk buttons is gone.

The set's verbs are on the menu, for this project's rule that an operation is entered from the object it acts on — and because five buttons appearing the moment a second row was picked moved every other control sideways at the one moment somebody was aiming at a row. The header counts ("11 branches"), a verb that cannot honestly apply to a set is absent rather than relabelled (no checking out eleven branches, no rename, no comparison, no proposal), and the destructive one names them.

A set operation reports every refusal, by name, once. Each is a loop over the single verb it is the plural of, so nothing about what is safe is decided twice — what they add is that eleven refusals are collected and emitted together rather than arriving in a toast that holds the last one.

docs.title: Upstreams
docs.text:
Set or clear what a branch tracks. "Nothing" is the first row of the picker rather than the last — it is the one answer whose position must not depend on how many remotes a repository happens to have.

There is no confirmation: nothing about it moves a ref or writes a file, and the dialog says so. What it changes is what the ahead/behind counts are measured against and where a plain push and pull go.

docs.title: Checking out a remote branch
docs.text:
A remote-tracking ref cannot be checked out, renamed or deleted by anything here, so a remote row is a different component rather than a local row in another mode — a mode would be one component every line of which asks which of two things it is drawing.

What it carries is the one verb that is available — Check out as…, with the ellipsis load-bearing, since this means making a local branch at that commit and calling it "Check out" would claim the app can put HEAD on a remote ref — and tracked by, so "origin/main, tracked by main" and "origin/spike, tracked by nothing here" are told apart.

The verb is absent once something tracks the ref: the local branch is a few rows up with its own Check out button.

docs.title: Stacked branches
docs.text:
A branch cut from another branch rather than from the trunk is an ordinary way to work — three changes that depend on each other, each reviewable — and git records nothing about it. That absence is the whole design.

Making one out of a branch you already have

A stack is usually recorded as you go, a branch at a time. To turn one branch that has grown too big into a stack after the fact — a commit, a file, a hunk or a few lines at a time — see Splitting a branch.

It is recorded, never inferred. After a base has moved on, the merge base of two branches says where they last agreed and not which was cut from which; and two branches off one trunk share a merge base that names the trunk. A stack inferred from the graph would be right about the common cases and confidently wrong about a rebase.

So it is a note — branch.<name>.sourcemanager-base in .git/config — and three things follow from where it lives:

  • It is this checkout's. A colleague does not receive it, because there is nowhere in git to put it where they would.
  • It is namespaced, so nothing git or another client writes can collide with it.
  • It survives every operation this app performs, because config does.

docs.title: What it buys
docs.text:
The drift is measured against the base. On feature-3 over feature-2 over main, "12 ahead of main" is the whole stack's work and says nothing about this link; aheadOfBase is the three commits this branch actually adds. The row draws one or the other and never both — two numbers about one branch with nothing saying which question each answers is worse than either alone.

And a proposal per link: each is that link's base against that link's head.

docs.title: Three refusals
docs.text:
A base that is not a local branch (a remote-tracking ref cannot be checked out, rebased onto or proposed against from here, so offering it would be an offer the app cannot keep); a branch on itself; and a base that would close a cycle — a on b on a is a chain with no trunk, and every reader of it would walk it for ever. The cycle check runs against what is stored now rather than trusting the refusal to have held, because .git/config is a text file somebody can edit.

A deleted base keeps its note and says so. Dropping it silently would lose the one record of what this branch was cut from at exactly the moment somebody is working that out.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Manage → Branches, open a branch's ⋮, choose Set base branch.
  2. Its drift is then measured against that base.
  3. Propose the links one at a time.

docs.title: What has been proposed off a branch
docs.text:
A badge on the row, from the pull requests this app already holds. It costs nothing and asks for nothing — a pass over the list in memory — so a repository whose proposals have never been read has no badge rather than a "no proposals" claim.

merged is sticky and the number is not: a branch proposed twice and merged once did land, which is the fact the delete warning must not lose. merged as #140 outranks merged into main and replaces it rather than joining it — they are the same fact at two strengths, and the forge's is the one that is right when they disagree.

docs.title: Changes and staging
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Staging, discarding, ignoring and deleting are free, at every granularity. What a licence adds

Two lists — staged and unstaged — a diff beside them, and the commit box. The tab carries a count of what it holds, which is the union of the two lists rather than their sum: a file with some of its changes staged is in both, and it is listed once.

docs.title: Three granularities
docs.text:
Stage Unstage Discard Revert File ✔ ✔ ✔ (asks first) ✔ from a commit Hunk ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Line ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔

Line-level staging reconstructs a patch from the lines you picked and applies it; hunk-level goes through the index API directly. Both key a selection to a line's index within its hunk, which is why the unified and split diff layouts cannot disagree about which line a click meant.

Space stages or unstages whatever is picked — the same verb the tick is rather than a second spelling of it, so a folder stages what is under it, a set of eleven stages eleven, and every refusal is the one the tick would have made.

docs.title: Flat or a tree, and one choice for both lists
docs.text:
Anything carrying a path becomes rows: a directory row per level with the count of everything beneath it, and files labelled by basename. The Changes lists and a commit's files on History are the same component with the same folds.

Which reading is in force is a habit rather than a decision per list, so it is remembered in the settings — a property on a surface would forget itself every time, since the surfaces are loaded on demand.

A tick on a folded directory stages everything under it. That case used to be broken rather than absent: it called a verb with a path git does not hold, so it silently did nothing.

docs.title: What a verb acts on
docs.text:
There are two different questions and they are kept apart. The file being read is one — a panel draws one diff — and what a verb acts on is a set, because somebody picking eleven files to discard is not asking to read eleven diffs.

The set comes from two places and they compose:

  • A multi-selection. ⌘/Ctrl-click adds and removes, ⇧-click extends from an anchor in the list's own order, and a plain click replaces the lot and sets the anchor. The anchor is written by a plain click and a ⌘-click and left alone by a shift-click, which is what lets a run be re-aimed by shift-clicking somewhere else rather than started again.
  • A directory — a verb chosen on a folder acts on every file under it.

The selection is scoped to one list, because "staged" and "unstaged" decide what every verb here means and a set spanning both would make Stage ambiguous by construction.

Every row of the set is lit, not only the one being read, because a verb acts on the set and the set has to be visible. Right-clicking inside the set keeps it; right-clicking outside it selects that row.

The wording follows the count: the menu's header says "11 files" rather than naming one of them, and two verbs are absent for a set rather than relabelled — Ignore writes a rule per path, and Blame is one file's story.

docs.title: A verb over a set is one operation, not eight hundred
docs.text:
Discarding a folder's worth of files used to lock the window for several seconds with nothing on screen saying anything was happening, and the cause was not that any one file is slow. It was that a set was eight hundred operations: per call, open the repository, build a whole status list to answer about one path, write the index, take a snapshot, append a row to the operation log, and emit a change that turns into a full status refresh of every list. None of those costs is per file; every one is per operation.

The same fault was in three more verbs, and the worst of them had no confirmation in front of it — "Stage all" was a loop, measured at 2806 ms for 800 files.

Measured over 800 one-line files:

Before After Opening the discard confirmation 1205 ms 9 ms Discarding 3972 ms 75 ms Staging 2806 ms 60 ms Unstaging 3056 ms 60 ms Longest single stretch the window is frozen the whole 5.2 s one 13 ms budget

All four are one operation now, over shared machinery: one status walk, one snapshot, one log row, one refresh, and the index and working tree written a chunk at a time against a time budget. Progress is in the operation banner, because a sweep of eight hundred files takes long enough to walk away from, and Stop is never gated.

Chunk sizes differ per verb because what a chunk costs differs: discard's is 32 (one index write and one tree walk however many paths), staging's is 16 (adding a path hashes the file, so the cost is bytes rather than calls), and resolving's is 8 (each file costing a three-way merge to write).

The refusals are collected and said once. A toast holds the last message, so eight hundred of them would report one.

docs.title: Discarding
docs.text:
Discarding a file takes it back to the last commit, index and working tree both — a verb that only reset the working tree would be the third of three overlapping half-undos and would leave the file still listed, reading as the button not having worked.

Discarding a hunk goes back to the index, and the asymmetry is a fact about where a hunk comes from rather than a taste for one: the only hunks on screen belong to one of the two diffs the panel draws, and undoing one can only mean undoing it against the side it was measured from.

A hunk of the staged diff has no discard at all, and that is the answer rather than a gap — undoing a hunk of HEAD-to-index is unstaging it, the button is already in that row, it is reversible, and an unrecoverable second spelling of it alongside would be a trap. Throwing staged work away is unstage, then discard.

docs.title: What it refuses, and what it offers instead
docs.text:
• A renamed file's discard undoes the rename — the old name comes back out of HEAD and the new one goes. This used to be refused, with a sentence telling you to untick the file and discard the old name: two operations to undo one, the second naming a path no longer on screen.
  • Deleting what no commit holds is the second answer, behind a tick. For an untracked file there is nothing to go back to, and the refusal was right about the verb and unhelpful about the intention. The tick is drawn from the same plan field the operation reads, so the offer and the operation cannot drift, and it is off every time the dialog opens — a destructive option still on from last time is one nobody chose.
  • A conflicted path is refused. Marker text is not the new side of a diff, and settling it belongs to Conflicts.
  • A selection with nothing undoable in it is refused. An empty patch applies cleanly and reports success for having done nothing, which is exactly how a destructive verb comes to be trusted.

docs.title: The confirmation lists every path
docs.text:
It listed eight and then "… and 412 more", defended on the grounds that a list which has to be scrolled to be counted is one nobody counts — but the count is in the title, so nothing there was doing the counting, and what the cap actually did was hide four hundred and twelve of the files about to be destroyed from the only place they are named.

A row also says what will happen to it where that differs from the dialog's sentence, since a set is the one case where the promise cannot be true of every path. One file keeps the exact sentence; a set gets a deliberately weaker one, because there is no sentence true of eleven files at once.

Nothing is confirmed at hunk or line level. A hunk is a gesture inside a diff and a line is a keystroke, and a dialog per line is a habit rather than a confirmation. What replaces it is refusing, and the fact that the result lands somewhere you can look at it.

docs.title: Ignoring a file
docs.text:
Entered from the file, and offering the four rules people actually ask for — this file, this extension in this directory, this extension anywhere, this whole directory — with the exact line on screen before it is written. A .gitignore is one of the few files in a repository that is composed rather than generated, and describing the intention while writing the line out of sight is how a client ends up being the thing whose output has to be checked afterwards.

Three things about it are load-bearing:

  • A tracked file is not ignored by a .gitignore entry at all. Ignore rules decide only what happens to paths git is not already following, so a file in the index goes on appearing in git status however many rules name it. A tracked path is refused by name, with the git rm --cached that would make a rule mean something.
  • The line is appended, and no code path can do otherwise. The file is opened in append mode, a missing final newline is made good in front of the new line, and the line ending is copied from what the file already uses — one LF line in a CRLF file is a whitespace change in every tool the repository passes through.
  • A rule that would lose is refused rather than written. The .gitignore files between the root and the path are read for re-inclusion (!) lines, and each is asked whether it covers this path — because libgit2 and git disagree here, and libgit2 reports a path a deeper file re-includes as ignored.

Rules that would mean nothing are absent rather than greyed: no extension rules for a file with no extension, no directory rule for a file at the repository root. A leading dot is part of a name rather than the start of an extension, so .env is offered one rule and not three.

docs.title: Applying a patch somebody else wrote
docs.text: Apply patch… beside the button that writes them. See Patches.

docs.title: The list is virtualised, and had to be
docs.text:
Both lists were built row by row, which is right for the forty changed files this surface is normally opened on and ruinous for a branch switch, a generated directory or a reformatting sweep. Measured through the shell, before a pixel was painted:

Changed files Build time 1,000 0.27 s 3,000 2.2 s 6,000 13 s

And a tap of the modifier then cost another 2.8 s, because every row declares two commands and the registry was growing at twice the rate of the list.

It is now 22 rows and 208 commands built, whatever the count is — 0.16 s at six thousand files. The section headings and the empty notes are rows of the same list, because anything that has to scroll with the rows has to be one of them.

One consequence you can see: the two bulk buttons ("Stage all", "Unstage all") live on a heading, and a heading three thousand files down does not exist — so each keeps a palette entry of its own that stands in while the button is scrolled away, and exactly one copy is ever listed.

docs.title: The gestures on a row
docs.text:
A double click stages or unstages — a third route to the tick, adding a hint key and no palette entry. On a directory the first click folds and the second is dropped, since a fold toggled twice lands back where it started and reads as a press that did nothing.

A right-click opens a menu, and every row of it is a second route to something the surface already draws — staging is the tick; Discard, Ignore and Blame are the three buttons above the diff — except Open in editor and File history, which are reachable nowhere else and are therefore the two rows that are in the palette.

Opening the menu selects first, because Discard, Ignore and Blame all act on the selection and each reads a plan taken at selection time. A menu acting on the row it was opened over while those plans described a different file would be right about the name and wrong about the offer.

docs.title: Writing a commit message
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. The box, the template, the marks, the trailers and recall are free. What the staged paths and the log are evidence of, and the subject-shape check, are commit-help; the drafting verbs are ai. What a licence adds

The box on Changes, and everything the app knows that would help fill it in. The rule the whole thing is built on is guidance, never enforcement: nothing refuses a commit for the shape of its message, nothing rewrites what you typed, and every control that does change the text goes through the field's own undo stack so ⌘Z takes it back.

docs.title: What is on it
docs.text:
• commit.template, laid into an empty box, with the surface saying which file it came from. Comment lines are stripped here, since this app has no editor session for git commit to strip them in.
  • The 50/72 marks, measured in the face the box is actually drawn in.
  • Co-author trailers, from a picker over the repository's recent authors, appended in GitHub's own Co-authored-by: spelling.
  • Conventional-commit type chips — a shortcut row you choose in the settings. Six by default; add perf, ci, build or your own, or empty the list and draw no chips at all. It is a habit rather than a fact about a repository: somebody who writes perf: writes it in every checkout they work in.
  • Recall of recent messages, from two sources kept in their own sections.

docs.title: Two sources of recall, and why they stay apart
docs.text:
The preference holds the last twenty messages typed into that box, globally. That is what your own wording looks like across every checkout you work in, and it is the only source that answers before anything has been read.

The repository's own log is the other, and it is what the preference cannot be: it is empty on a clone made this morning, which is precisely the moment somebody most needs to see how this repository writes its subjects, and it holds twenty messages where a convention is visible in two thousand.

Choosing the log rather than a second file of the app's own settles three things at once: there is no schema to version, no rows to drop when a repository leaves the fleet, and no copy of anybody's prose on disk — a commit message is the words you wrote, and the only defensible place to keep those is the one git already keeps them in.

One walk, two readings:

  • The vocabulary is everybody's, because which types and scopes a project uses is a fact about the project, and inferring it from one address would answer nothing at all on a fresh clone.
  • The recall list is filtered to this checkout's own user.email — the address git would sign the next commit with — because offering another person's whole message to be committed under your name is not recall.
  • The completions are everybody's with your own ranked first.

Nothing is walked because a surface was opened: the log is read by the first keystroke in the box, or by the recall list being opened. What is read is then kept and re-walked only when the repository or HEAD has moved.

docs.title: The suggestion strip
docs.text: Under the box, and it is where the two kinds of help sit side by side — which is the thing nothing else in the field ships.

docs.title: The offline half: inference that states its basis
docs.text:
suggestionsFor() answers a row per suggestion and the basis is never empty. This app's rule everywhere is that an inferred thing names its evidence, and a commit type is the most consequential inference in the set: a wrong feat: is wrong in the changelog, in the release notes and in whatever reads the log a year later.

So there is deliberately no "the source files changed, so this is probably a feature". A feature and a fix touch the same files in the same directories, and where the paths decide nothing the answer is empty, with the sentence saying so — which is also the sentence that teaches where the line is. The paths decide a type only where they genuinely do: every staged file a test, a document, a build file or CI configuration.

Once a type has been typed by hand, the one thing left that the paths do decide is where the change lives, so the second kind of row adds the deepest directory the staged files share. A scope is only offered where this repository's subjects carry scopes; a segment that only names a layout convention (src, lib, app) is not a scope, since fix(src): says nothing fix: does not; and a scope that repeats the type is dropped, test(tests): being the same word twice.

A declaration outranks an observation. A commitlint type-enum array is lifted out of the JSON, YAML or JavaScript spelling and those are the types that may be suggested, because a declaration is a rule somebody wrote down and the counts are a pattern somebody noticed. Nothing is evaluated — a commitlint.config.js that computes its types from a required module is a program, and running one is not something a git client does.

docs.title: The generated half
docs.text:
A model's draft, in the same strip, marked as generated and naming the model that answered. See Asking a model, including @ai — write the part that carries intent, mark where the machine should fill in, and the two are blended.

The offline inference is not a fallback for when no model is configured: it is cheaper, it is offline, it needs no key, and it states its basis, so where the paths genuinely decide something it is the better answer, because you can check it.

docs.title: Reaching the strip by keyboard
docs.text:
The keyboard really moves into it, by Tab and by ↓ alike. A highlight that walked a list while the caret went on blinking in the box would be two cursors, and which of them Enter belongs to is not something a reader should have to work out.

  • Tab is the shape everybody has met under a box of completions.
  • ↓ steps in from the subject or from the end of the message. Not only from the end: the suggestions are about the subject, so a reader who had typed both could never have reached a suggestion about the line they were on.
  • ↑ off the top, ↓ off the bottom, Enter having taken a row, Esc having taken none, and Tab again all hand the keyboard back.
  • Nothing is highlighted until ↓ is pressed. With a row pre-selected, Enter would commit a line the app guessed rather than the one you typed.

Both keys fall through with nothing to suggest, which is the common case, so Tab goes on indenting and ↓ goes on moving the caret.

Pressing a row writes the subject line only, so a paragraph already typed under it survives being offered a better subject.

docs.title: The shape a subject is expected to have
docs.text:
A regular expression the first line is matched against, a warning sign beside the box when it does not match, and the sentence behind the sign. Nothing else.

It warns and never refuses. No commit is blocked, no button is greyed, no word is rewritten. A client that enforced a convention would be enforcing somebody else's rule with no way to see it — the app is not a linter.

A regular expression rather than a switch, because "which shape" is the whole question: a project with PROJ-88: … subjects is as entitled to a check as one with feat(scope): …. The default is Conventional Commits in commitlint's own type set, spelled out rather than derived from your chip row — taking perf off a chip row is not a statement that a colleague's perf: commit is malformed.

Three states and never two: no pattern at all is a project with no convention and the mark is absent rather than green (a tick beside every message anybody types is chrome), and a pattern that will not compile is reported as not ok with a sentence naming the setting rather than the message.

A repository's own pattern outranks the setting, in .git/config under the app's own key — which shape a project's subjects take is a fact about the repository, the same for everybody who works on it, where a setting is one reader's habit. Per checkout rather than committed, because .git/config is not cloned, which is also what makes a stored pattern safe to act on.

docs.title: Amending HEAD
docs.text:
A tick on the commit box. It amends over the tree the index currently writes, which is what makes it pick up newly staged work and what makes an untouched index leave the content alone. An empty message keeps the one the commit has, which is --no-edit. The author and their timestamp survive and the committer does not, as git does it: who wrote the change and when are facts about the change.

Only HEAD, and it says so. An older commit is reworded by stopping on it in a rebase, which this app has — see Rewriting history. Nothing amends while an operation is in flight.

A published commit is warned about, once, and amended anyway. Rewriting a pushed commit on a branch of your own is ordinary, and refusing it would be this app deciding how somebody else's branch works — but the consequence is not visible from the button. "Published" is ahead == 0 against the upstream: local, no network, and no promise beyond what the last fetch left.

The tick is absent rather than present-and-refusing on an unborn branch or during a stopped operation.

docs.title: Reading a diff
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Every reading of a diff on this page is free. What a licence adds

One panel, used everywhere: the working tree, the index, a stash, a commit, a comparison, a file's history, and somebody else's pull request. Which verbs it offers changes; how it reads does not.

docs.title: Unified or split
docs.text:
Unified is the default — it is what git diff prints, it survives any width, and a hunk that only adds lines gains nothing from a gutter down the middle. Split earns its width on a rewrite, where the before and after of a line are otherwise rows apart.

It is a habit rather than a per-panel switch, so it holds for the working tree, the stash viewer and a commit's files alike. Both layouts draw the same cell and both key a selection to a line's index within its hunk, so staging cannot tell which layout a click came from.

Below about 889px of panel — 55 columns a side, derived from the monospace font rather than a pixel figure somebody picked — the split chip is hidden and the panel says "split view needs a wider panel" rather than lighting a control it is ignoring. Dragging a splitter narrow falls back to unified and keeps the preference, because dragging a splitter is a statement about this window rather than about how you read diffs.

docs.title: What is drawn
docs.text:
Syntax highlighting, from the file's extension. Anything unrecognised renders as plain text, exactly as before, because unknown must not look like broken.

Intra-line marks — a word-level comparison between a line and its partner, drawn in both layouts as washes behind the text rather than in the markup, which is what keeps the plain string authoritative for measuring.

Rows pair by likeness, not by position. Within a change block a removal is shown against the addition it most reads like, and anything with nothing alike opposite it takes a gap. Pairing by position was tried first and was wrong as often as it was right, confidently showing two unrelated lines as one line's before and after. A gap reads as absence rather than as a mark: a wash a shade deeper than the ground and a hairline at a fifth of the divider's weight, because a divider-weight rule struck across the row was the loudest thing in the panel.

docs.title: Four dials
docs.text:
Control What it changes Context 3 / 10 / 25 / the whole file Whitespace nothing → whitespace → whitespace and blank lines Split unified or side by side Wrap fold long lines, or scroll sideways

The first two change what libgit2 was asked rather than how the answer is drawn, so the panel re-takes its diff — and it is the controller that knows whether those hunks came from the working tree, the index, a stash or a commit.

Whitespace and blank lines are separate switches because they are separate in git, and for a reason: -w disregards whitespace within a line, and a blank line has none to disregard, so no amount of ignoring whitespace hides one. A reformatting sweep normally needs both, so one chip cycles all three states.

Ignoring whitespace stands the writing verbs down

Staging, reverting and discarding rebuild the hunk as a patch and apply it, and a diff hiding a re-indent is not a patch of the file on disk. Those verbs are hidden rather than greyed while a filter is on, which is also what makes them genuinely unavailable — a hidden control is in neither keyboard route — and the panel says why, because a missing Stage button reads as a broken Stage button.

Wrapping is a preference rather than a per-panel switch for the same reason split is: it is a reading habit, so it holds for every diff surface at once, including the three-way conflict columns, which run out of room first at a third of the width. Scrolling is the default — a diff reads by column as much as by row, and a fold pushes everything under it out of alignment.

docs.title: A ten-thousand-line hunk
docs.text:
The panel used to virtualise the hunks and build every line of one, so forty small hunks were fine and one contiguous hunk was not — and the context dial's "Whole file" step turns any large file into exactly that. Measured at ~116 KB of resident memory per built row, a thousand changed lines cost 234 MB and ten thousand cost 2.3 GB; that was the whole of the "the app is using 400 MB" report, and nothing on screen said so.

Slicing the long hunk into smaller pieces was tried and made it strictly worse at every size, which is the finding the present design is built around: a list fills its viewport by creating rows until their heights add up to it, and a row whose height is not known at the moment it is created never adds anything up. Smaller rows only made more of them.

So the panel draws one flat list of rows whose height is arithmetic — with wrapping off, a row is exactly one monospace line. Hunk headers, file bands and every line are rows of one list, each reporting a floor height from the start. Live cells drop from one per line to a screenful, and a bound test asserts that in all three layouts, because the fix is otherwise undone by the next feature.

Three consequences are deliberate: the floor is a floor rather than a claim (a row settles to whatever it lays out to); wrapping is virtualised too, one line being a floor for a folded row rather than a guess at it; and the pinning moved with the rows — the header, the file band and a split pair hold themselves at the viewport's width and slide back as you scroll sideways, so the staging button stays reachable instead of riding off the right-hand edge.

docs.title: Binary, images and LFS
docs.text:
libgit2 answers a binary delta with no hunks at all, and the panel used to draw that the only way it could: "no textual changes in this file", over a screenshot that had just been replaced. That sentence is true of every binary file that ever changed and is therefore not an answer.

The provider reports a kind and the panel picks a renderer:

  • binary — a change with a size readout, and the reasons told apart. GitHub withholds a patch for three unrelated reasons and "no textual changes in this file" is true of all three.
  • image — a promise that at least one side is drawable. png, jpeg, gif, bmp, webp and ico, because those decode everywhere this ships and anything whose plugin is optional would draw on the developer's machine and not yours.
  • lfs-pointer — see Git LFS. A pointer is text, so it diffs perfectly well as three lines of the wrong file; the pointer question is therefore asked before the binary one.

docs.title: Three ways to compare two pictures
docs.text:
Side by side answers "what are these" and is nearly useless at "what moved": the eye cannot hold two images a panel's width apart well enough to find a few pixels, and each is drawn at whatever scale its own half allowed.

Swipe puts a boundary through one frame. Onion skin fades the versions into each other. Both are one frame, one scale, and the top-left origin rather than the centre — where the two versions are different sizes, centring shows both of them shifted and reads as a change to each.

The reading is a preference, like split and wrap. Both overlays are absent where there is one picture: an addition has no "before", and an overlay would be one version drawn under a blank frame, which reads as the other having been erased.

Nothing in the binary branch writes, and that is the answer rather than a gap: a hunk is what staging, reverting and discarding act on and there is not one, so those verbs — and the whole option row above them, every one of which is about lines — are absent, with a sentence saying so.

docs.title: Where a diff cannot be staged
docs.text:
canStage is off for a commit's diff (there is no index behind history), a comparison, a file's history, and somebody else's pull request. Per the absent-not-greyed rule those verbs are not drawn at all rather than drawn dead.

A forge's diff additionally cannot be re-read, because re-reading matches on the path — so a pull request touching a file also open in Changes would otherwise have the local version silently swapped in the moment a context option changed.

docs.title: What a hunk header carries
docs.text:
Beside the @@ line: staging, unstaging, reverting or discarding the hunk; copying a permalink to the lines picked; holding the hunk back for a patch you assemble out of several commits; and on a proposal's diff, Comment.
