Comment is in the header rather than on every line for the reason the permalink is: a button per line is a keyboard entry per line, and the alphabet does not stretch to a diff. It acts on the panel's own selection, which is how staging has always worked here, and a forge takes a comment on a range — so two lines picked and one comment written is exactly the shape both ends already have.

docs.title: A comment under a line
docs.text: The panel takes a map from path|side|line to whatever is there, plus something to draw it with, and puts a row of its own under any line that has something under it. Two things follow: the panel stays a diff viewer, so nothing in it knows that forges exist and the same mechanism would hang a blame annotation off a line; and a thread is a row rather than something inside the line's cell, because a thread's height is only known once it has laid out, and as a sibling it reports the same one-line floor a wrapped row does and grows past it. A test builds five hundred threads and asserts the list still holds a screenful.

docs.title: The whole diff in one scroll
docs.text:
A file at a time is the right way to review a file and the wrong way to read a proposal, and both readings exist. The combined one is every file's hunks in one scroll, in file order, with a band naming each file as it goes past.

It travels as one hunk list with a marker entry carrying a file where a hunk carries lines — the same shape a binary change already uses — which is what makes it cost nothing to draw: one list builds only the rows near its viewport, so a 200-file diff realises incrementally, and the highlighting, the split and wrap preferences and the intra-line marks all apply for free.

Two things about it are load-bearing. Every hunk carries the path it came out of, because the extension changes as you scroll and without it a column of Python, YAML and C++ would all be highlighted as whatever the first file happened to be — worse than no highlighting, because it is confidently wrong. And a file the forge withheld a patch for keeps its band and its sentence rather than dropping out: a whole diff that quietly omits three files is worse than no whole diff, because the omission is invisible to exactly the reader relying on it being whole.

docs.title: Taking pieces out of a proposal
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. The extraction itself is stacked-branches; the proposal it opens and the retarget are forge-write. What a licence adds

"This proposal is too big, take the API change out into its own" is the commonest thing anybody says about anybody else's work, and until this existed the answer was to leave the app for a terminal: a branch cut, checkout -p twice, a force-push, and a proposal retargeted in a browser.

It is splitting a branch's other verb, and the only one here that moves a branch that already exists. Everything the split writes is a name that was free; an extraction writes one of those and moves one somebody may be reading.

docs.title: How it goes
docs.text:
1. On a proposal's page, press Extract. The chip lights, a strip appears above the file list saying what the ticks mean now, and the pane beside it starts drawing this checkout's diff rather than the forge's patch.
  2. Pick what comes out — a file's tick, a hunk, a run of lines, or a commit, whose Take puts every file it touched into the set.
  3. Choose a mode, name the new branch, and press. The extraction is written locally and refuses in its own words if it cannot be.
  4. The propose dialog opens on the new branch — the same push, reviewers, labels and draft tick the ordinary Propose button uses.
  5. Only then is the original branch pushed, and in stacking mode the proposal is retargeted.

The order cannot be reordered. Until the extracted branch exists on the forge, retargeting names a branch the forge does not have — and a proposal whose branch has lost the extracted code while nothing holds it yet is work that looks deleted. Every failure between the steps gets a sentence, because each leaves a coherent state that is not the one asked for: a refused push leaves both branches here as the extraction left them; a refused lease means somebody has pushed since your last fetch, so the rewrite is here and the forge still has the old branch.

docs.title: The three modes
docs.text:
Each is named after what happens to the branch the code came out of, and the whole of the difference is the parent of the one commit that branch is left with.

Mode The branch's new commit sits on Its tree The push Remove the branch's own tip the remainder ordinary Rewrite the base the remainder with a lease Stack the extracted commit the branch's own with a lease

Remove is the default because it is the only one that keeps the branch's history: every hash on it survives, the push is an ordinary fast-forward, and the proposal's diff loses the extracted code because a commit on top took it back out.

Rewrite is what you want when the branch should read as though the extracted code was never on it.

Stack gives the branch its own tree rather than a synthesis, which makes "the two add up to the branch" true by construction: what it then adds over its new base is exactly the remainder. It is the mode that wants the proposal retargeted, and the only one that asks the forge for anything.

Both rewriting modes force, and force means a lease. A branch somebody else has moved is refused by name rather than overwritten, and with no remote-tracking ref it refuses as git does. A plain --force is never reached from here — the transport's rule, and the one place you would most regret it.

docs.title: The two sides are exact complements
docs.text:
What the branch is left holding is derived from what you picked rather than gathered alongside it, because this is the one thing in the operation that could be quietly wrong: a synthesis that dropped a line produces two branches that both commit, both push, and are both plausible.

  • A file nobody picked is taken whole, being entirely what is left.
  • A file picked whole is absent from the remainder, and absence is right rather than empty: the tree is built from the base, so a file nothing says anything about stays as the base has it — which is precisely "this file's change went elsewhere".
  • A partly picked file keeps every line the pick did not name.

The guarantee is asserted as blobs compared string for string, not as "something was written".

docs.title: It refuses before it writes anything
docs.text:
• A branch another worktree has open is refused by name, with that worktree's path in the sentence. libgit2 refuses it too — but at the second of the two calls a move is, having already written the tree, which reads as "I extracted four files and now every one of them is a staged change".
  • A dirty working tree, where the branch is the one you are on, is refused first and in this app's words naming the file. Untracked files are deliberately not counted: nothing this writes touches a path git does not know about, and refusing over a stray build artefact would make the operation unusable in exactly the repositories it is for.
  • A branch this checkout does not have — which is what a proposal from a fork is — cannot be extracted from, and the chip that starts the mode is absent rather than greyed.
  • Taking everything is refused: that is not an extraction.

Where the branch is the one you are on, the working tree and the index move with the ref, so you are not left standing on a commit that no longer exists.

docs.title: The ticks mean something else while the mode is up
docs.text:
The box beside a file is "I have read this" everywhere else on a proposal's page; while an extraction is being arranged it picks the file. One box with two meanings is a real cost, and the alternative — a second tick in a row that already carries a fold arrow, a status letter, a diffstat and a comment count — is worse.

What pays for it is that the mode is loud: the chip is lit, the strip above the list says what the tick means and which diff is on screen, and the pane beside it is drawing a different diff. It is a strip rather than a dialog because this takes several minutes and several places, and a thing you can walk away from mid-way must not be possible to lose track of.

The picking is against your local diff, deliberately. The forge's patch is a different rendering of the same change — its context, its hunk boundaries — so a pick made against it would take out lines nobody chose, silently.

A commit's Take is a gesture over its files rather than over its own lines, and that is honest rather than lazy: a commit's contribution to a file a later commit rewrote is not in the cumulative diff at all, so claiming to take its lines would be a number that is right about the easy case and confidently wrong about the interesting one.

docs.title: Retargeting, and where it is not offered
docs.text:
Re-basing a proposal is not a small thing — it moves the merge base, so the diff every reviewer is reading is a different diff afterwards. It is here for the one errand that cannot be finished without it, it is one named write, and the app sends a base and nothing else, asserted by reading the bytes that go out.

It is its own capability rather than riding on "can this forge change a proposal's state". Where a forge does not have it, stacking still runs and the dialog says — where the choice is made, not afterwards — that the proposal will have to be retargeted by hand.

The result is re-read rather than claimed. What a claim would buy is a branch name changing a second early, in exchange for the page having to be right about what else moved: every file in the diff, the file list, the size estimate and every comment's anchor.

docs.title: Undoing one
docs.text:
The operation log carries an extract-branch row that offers both writes back: the new branch dropped and the old one put where it was. An inverse that only deleted the new branch would leave the original holding the commit the extraction gave it — the state you are trying to get out of.

Both ends are guarded. The extracted branch is dropped forced, its commit being a synthesis nothing else reaches, and what earns that is its tip still being exactly where the extraction left it. The original is put back only if it is still there too; a commit made on it since is work this would throw away, so it is refused by name.

It cannot un-push and it cannot close a proposal, and the row's own sentence says so: if you have already pushed, you get your refs back and still have a proposal to close on the forge.

docs.title: The fleet
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. A fleet of up to three repositories is free. An unlimited one (fleet-unlimited), importing a folder (fleet-scan), a second window (windows) and the proposal and CI summaries on a card (forge) need a licence. What a licence adds

The page the app opens on, and the answer to "what is the state of everything I work on". One card per registered repository, carrying its branch, its drift, how much uncommitted work is in it, and whether an operation is stopped in it.

Nobody else in the field has this on a home page with drift and stopped operations beside each other; GitKraken's Workspaces are the nearest thing and are a paid feature there.

docs.title: Four ways in
docs.text:
Add ▾ is one control with four rows, ordered cheapest to most:

Row What it does Import repository Take on a checkout that is already on disk Clone Bring one down, with a depth dial and what shallow gives up New repository git init here — and, where a token says it can, the same repository on the forge with origin wired up Scan a folder Walk a directory and offer every checkout beneath it

The path fields are asked for rather than always there: two mono text boxes stating a question that is answered once would push the cards down on every visit, so each sits behind a button that reveals it, focused, and Esc puts it away.

docs.title: Scanning
docs.text:
Registering twenty checkouts one typed path at a time is what a single path field cannot do. The walk is breadth-first, a batch per turn of the event loop against a time budget — a scan of a home directory has to leave the window alive, and has to be abandonable.

Nothing is registered by the walk. What it finds is offered, to pick from, because a scan of anyone's home directory turns up plenty nobody wants in the fleet.

A repository is a directory holding a .git directory, which is the single test that excludes both submodules and linked worktrees — theirs is a .git file — and neither belongs in the fleet on its own, since each is reached through the repository that owns it. A found repository is never descended into; node_modules, build, Pods and DerivedData are never entered; hidden directories and symlinks are skipped, because a symlink back up the tree is how a walk like this loops.

docs.title: A repository that does not exist yet
docs.text:
New repository does git init in a folder you name, and optionally creates the same repository on the forge and points origin at it. Four things about the forge half are deliberate:

  • auto_init is off. A forge-made initial commit is exactly what turns your first push into a rejected non-fast-forward, and the only ways past that are a force or pulling a commit nobody wrote.
  • Nothing is pushed. The remote is wired up and Push — which knows about leases and upstreams and refuses in its own words — is how the first commit gets there.
  • Private is the default, and the tick says so: a public repository is visible to everybody the moment it exists, and that is not a state to arrive in by not reading a dialog.
  • The order is local, then forge, then remote, each only if the last succeeded. A repository on the forge with nothing local to push into it is litter somebody has to delete by hand.

It refuses rather than clobbers three times: a folder that is already a repository (it offers to import it instead), a folder that holds anything at all, and a path inside another repository's working tree — a nested repository is invisible to the outer one's status, because git does not descend into one.

docs.title: What a card says
docs.text:
The branch, ↑ahead ↓behind, the count of uncommitted files, tags for a stash, a worktree or submodules, and a marker when an operation is stopped in there.

The whole tile opens the repository — a card is a repository the way a row is a file, and the Open button in the corner is the label on the target rather than the target.

An unread card says so

Summarising a repository costs an open, a status walk, an ahead/behind, and three list reads. Doing that for nine checkouts of twenty thousand files blocked the window for 4.1 seconds, so it is batched now: the list is immediate, and each entry's git fields fill in over the following turns.

An entry that has not been read yet carries summarised: false and the card says so, because every one of those fields is a claim if it is drawn as an answer: no branch is "detached", nothing ahead or behind is "in sync", and nothing dirty with nothing untracked is "clean" — the last being the one somebody reads to decide a checkout needs nothing doing to it.

The fleet is deliberately outside the app's general refresh: summarising it opens every registered repository, so it is refreshed when the page is shown rather than after every staged hunk.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Free-text labels you assign. A repository belongs to at most one, and one that belongs to none still renders, in a section of its own at the end.

Four verbs sit behind one control — make a group, rename one, delete one, and file a repository into one — and none of them re-summarises anything: a label is a fact about the fleet rather than about the repository, so assigning one rewrites the cached entries in place instead of opening every registered repository again.

Deleting a group deletes a label and never a repository. Its members are un-filed into the section at the end, still registered and still on disk, because losing a checkout while tidying up a name is not a trade anybody would make knowingly.

docs.title: Three things about grouping that are separate on purpose
docs.text:
• Drawn — whether sections are shown at all. Turning it off leaves every label where it was, so turning it back on returns to what was there.
  • Declared — a group can exist with no members, so "make three groups, then sort thirty checkouts between them" no longer has to be done one card at a time and in the wrong order.
  • Inferred — group by parent directory is a shortcut, and it is reversible because every label it writes is recorded as derived. Undoing it takes back exactly those and cannot discard a name you typed. A label stops being derived the moment you touch it.

docs.title: The order is yours
docs.text:
Alphabetical was the first answer and the objection to changing it was that any other order would have to be persisted, migrated and given a way to change. It is all three now: sections are dragged by a grip, or moved with arrow buttons that are visible always rather than on hover — a hover-revealed button is invisible to the palette and to the hint keys.

A name the arrangement has never heard of ranks past the end of it, so with no arrangement every name ties and the alphabetical tie-break decides the page. There is no second mode to keep in agreement with the first. The unlabelled leftovers stay pinned last.

Dragging a section by its grip and a card by its body carry different things, so the shared drop target tells the two gestures apart without guessing, and they draw different marks: a wash for "file into here", an insertion rule for "put it between these two".

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text: Chips narrow the page — dirty, ahead, behind, stopped — and the sections are computed from what the chips left, so filtering and grouping compose.

docs.title: Removing one
docs.text:
Three answers, not a boolean, because they are three different acts and a tick beside one button would make the destructive one the same press as the harmless one:

  1. Forget the entry — the checkout stays on disk.
  2. Move the folder to the trash — offered first, and the primary, because a checkout is often the only copy of something and this is the one form the operating system can take back.
  3. Delete it permanently — deliberately not the primary.

Three rules keep the offer honest. The folder goes first and the entry only if it went, because a fleet that has forgotten a repository whose files are still there is recoverable while the reverse reads as "deleted" and is not. The trash failing refuses rather than escalating — quietly turning a reversible request into an irreversible one is the worst thing that function could do. And the dialog is composed from the same plan the operation consults, so it says what is actually in there: uncommitted files, untracked files, stashes, and commits no remote-tracking ref can reach — the one figure that says the folder holds something that exists nowhere else.

The repository being open is not a refusal: it is a reason to close it first, which the app can do and you cannot conveniently. The dialog says the app will go back to the fleet.

docs.title: Two windows
docs.text:
New window opens an empty one on the fleet — somewhere to put the next checkout — and a card's Open in a new window opens that repository beside whatever is already open, landing on Changes.

A second window is a second repository, genuinely: each window holds its own set of controllers. What is shared is everything about the reader rather than about a checkout — the preferences, the fleet, the command counts, the language, the editor template, the keychain, the snapshot store. So the theme you pick in the second window is the theme the first one is drawn in, because there is one preferences object rather than two agreeing by arrangement.

A repository open in one window draws as open on the other window's card, and removing it closes it everywhere.

Repository tabs are recorded as the shape that could not have delivered this

A tab strip over one set of controllers is a visible drawing of the ⌃Tab list: pressing a tab swaps the repository underneath every surface, which is what the switcher already does with no chrome at all. Two repositories side by side needs two windows.

docs.title: The free tier keeps three
docs.text:
The fleet cap is the one licence limit with a number in it, and it bounds growth and never the fleet: forty registered repositories still list, still open and still refresh under a lapsed licence, and only the forty-first is refused. Nothing deletes an entry to enforce anything.

The Add control is disabled with a sentence beside it when the fleet is full — disabled rather than absent, which is a deliberate exception to the absent-not-greyed rule, because the verb applies, it is the one about to be wanted, and a control that vanished would take the sentence explaining it with it.

docs.title: Pull requests and CI
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. Reading is forge; proposing, reviewing and labelling are forge-write; GitLab and Bitbucket are forge-providers; permalinks are forge-links; writing while the forge is unreachable is offline-comments. What a licence adds

Pull requests, reviews and CI results come from whichever forge hosts the remote, behind a provider seam the interface never looks past.

Forge Reads Writes GitHub everything proposals, reviews, comments, labels, reviewers, repositories GitLab ‡ everything but check runs and a review decision proposals, reviews, comments Bitbucket Cloud ‡ everything but per-file patches nothing

‡ Fixture-proved and never live-proved: the tests pin the URLs built, the JSON mapped onto the documented fields, the errors told apart and what the transport will and will not let through. No live instance has ever answered.

Self-hosted instances work, including GitHub Enterprise, GitLab on your own machine — see declaring a host.

None of this is git transport. Moving objects is a different protocol with a different credential, and nothing on these two surfaces fetches, pushes or pulls anything.

docs.title: What the app may write, in one list
docs.text:
Ten endpoints, spelled out in one array in the transport, and a provider cannot add one:

  • Submit a review, and send one that was already begun
  • Comment on a line, and take that comment back
  • Append a comment to the review being written, and throw that review away unsent
  • Open a proposal, ask for a review, put labels on it
  • Create a repository under the signed-in account

There is no PATCH and no PUT. So nothing retitles, re-bases, closes or merges a proposal; nothing dismisses somebody else's review or rewrites the body of one; and nothing replaces the reviewer or label set somebody else chose — a POST on the labels path adds where the PUT on the same path would replace.

No read path writes at all, and that is asserted rather than promised: a test drives every read there is — both diff readings, a re-read, both refreshes, a whitespace switch — with a draft open the whole time, and requires the write log to come back empty.

Nothing writes without a user action. Nothing on a refresh, nothing on a timer, nothing as a side effect of reading.

The one row that names no operation

Nine rows name one operation each: read the pattern and you know what may happen. POST /graphql is a single URL behind which every mutation GitHub has lives, and which of them a request performs is decided by a body nothing in the list inspects — so for that row, "what may this app write is answerable by reading one array" is false, and no arrangement of the array makes it true again.

It is there because the review being written moved onto the forge and REST cannot append a comment to a pending review. The alternatives were a delete-and-recreate on every keystroke, or keeping the draft local. What stands in the guarantee's place is narrower and asserted rather than promised: exactly one mutation is spelled in this app, from a fixed template with its arguments as typed GraphQL variables rather than text spliced into a query, and it is sent only from a control somebody pressed.

A GraphQL read — the review decision, and the id lookup — goes down its own channel with its own allow-list, and the document is checked: it must be a JSON object whose query begins with the query keyword, carrying no operation name, and containing the word mutation nowhere at all. So the one thing the write row cannot promise about itself, that channel does.

docs.title: Every state is a state, not an empty list
docs.text:
no-repo, unsupported, unconfigured, idle, loading, ready, failed — and the surface renders the ones that are not a list.

An empty list is only ever allowed to mean "this repository has none." Rendering "no token" or "the forge said no" the same way is how a network feature earns its reputation for lying.

A forge that cannot answer a question refuses with a sentence rather than an empty list. GitLab has no per-commit check concept, so check runs there is Unsupported with a sentence naming the Runs page — that repository's pipelines work perfectly.

docs.title: A token is read, never kept if it can be helped
docs.text:
GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN, then gh auth token (asynchronously, and only once a surface asks, so an app never pointed at a forge never shells out), then a token typed into the app.

That last one lives in the settings file in plain text and the surface says so in as many words, because somebody choosing it deserves to know before rather than after. No token is logged and none reaches an error message.

With no token nothing is requested at all, since an unauthenticated call to a public repository works and then stops, mid-session, at sixty requests an hour.

docs.title: Signing in through the browser
docs.text:
The OAuth device flow — the only mechanism a desktop app can honestly use, since an authorisation-code flow needs either a client secret it cannot keep or a loopback socket it cannot count on. It honours the server's polling interval and keeps a raised one.

This build ships no client id, because one belongs to whoever registered it. Register an OAuth app, enable device flow, and supply the id through an environment variable or the field the panel offers — "no client id" is a first-class state with instructions, exactly as "no token" is.

The granted token joins the same order and lands in the same unencrypted settings a pasted one does. The browser removes the copying, not the storage.

docs.title: Declaring a host
docs.text:
A host resolves to an instance — which software is there, and where its endpoints are — rather than straight to a class. That is what makes GitHub Enterprise and a private GitLab work: the same class, against <host>/api/v3.

Four things about it are load-bearing:

  • The URLs are derived from the host, never typed. You declare a host and which software runs there — the two facts nothing in a remote URL can say — and the rest is worked out. Three fields would let somebody point the API at one machine and the browser links at another, which is a phishing shape rather than a configuration.
  • The write allow-list is derived rather than written out. Declaring a host widens where this app may send a body, which is exactly what declaring one is for — and the operations are still fixed: nothing typed into a settings page adds a verb, changes a method, or reaches a path no provider was written against.
  • Everything that is not a bare host name is refused rather than repaired. A scheme, a port, a path, userinfo, a wildcard: each is a way to make one URL look like another once it reaches a derived pattern. A stored row is vetted on the way in exactly as hard as a typed one and dropped rather than fixed up, because the settings file is text somebody can edit and this is the one setting that widens where a credential may be sent.
  • The sign-in panel says which instance is in force, above everything and not optionally. What is about to be pasted is a credential, and "Sign in with GitLab" drawn over somebody's private instance is the one sentence that panel must not print.

Declaring a host lives on the sign-in panel rather than the settings page for that reason: it is the one control in the app that widens where a credential may be sent, and the panel that hands the credential over is where that belongs.

docs.title: What is kept, and asking again is a decision
docs.text:
Every answer goes into a cache under a key naming the question — pulls:owner/name, checks:owner/name@<sha>, detail:owner/name#12 — which is what makes the two verbs different:

  • Load serves what is held and fetches only when nothing is.
  • Refresh means spend a request now, which is what Reload does.

The slug is in every key, so switching repository invalidates nothing and coming back is free; the commit is in the checks key because HEAD moving asks a different question rather than staling the old answer.

On GitHub a refresh is cheap as well as explicit: a conditional request earns a 304 that does not count against the rate limit — and a tag is kept only for an answer that arrived in one page, since it identifies one URL and a list assembled from three is not revalidated by the first being unchanged.

Answers outlive the process, in a database beside the settings, and a stored list is served labelled and refreshing: "stored, read 14h ago · refreshing". Serving one spends the request that will replace it, so the screen is instant and converges without anybody waiting in front of a blank one. What was never acceptable is a stored list wearing a live one's face, and that is a different thing from serving one that admits what it is.

A failed refresh keeps what it failed to replace. The state stays ready and the refusal is drawn beside the list rather than instead of it, because "showing what was read yesterday, and today's attempt failed" is a state, and a more useful one than an empty frame with a red box in it. That is also why a missing token no longer folds a list already on screen into "unconfigured": signing out should stop the fetching, not erase the reading.

Signing out is a hard forget — memory and disk both — because a private repository's proposals sitting on disk after the account that read them was forgotten is exactly what somebody pressing that button is asking not to happen. It forgets answers: there is no column a token could occupy, and a test reads the file's bytes back.

A repository leaving the fleet takes its rows with it, by both path and slug: the path is exact and survives the directory's deletion, the slug catches what a second checkout of the same project overwrote the path of.

docs.title: The proposal list
docs.text: Number, title, author, state, branches, labels and awaited reviewers draw immediately; selecting one adds the description, the counts and the assignees; two more requests add the files and the reviews. Each wave has its own state, so the panel draws what it holds and says what is still coming. Commits are a fourth request spent only when asked for.

docs.title: A row before it is opened
docs.text:
The state is on the number, in the four hues every forge's own web UI uses — green open, grey draft, the accent for merged, the failure hue for closed-without-merging. Somebody who has read a proposal list before does not have to learn this, and the tooltip names the state in the forge's own word, which is the only thing separating merged from closed for the one person in twelve who cannot separate the hues.

Which of the four it is comes out of three fields, and the order they are asked in is load-bearing: state is only ever "open" or "closed", a merge is a closed one with a timestamp, and a draft is a flag. GitHub leaves draft set on one that was closed while still a draft, so asking about the flag first filed an abandoned draft as a draft — drawn in the grey that means "not finished yet", filed under the Open chip, and counted as open by the waits reading, which then flagged it for having waited months on a decision that had been taken.

The size is a band, not a figure. Five bands over four colours: XS and S share one, because "small enough to read now" is a single answer; L and XL do not, because that is exactly the pair somebody is choosing between when deciding what to pick up before lunch.

The size genuinely is not in a list — a forge fills the counts only when one proposal is asked about by name, so "a size on every row" is a request per row. They are spent lazily as rows scroll past, capped at thirty per list and never without a token, and the answer lands under the same key the panel and the metrics sample already use, so a proposal is bought once ever including across launches.

The state matters as much as the figure: a blank column reads as "this proposal has no size", which is the one thing it never means, so a row draws a figure, an ellipsis or an em dash — with a sentence under the list, once the ceiling is actually reached, saying why the dashes are there. A ceiling nobody can see is indistinguishable from a bug, and this one is reached by scrolling, which is exactly the gesture that would make somebody wonder.

The row bands the forge's raw total and the panel bands a counted one — with lockfiles and vendored directories set aside — so the two legitimately disagree about which letter a proposal earns. What they must never disagree about is what L means, which is why one component draws both. The tooltip says which arithmetic this is and that opening the proposal buys the other.

Labels arrive with the list and were simply never drawn, which is the odder gap of the two, because the search box and the whole filter vocabulary already match on them. They are capped at two with the rest counted: a repository whose convention is eight labels a proposal would otherwise push the author and the branch off the end of the line, and those are the two facts that tell two similarly-titled rows apart.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
By creation or by update, created by default because it is the only one of the two that is stable: ordering by update time alone reorders the page under you while you are reading it, and a row that was third yesterday is fifteenth today for reasons nothing on screen shows.

It is remembered, and the chips are drawn as their own labelled pair rather than beside the filter chips — a filter decides which proposals are here and a sort decides where each one sits, and one row of identical chips would make the exclusive-group rule read as covering both.

docs.title: Filters are a vocabulary, not four chips
docs.text:
A filter is a name and a list of conditions over the documented fields, all of which must hold. The four state chips are built-in filters in that same vocabulary, differing only in being code and in declaring an exclusive group.

A filter's definition travels everywhere its name does, because a filter is named by its author and a name is a claim. Everything is evaluated over what was already fetched, so the surface says when the fetch stopped at the provider's ceiling — "3 match" must never read as "3 in this repository".

docs.title: Two review fields that are each half of a qualifier
docs.text:
This is the part of the vocabulary that was reported three times, and each report was about a different half:

Field What it is Wrong about awaited reviewers The forge's review-requested: — who is on the hook right now A forge drops somebody the moment they answer, so a proposal whose reviewer objected has an empty list and is still owed a review. Lists fewer rows Merging requires a review The base branch's protection Knows nothing about approvals, so a proposal already approved still demands one. Lists more Review outcome so far The forge's own decision — required, approved, changes-requested, none, unknown Only the forge can put the two together

The labels are the third fix. "A review is required", offered beside a "Review decision" whose values include required, reads as two spellings of one thing — and somebody who picks the wrong one gets a list that is right and unexplained. Each one's caveat now points at the other, and the pair is asserted against the labels rather than against literals, so a rewording cannot leave two sentences naming fields that no longer exist.

unknown is a real answer and a common one: reading branch protection needs admin rights on some repositories and a forge answers 404 both for a branch with no protection and for a token that cannot see the protection it has. Reporting it as "no" would quietly drop every proposal on a repository you merely lack a scope for.

The decision costs one round trip for the whole list — which is why it exists at all, a field on every row not being buyable a request per proposal — and only the open proposals are asked about, that being the only state the question means anything in.

docs.title: Other things worth knowing about the vocabulary
docs.text:
• @me resolves at match time, and a saved filter keeps the word rather than the name, so the same filter means the right thing under a second account. An empty login matches nothing, including under the negative operators — not @me with nobody known would be "not nobody", which is everything.
  • state anyOf open excludes drafts, which is the vocabulary rather than an accident: a draft's state is draft, so this clause is the forge's is:open draft:false. A filter wanting both says state anyOf open, draft.
  • "Someone is awaited" counts teams, and naming a login matches people only. A review asked of a team and nobody else is a proposal with somebody awaited, but putting a team in the people list would make "waiting on kate" quietly true of a proposal awaiting a team kate happens to be in.
  • The whole vocabulary is documented in the editor — every field carries one line saying what it is, in a glossary fold beside "Add condition", plus the longer caveat printed under the conditions when that field is in use. Two separate strings on purpose: a glossary of paragraphs is not scanned, and a warning buried among a dozen definitions is not read.
  • A saved filter and a state chip are exclusive, and two saved filters are not. A saved filter is a complete question in a vocabulary that already contains state, so leaving Open lit beside it ands in a condition its author did not write — and a saved filter that "finds nothing" because of the chip nobody looked at is the commonest way one appears broken. Turning off the last thing in force falls back to All rather than Open.
  • A typed query is not a filter. Three characters you are holding in your head for ten seconds live on the surface rather than in the vocabulary, and both hold at once. It is reset when the surface is built, unlike the filters: a list narrowed by a query nothing on screen is showing would be a bug rather than a choice.

docs.title: The list was short, and there were three reasons
docs.text:
Worth recording because the fix took three passes:

  1. Teams were dropped from the awaited list, so on a repository whose convention is review teams that was most of the rows.
  2. The window was full of closed proposals — the list is bounded at five pages, and that ceiling is reached by merged ones, so an open proposal nobody had touched in a month was not in the data any filter ran over. The open ones are fetched on their own now, sorted by creation ascending because that pass exists to be exhaustive.
  3. review:required is not the awaited list, which is the part no amount of fixing a clause could reach — see the table above.

docs.title: The strip along the foot of the window
docs.text:
A saved question is worth more than the page it was written on, so it earns three routes: a count on its tab's badge, a watch, and a chip on the strip along the foot of the window — which is drawn on every surface, so a count you want in the corner of your eye survives walking to Changes, to History, to the fleet and to Settings.

A widget there is a filter and a kind — a proposal question, a CI question or a ticket question — so a chip is the filter answering for itself. Pressing one goes to that list with that filter in force.

Nothing on the strip fetches. A list this window has not read draws — and never 0: a zero is a claim that there is nothing, and the strip is the last place that should be guessed at. The counts follow each list's own change signal, so they move when the page they belong to is read.

The strip is absent until you add a chip, kept per checkout in .git/config, and the order you put them in is the order they are drawn in. A chip whose filter has since been deleted is kept and says so, rather than vanishing with the question it was asking.

docs.title: Which proposals have been waiting too long
docs.text:
Three readings rather than one "stale" flag, because the three ways a proposal gets stuck have different people on the hook:

open Opened, and still open approval Open, and nobody has approved it merge Open, approved, and still not merged

Collapsing them would report one figure to the reviewer who has not looked, the author who has not merged, and nobody in particular — which is how a badge comes to be ignored.

Mode and value are per reading. The values are on different scales — a fortnight open is ordinary and a fortnight approved-and-unmerged is not — and the mode does not transfer: "above the team average" is a meaningful reading of review latency and nearly meaningless of "open too long", where a mean is dragged by whichever proposal somebody abandoned.

In average mode the value is a multiple of the mean, defaulting to 1.5 rather than 1.0, because these distributions are right-skewed and a mark that fires on a third of the rows is decoration. Below eight observations the average mode does not answer — not a statistical threshold, there being no honest one for a mean over whatever the forge last changed, but the point at which one abandoned proposal stops being a quarter of the answer.

The two review-based readings can only be computed for a proposal whose reviews this app happens to hold, so such a row is unjudged, drawn as ?, and counted separately — which is also why those two are off by default: switching one on is the moment somebody accepts a column that mostly says "not read yet", where the open reading needs only the list.

A row draws one mark and the most actionable wait wins — merge, then approval, then open — because a proposal that is agreed and sitting there needs one press from somebody already convinced. Colour says only look at this, and the four glyphs carry which.

Nothing here costs a request: the verdicts are recomputed over the list in memory and the reviews already held.

docs.title: CI has two questions
docs.text:
Neither list answers the other, and the sentence under the chips saying which is on screen is the load-bearing part — the two lists look alike, and somebody who takes one for the other will conclude their own commit passed on the strength of somebody else's push.

Page What it holds Runs What the forge's own CI has been doing — a run of a workflow, on a branch, with an event behind it, holding jobs holding steps Jobs What any CI reported against one commit — the honest question, and the only reading that works for a repository built by something that is not the forge's own CI

Runs is the page that opens, which reverses what this surface used to do. The old default was the reading keyed to what is checked out; the trouble with it is that a commit's checks are empty far more often than CI is idle — nothing is pushed yet, the fetch is stale, the work is on a branch the forge has not seen — so the page opened on a blank list on a repository whose CI had run forty times that week.

The keys differ in what they carry, and that is the whole design: the checks key moves with HEAD and the runs key does not, so committing re-asks one and leaves the other alone.

Jobs are one request per run, bought when a run is opened and never for the list — and served outright rather than served-and-refreshed, which is the one place in this layer that is right: a finished run is immutable, and asking again would spend a request to confirm something that cannot have changed.

A run is opened rather than unfolded. In-place expansion works for the two or three jobs of an ordinary build and stops working exactly where you need it: a matrix build is twenty rows pushed in under one, and the list you were reading has lost its place.

A verdict is a colour and a shape, and the palette is broken here on purpose — everything else in the app is one accent and a neutral ramp, because "is anything broken" is the entire question this tab is opened with and a column of identical marks answers it only to whoever stops and reads each one. Three rules keep it from becoming a second palette: colour is never the only channel (every verdict keeps its own glyph and a tooltip naming it); four verdicts, not nine; and the hues are tuned for this ground rather than taken off a stock palette.

A duration column falls back to the status only while there is still something to be doing — never "how long since it started", which would report a queued run as having taken four hours. But a skipped check is completed with no timestamps at all, so the fallback printed the word "completed" under a heading whose every other value is a length of time. A finished thing with no duration took no time, and nothing is the honest figure there.

docs.title: Proposing one
docs.text:
From the Pull requests surface for the branch that is checked out, from a branch row's ⋮ for that branch, or from the comparison page with the left as the base and the right as the head.

The proposal is the operation; the other two are courtesies. Asking for reviewers and putting labels on are spent afterwards, on a number only the first request can supply, and a failure in either leaves the proposal open — reported as a notice rather than an error, because calling that a failure would report a success as one and this app has no verb for taking a proposal back. Somebody told "it failed" would go looking for a proposal that is sitting there open.

draft is sent both ways round rather than omitted when false. A repository whose plan has no draft pull requests answers 422 for true, which is a refusal you can act on; omitting the field would quietly open a proposal that is ready for review when a draft was asked for.

The push is a tick, default off, and the surface owns the order. A forge cannot open a proposal for a branch it has never seen, and getting it there is git's side of the house — so the dialog offers the tick, the surface pushes and waits, and the proposal is opened only if the push landed. A proposal of half a branch is worse than a refusal, and nothing leaves the machine because a dialog was opened.

What is prefilled comes from the commits it would land: one commit gives its subject and body, several give the branch's name and the list of subjects. Anything else is a form filled in twice.

docs.title: The template a proposal starts from
docs.text:
A repository that carries a proposal template expects every proposal to start from it, and this app opened its dialog with a description assembled from the commits — so a project with a checklist got one that skipped it, silently, every time.

They are read off disk and not fetched. The file is already in the working tree: reading it costs no request, needs no token, works offline, and — the part that decides it — is the same file the forge would use, so what this app prefills and what a browser prefills cannot come to differ. The cost is stated: a checkout that has not fetched the commit adding a template does not have it.

Where they live is the provider's — GitHub looks in three directories under two spellings plus a directory of several; GitLab has only a directory and no single file at all; Bitbucket has no convention, so the picker is absent.

The first single file wins and the rest are ignored, which is the forge's own resolution: a repository carrying two has exactly one as far as anybody else is concerned. A directory contributes all of its templates, that being the whole point of the form.

The picker is absent below two: none at all, and one — a repository that has already made the choice, where a picker would only ever say what happened when the dialog opened. "None" is the first row rather than the last, because its position must not depend on how many templates a repository happens to have, and choosing it restores the commits' prefill rather than emptying the box.

The title stays the commits' — a template is a description and says nothing about what to call the thing.

docs.title: A link somebody else can open
docs.text:
A url to a file, at a commit, at the lines that are picked — for pasting into a chat message or a ticket, where it will be read days later by somebody who was not there.

It is keyed to the commit and never to a branch. That is the whole reason it is a verb here rather than something you assemble from the repository's front page: a link naming a branch means a different file every time anybody pushes, and this one goes on meaning the same lines next week.

The shape is the provider's, because GitHub writes #L4-L9 and GitLab writes #L4-9. A forge with no such page leaves the capability false and the verb is absent rather than copying an empty string to the clipboard.

It costs nothing and asks nobody. A link is a string: no request, no token, and it works on a signed-out repository with a remote.

Three verbs because there are three questions: the file header's copies a link to the file as this commit left it, the diff's hunk header copies one to the lines picked, and Blame's copies one to the lines picked there — keyed to the commit the file was read at, resolved from whatever was typed in the revision box, because "HEAD" means a different file every time anybody pushes.

The new side's numbers, and nothing invented. A selection of removals alone has no line to point at in that revision — those lines are in the parent — so it falls back to linking the file rather than pointing somebody at a line number that means something else there.

What was copied is printed for a few seconds rather than toasted, because somebody about to paste a permalink into a channel can see which commit and which lines they are about to claim, which "Copied!" would not tell them.

docs.title: A ticket id, and the page it names
docs.text:
Everything a commit message says about why tends to be one token long — #412, PROJ-88 — and the rest of that reasoning is on a page this app is not.

A rule lives in .git/config, not in the app's settings: which tracker a repository files its work in is a fact about the repository — the same in every checkout of it and for everybody who works on it. Per checkout rather than committed because .git/config is not cloned, which is also what makes a stored rule safe to act on.

The forge supplies one by default, so most repositories need no setup: #123 against whichever tracker hosts the remote. It is a template rather than one url, because an issue link is a rule — something that turns a token in prose into a page — and the shape is the provider's, GitHub writing /issues/123 and GitLab /-/issues/123.

A rule written by hand outranks it, which is why the default is ranked last: a repository whose # means a ticket in somebody else's tracker says so in its own config, and a default that outranked it would be this app overruling a statement somebody made deliberately.

A Jira/Linear-shaped id (ABC-123) is recognised out of the box once it has somewhere to go — matching the shape costs nothing, and what this app cannot do is guess where it points, since the same id means two different companies' trackers. So the shape is built in and the destination is one line you write once. With no destination there is no rule at all rather than a rule with an empty url.

Two things about git's config syntax fail silently and are therefore stated everywhere: # opens a comment there, so an unquoted #([0-9]+) is an empty pattern; and a backslash is an escape, so an unquoted \b is a backspace character. Neither arrives as an error, and the symptom is no link at all — which is exactly what a repository with no rules looks like. Writing a rule from the settings page quotes and escapes it, so the trap stops existing for anything typed there; what the page still draws is which rules are in force, which came from the forge, and which were dropped and why.

Only http and https are allowed, checked on the template before anything is drawn: the answer is handed to the desktop, and a file: or a javascript: there is a different kind of thing entirely. The capture is percent-encoded on the way in, since a loosely written pattern capturing a space is the ordinary way a rule produces something that is not a url.

docs.title: Somebody else's Markdown
docs.text:
A proposal's description, a review's body and a comment on a line are all prose somebody typed into a forge, and one component draws all of them.

Images are stripped before the text is parsed, and this is not a nicety: Qt's Markdown renderer loads images and has no switch for turning that off, so an ![](https://…) in somebody else's description would make opening the panel a read receipt delivered to whoever wrote it, from a private repository, with your address on it. A line saying an image was there replaces it — refusing to fetch and refusing to say anything are different things. A badge is a linked image, so the picture goes and the link stays.

Blocks rather than one text item, because Qt's importer gives a paragraph no margin at all and there is no property for block spacing — so a description of any length reads as one wall. The source is cut into top-level blocks and the layout puts the space between them, which is also what lets a fenced block sit on a ground of its own.

The splitting is conservative on purpose: a fence is atomic, a loose list stays one block (cutting at the blanks would make each fragment its own list and restart the numbering at 1), and a construct it does not recognise is passed through whole. Nothing is dropped, and a test walks the input back out of the blocks.

A numbered list that does not start at 1 cannot interrupt a paragraph, which is CommonMark rather than a Qt fault and is the single commonest way a description renders wrongly: somebody writes a sentence and then a list beginning "2.", and the whole thing comes out as a run-on paragraph with the numbers inline. A blank line is inserted.

A GFM table is laid out here, because Qt parses one and will not draw it — every column collapsed to the width of its own content with no padding, readable only by somebody who already knows how many columns there are. The parse is bounded at where the pipes fall: a cell's content is handed back as Markdown for the renderer to draw inline, so emphasis, code spans and links go on being somebody else's parser's business. The overflow is the table's own rather than the panel's, so one wide table in the middle of a proposal does not put a horizontal scroll bar under the whole of it.

docs.title: History, graph and search
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. The walk, the graph, the search, blame, file history and comparing two refs are free. A permalink is forge-links, the proposal and CI columns are forge, and bisecting from a commit is bisect. What a licence adds

The graph on the left, a commit's message, files and diff on the right, and a search box that narrows the walk rather than the rows on screen.

docs.title: The surface opens where you are
docs.text: On your own branch's tip rather than at the top of the list, with that commit selected so its files and its diff are already on screen. The list positions there once, when it is first filled for this repository — doing it on every refresh would drag the view back after every staged hunk, and moving a list somebody is reading is worse than opening in the wrong place. Nothing is hidden by it: the newer rows are one scroll up.

docs.title: Lane 0 is the branch you are on
docs.text:
Lanes used to be handed out in the order commits came off the walk, which is by time across every ref — so which branch got the leftmost column depended on who had pushed most recently, and your own branch wandered between columns from one refresh to the next. That is the one lane worth being able to find without reading it, because a graph is scanned down a column.

A colour belongs to a lane, not to a column. When the colour was the column, a recycled column handed its colour to whatever branch took it next, so a thread you were following changed colour at the row where an unrelated branch ended — and the trunk's colour was whichever column it landed in, so "which branch does work land on", the one question a graph answers without a label being read, was answered differently from one refresh to the next.

Colour nought is now reserved for the default branch and handed to nothing else, from the row where the trunk's tip is drawn and down: above that row those commits are the branch that is ahead of the trunk, and colouring them as the trunk claims the thing the graph is there to disprove.

The ref chips wear that colour, so a branch's pill and the column its commits are drawn in are one thing rather than two — with the hue driving the ground and the border while the label stays the ordinary ink, because a lane colour is tuned to be a stroke on the window and asking it to be small text over a wash of itself is a second job it cannot do. A tag keeps its outline, so a tag and a branch at one commit are not the same object with only the name to tell them apart.

Chips are drawn before the subject, in the same column. They spent a while as a column of their own after it, on the argument that the subject should start in the same place on every row — which is true and cost more than it bought: a chip at the end of a line whose subject had already elided into the gap sat inches from the commit it labels.

docs.title: Six search scopes
docs.text:
Any field is the default and is the union of the rest — and it tries the cheap fields first, so a hit on message, author or hash costs nothing extra and skips the diff entirely. Only a commit none of them match is diffed, and paths and content are then checked off a single diff.

Scope Matches Message subject and body Author name or address Hash full or abbreviated Path files the commit touched Content text on added or removed lines — git's log -G Issue a ticket id one of your link rules recognises, or the url it points at

Content matches changed lines only, which is -G rather than -S: a commit that merely sits near the text did not change it.

Every match says why it is in the list, when the reason is not already on screen — the body line, the path, the changed line. The row renders only a subject, so a match against the message body reads as a match against nothing without it.

docs.title: The search is batched and abandonable
docs.text:
Doing it synchronously froze the window: on a 4000-commit repository with thousand-line files a content search blocks for ~2.3 s, and since changing the scope re-ran it, clicking through the chips meant six of those back to back.

Each batch runs to a time budget rather than a commit count, because what a commit costs varies by orders of magnitude between comparing a field and diffing a large file. Measured, that holds the longest freeze at 11–14 ms on both a light and a heavy repository.

Starting a search cancels whatever was running; Stop keeps what has already been found. It stops after 5000 commits and says so, since even responsive scanning has to end somewhere.

docs.title: The same question is answered once
docs.text:
A refresh runs after every staged hunk, on every working-tree event, and whenever the window comes back to the foreground. Each of those used to re-run the whole walk — or the search — from the first commit, which is what people saw as the list flicking, and what threw away a search that had been running for several seconds.

The walk is a pure function of the refs, HEAD and the narrowing, so an unchanged reading is an unchanged answer and there is nothing to do. Three skips follow:

  • A question already answered serves the list it has.
  • A question already being answered is left running.
  • A question you stopped is left stopped — pressing Stop is an instruction, and a refresh that changes nothing has no standing to overrule it.

Search is its own verb for exactly that reason: after a Stop the query is unchanged, so pressing Search used to do nothing whatever.

docs.title: Filters, which compose with the search
docs.text:
The scope sits against the search field with no gap, because "search the messages for X" is one question and it used to take reading a placeholder, finding the matching chip on a row of its own below, pressing it, and then typing.

Three more are folded behind one chip that carries how many of them are in force. That count is not decoration and is the whole reason folding them is safe: a narrowing nobody can see is indistinguishable from a repository with nothing in it. The section also opens by itself whenever the count is above zero.

  • Author — name or address, anywhere in either. Not the same thing as the Author scope, which decides what the query is matched against and can only be one thing at a time; the filter is what makes "content search for foo, by kate" askable.
  • A period — two dates, typed or picked. The committer's time is what is compared, because that is what git log --since compares and what the row beside it draws; filtering on the author's date while printing the committer's would put a rebased commit outside a period its own row says it is inside.
  • Signature — any, signed, not signed, signed with a key. A filter rather than a seventh scope, because "does it carry a signature" is a fact about the commit and filing it among the scopes made it exclusive with searching the message — and left the commonest reading of it, "which of these did nobody sign", unaskable at all.

Everything is filtered during the walk, so the ref filters, the query and these compose: narrowing to a branch narrows the search with it. That also means a period can make the walk cross a hundred thousand commits to reach a fortnight in 2019, which is exactly the shape that must be abandonable.

Both the author and signer pickers are filled from what the walk scanned rather than from what it kept — built from the matches, narrowing to kate would leave kate as the only suggestion, so the field would stop suggesting the moment it was used.

Nothing here is persisted: a period restored on launch hides most of the history behind a control nobody remembers setting.

The empty state names which narrowing emptied the list — the author and both ends, with "anyone", "the first commit" and "today" standing in for the ends that are not bounded. "No matches" reads as a repository with nothing in it.

docs.title: The walk is batched too
docs.text:
Unbounded, linear, and most of a second at thirty thousand commits — on the thread that draws. It is batched now, with one budget spent before returning, so almost every repository anybody opens is complete when the surface asks, with its graph in hand and no flicker through an empty list on the way to a full one. A large one has done exactly one budget's work and yielded.

The lane pass is deliberately not batched: it needs the whole list, so running it per batch would be quadratic in the size of the history. The graph is drawn only once it is ready — a graph over a growing list would show connections to commits that are not on screen, which is why a filtered list draws no graph either.

docs.title: What a commit row says
docs.text:
The subject, and up to five more columns you can switch off individually. Two of them are worth explaining:

The proposal is a number the forge wrote into its own merge or squash subject, naming a page this window already draws — so pressing it goes to the Pull requests surface rather than out to a browser. A commit that landed by fast-forward or rebase carries no number anywhere, which is a blank rather than a guess (drawn as nothing rather than as a dash, which reads like a value), and where the subject cannot say, the forge is asked — a request per commit, spent lazily as rows scroll past, with a cap, and answered from the cache thereafter. A negative answer is stored too, because "this commit went through no proposal" is a real answer and the commonest one on a branch anybody pushes to directly.

The ticket is somebody else's system, and opens there. A number in ordinary prose is deliberately not read as a proposal: #142 in a subject somebody typed is a ticket, and matching it as a proposal would put a link to the wrong system on half the rows.

The column set is stored as the off list, because an enabled-list cannot tell "nobody has chosen" from "everything is switched off" — and a column added by a later build would be hidden by an enabled-list written before it existed, silently, on exactly the machines that have been running longest. The ticks live on the History page, where the width each column costs is in front of you.

Rows are tight by default, and the roomier reading is a preference: a history is the one list somebody scans thousands of rows of looking for one, so how many fit on a screen is most of what makes that quick.

docs.title: A commit's contents
docs.text:
Selecting a commit reads what it changed — the file list, then the one file being read — on demand, once per selection, because History is thousands of rows and none of it is worth knowing until a row is chosen.

A commit is diffed against its first parent. For a merge that means the side it brought in, which is what git show prints and the only reading with a per-hunk shape; a root commit is diffed against the empty tree.

The message sits above the file list in a fixed-width column, capped and scrollable rather than elided. It used to elide on the last line that fitted, which said there was more and offered no way to reach it: the one place in the app that draws a whole commit body could not be used to read one, and the message that happened to be cut is exactly the one worth reading — the one whose author had something to explain.

docs.title: The commit menu
docs.text: Right-click, or the ⋮. Reset, detach, restore a file, revert, cherry-pick, rebase onto this, bisect from here, reword, edit, a permalink, a patch, notes, "Explain this commit", "Changelog since this", and open on the forge.

docs.title: Blame
docs.text:
Per-line, with the file's revision list beside it. A plain click picks the line and lights the commit that last touched it; ⇧-click extends the range and leaves the commit alone, because somebody selecting fourteen lines is not asking to relight the graph fourteen times.

A blame survives a refresh. It used to be cleared outright, and the complaint that ended that was exact: open a file in Blame, click away to another application, come back, and the panel was empty. Nothing about the window regaining focus changes who last touched a line. What actually invalidates an annotation is HEAD moving, so that is what re-blames it — and it re-asks for the revision as it was asked for, because somebody who opened HEAD means "as it stands now" and re-blaming the sha HEAD was would pin the panel to a commit that has since been rewritten.

docs.title: File history
docs.text:
"What happened to this file", which is the question next to Blame's and not the same one: blame says who last touched each line as the file stands now, and is therefore silent about a change that was later overwritten and about the day the file was moved.

Reached from a file row's menu on Changes, or by name from the palette.

The tracked path moves as the walk goes back, and that is why every row carries its own. Rename detection is paid for at the one step where a rename can be found, and from there down the file answers to its old name — so the row that moved it prints both names with an arrow between them, and the diff beside it says that a first-parent diff of the new path necessarily reads as an add. A list whose paths silently change halfway down reads as a bug in the list.

Most commits are answered without a diff at all: the commit's blob id for the tracked path is compared against each parent's, and one that matches any of them is skipped. That is git's own history simplification, and it is why a merge that took one side's copy is absent — the commit on that side did the work and the walk reaches it anyway.

An empty answer says which one it is: no repository, an unborn HEAD, a path nothing has ever held, a walk stopped at its limit, a walk cancelled. None of them is an error, because none of them is a failure, and rendering "the path is misspelt" the same way as "still going" is how a reader learns not to believe a surface.

docs.title: Where change has landed in a file
docs.text:
A strip beside the file history, banded top to bottom, each band the count of commits whose diff touched that part of the file. It answers "does change cluster at the top, the middle or the end", which a list of commits cannot show.

It is a proportion and never a line number

Line 40 in a commit from 2019 is not line 40 today, and following a line forward through every subsequent change is what blame does at blame's price. So a hunk is banded against the length of the file as it stood in that commit, and the sentence under the strip is not optional — a strip drawn beside a list of commits is read as line numbers by everybody unless something says otherwise.

The hunk ranges are free; the denominator is a blob read per commit, which is exactly the cost a batched walk exists to refuse. So the banding sits behind a control that prints the price, and it publishes once rather than as it goes: a distribution over the first tenth of a history is not "the distribution so far", it is a different number that would move under you. For the same reason cancelling keeps nothing.

docs.title: Comparing two refs
docs.text:
The Compare surface, reached by name. It answers "what lies between these two", and its whole design follows from the fact that the question has two answers and they are routinely confused:

  • A..B diffs the two trees as they stand.
  • A...B diffs from the merge base of A and B to B.

On a branch that is merely ahead they agree, which is why the confusion survives — the difference is invisible until the day it matters, and then it says a branch deleted a file it never touched.

The label is the feature, and it is computed beside the trees that were actually diffed, so a label composed somewhere else cannot drift from what is on screen. A mislabelled diff is worse than no diff, because both readings render as something plausible and neither announces itself.

Both commit lists are read in both readings: in two dots the left-only commits are the ones whose work shows up as removals; in three dots they are exactly what is being ignored. One list would have made the distinction invisible again at the one place somebody is trying to learn it.

Three dots across histories that never met has nothing to diff from, so it is refused by name and points at the other reading — rendering an empty file list there would say "these two agree", which is the one conclusion somebody will act on and the opposite of the truth. Two dots is unaffected, and says so without it being an error.

From the page you can write a patch in the reading on screen, or open a proposal with the left as the base and the right as the head.

docs.title: The reflog
docs.text:
Every ref update git makes is journalled, and that journal is the only record of a commit nothing points at any more. It is therefore the answer to "I have just lost an hour of work", and the reason a hard reset is survivable at all.

The claim other clients make here is false

Tower sells "Undo everything", one keystroke, no qualifications. The reflog records refs, not files. A commit that left a branch is still in the object database and can be reached again; an uncommitted edit that reset --hard wrote over was never in an object at all. A button that cannot tell those apart is at its most confident exactly when it is most wrong, because it is pressed at the moment the work was destroyed.

So the surface prints two sentences and never merges them — the commits come back, the working tree does not — and the verb is "Put HEAD back", not "Undo".

The mode is always mixed and is not a parameter: soft would leave the index holding the tree of the commit you are walking away from, which reads as a pile of staged changes nobody asked for; hard would overwrite the working tree, which is the one thing no reflog can give back.

An emptiness has three causes and they are not the same news — a ref with no history, a journal pruned to nothing, and reflogs being switched off in config. Only the third means there is no undo here and there will not be one later either.

refs/stash has a reflog too, and so does every local branch. All of them are listed and any can be read, because the entry explaining where a branch went is in the branch's own log when the move was made from another worktree. Only HEAD's entries are restorable — moving somebody else's ref from a log viewer is a branch write.

docs.title: Git LFS
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Pointers, the probe, fetch, checkout and the locks. What a licence adds

A path matched by a filter=lfs attribute is committed as a pointer — three or four lines naming an object stored somewhere else — and the real content is fetched separately. Everything here follows from that one sentence: a diff of a pointer is not a diff of the file, a checkout that never fetched holds pointers rather than content, and a row that says nothing about it is a row claiming a 40 MB video is a 130-byte text file.

docs.title: Reading needs no git-lfs; writing does
docs.text:
Whether a path is LFS-managed is answered through libgit2 reading the same .gitattributes git reads, with the same precedence and the same subdirectory rules. That is worth having for its own sake — a reimplemented glob matcher is one more thing to be subtly wrong about — and it is worth more for what it buys: every reading feature works on a machine with no git-lfs installed at all.

Only the verbs that move objects need the program. With none, the tab draws the state and the sentence rather than controls that cannot work.

docs.title: A pointer is the whole format, never its first line
docs.text: The cheap test — "the first line mentions git-lfs" — would draw a document about LFS as a file whose content is missing. So a pointer must be a version line first, then key/value lines with an oid and a size among them and nothing that is not a line of that shape, bounded at 1 kB: a pointer is small by definition, and reading a gigabyte to find out it is not one is the cost being avoided.

docs.title: In the diff
docs.text:
The pointer question is asked before the binary one, because a pointer is text — the binary tests both say no, and libgit2 produces a perfectly good three-line diff of oid sha256:… under the name of a file you believe you are looking at. Nothing about that reading is broken, which is what makes it worse than a failure.

The entry carries the size the pointer names rather than the pointer's own hundred-odd bytes: reporting a replaced video as a forty-byte change is the wrong number drawn in the right place.

One side not being a pointer is its own piece of news. A file moved into LFS and one taken out of it each get their own sentence rather than both reading as "the object changed" — those are the two changes somebody is most likely to be looking for an explanation of.

docs.title: On a file row
docs.text:
Three answers and not two:

(nothing) LFS does not manage this path LFS The real file is here LFS ↓ This is still a pointer — the objects were never fetched

"This is not an LFS file" and "this is an LFS file that is not here" are opposite pieces of news, and a boolean draws them alike. It is a word rather than a tint, because colour is never the only channel and here the two states it can be in are ones no amount of tinting separates for somebody who has not been told there are two.

It is asked per row, which is affordable because the list is virtualised: only a screenful of rows exists at a time.

docs.title: Fetch and check out are two verbs and never one
docs.text:
A fetch fills the local object store and leaves every file exactly as it was, so somebody who ran only that would see nothing change and reasonably conclude it had not worked; a checkout writes only what has already been fetched. Folding them into one control would make the cheap local step inherit the expensive network one's failure mode — which is the argument the submodule tab's Init and Update already make.

Neither is ever automatic. An LFS fetch is a transfer of possibly several gigabytes, and nothing here spends that because a surface was opened.

Both are absent with no git-lfs, and the sentence under the list says which half is missing rather than reading as "LFS does not work here".

docs.title: Tracking a pattern
docs.text:
The exact line is on screen before it is written, and the file is appended to — so a comment, a section or an order somebody chose cannot be lost to a rewrite even in principle. The line ending is copied from what the file already uses, a missing final newline is made good in front of the new line, and the whole thing is taken back out if it did not land in full.

Untracking appends too, and this is where the app deliberately does something other than git-lfs. git lfs untrack deletes the line, and deleting a line means rewriting the file — which is exactly what the append-only rule exists to protect against. Within one .gitattributes a later line overrides an earlier one per attribute, so <pattern> -filter -diff -merge is git's own spelling for "stop applying that".

The cost is stated rather than hidden: the file grows, and both lines are visible in it. So the list reads the order — the last mention of a pattern decides — and a superseded row is still listed, saying "no longer applied", because it is there and a list that dropped it would be describing a file you can open.

That is also why lfs track has a printed git command and untracking has none: git lfs untrack does something else, and printing it would teach a command that produces a different file.

Tracking needs no git-lfs and the two object verbs do, so the Track button is drawn whatever the probe said. A repository can perfectly well declare its LFS patterns on a machine that cannot yet move the objects, and refusing to let it would be this app deciding what may be installed tomorrow.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
Read from the server, so they are asked for and never guessed at — and read only when you press Read locks, which is the fetch's rule for the same reason. An empty map draws no badge rather than "nothing is locked": those are different claims and only one is knowable without asking. The state is idle / reading / ready / failed, because an empty map means all four otherwise.

The verifying form of the listing is used rather than the plain one, and the difference is the whole feature: the plain listing carries an owner's name, which is not the question — two people can share a display name, and "is this mine" is what decides whether a verb is offered at all.
