The verifying form answers two arrays, and which array an entry is in is the only thing that says whose a lock is. A server that will not verify is a failure with a sentence rather than a column of rows nobody can act on.

Somebody else's lock is refused, and there is no force. git lfs unlock --force exists and is deliberately never passed: a lock is a claim somebody made about work they are doing, and an app that makes breaking it as easy as honouring it has implemented the opposite of the feature. The refusal names who, since "it is locked" leaves you nowhere to go and "kate holds it" tells you what to do — and the menu row is absent rather than refusing, because what you see instead is her name on the row itself.

docs.title: A patch of LFS files says so before it is sent
docs.text:
What travels in a patch is the pointer rather than the content, so it applies cleanly on the far machine and leaves somebody with a hundred and thirty bytes of metadata naming an object they may not have — a patch that "worked" and produced no picture.

Every patch route inherits a count and a sentence naming what the recipient will still need. It is a note and never a refusal: the patch is valid, the button stays live, and what is wrong with it is on the other machine.

docs.title: The fleet says nothing about LFS, and that is a decision
docs.text:
What was asked for is a card that reports a checkout with unfetched objects, and the answer cannot be had from what a fleet summary already reads: "still a pointer" is a file read per managed path, per repository, across every repository in the fleet. That is exactly the cost the fleet page is designed to refuse.

The tempting substitute is worse than the absence: a root .gitattributes naming filter=lfs is cheap, and it answers "this project uses LFS" — which is not the question. Drawn as an LFS badge on a card, it would be read as "something here needs fetching", which is true of a checkout that has never fetched and false of every properly checked-out one, with no way to tell from the card which kind you are looking at. A badge that is right by coincidence on some cards is worse than no badge.

The figure lives on Manage's LFS tab, where you have asked about one repository and the walk is affordable.

docs.title: With no git-lfs, a commit warns and is allowed
docs.text:
That is git's own behaviour and this app does not improve on it: with the filter absent, git writes the file's content whole where a pointer should have gone. Refusing would be this client inventing a rule git does not have.

What it must not do is repeat git's silence, because the result is a commit that looks right, pushes, and has to be rewritten — so the warning says what was written and what it will cost, and it warns afterwards, because that is when it is true.

docs.title: What the git directory is made of
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. The breakdown and all nine verbs. What a licence adds

Manage → Maintenance is a breakdown of .git — where the bytes are, how many objects are loose, what is reclaimable — and nine verbs that change it.

It exists because the two questions a reader actually has are "why is this checkout four gigabytes" and "is there anything safe I can press about it", and the usual answer is a command somebody found on the internet, run in a terminal, whose destructive half is indistinguishable from its harmless half at a glance.

docs.title: The breakdown reads with no git at all
docs.text:
The walk is of the directory itself, so it works on a machine with no git command line — which is the ordinary state of somebody who has only ever used this app.

Part What it is Reclaimable Loose objects One file per object, before anything packs them yes Packs The packed object database yes Reflogs Where HEAD and every branch have been yes LFS The local LFS cache — drawn only where it holds something no Worktrees Linked worktrees' admin directories no Submodules Submodules' whole object databases no Other Refs, the index, config, hooks, everything else no

The total is the directory's own size, not the sum of the rows, and Other closes the gap — so a part this app does not know about is reported rather than silently dropped. Anybody comparing this page against du has to get the same number or the page is worthless, and a test asserts the two agree.

A count of — is not a count of zero. A pack directory holding no packs and a directory whose files nobody counts are different facts, and "0 files" beside a row holding 40 KiB reads as a bug.

It is asked for rather than refreshed: a stat per loose object is tens of thousands of them on an unpacked repository, so arriving on the tab takes the reading, exactly as Blame and the metrics page are asked for. It is dropped when you change repository, a breakdown of the previous one drawn under this one's name being a claim rather than an answer.

docs.title: The verbs need git, and say so rather than disappearing
docs.text:
libgit2 has no gc, no repack, no prune and no maintenance — not reduced versions of them, none of them. So every verb runs git, and where there is no git the controls are drawn, disabled, with the sentence that says why.

That is the one exception to absent rather than greyed: the refusal is about this machine rather than about the verb, and a page that vanished would leave a reader with no way to discover the feature exists or what it needs.

Verb Runs What it loses Run maintenance git maintenance run Nothing Write a commit graph git commit-graph write --reachable Nothing Collect garbage git gc Unreachable objects older than two weeks Repack git repack -a -d --depth=250 --window=250 Nothing Aggressive gc git gc --aggressive The same as gc, slowly Prune git prune Every unreachable object Expire the reflogs git reflog expire --expire=now --all Every reflog entry Start background maintenance git maintenance start Nothing Stop background maintenance git maintenance stop Nothing

Run maintenance is the primary button, and that is a recommendation rather than a layout decision. It is git's own modern answer — an incremental repack, a commit graph, a loose-object pass — and the only one here you can press without first having to think about what is reachable.

Writing a commit graph is on this page because this app benefits from it. Every history walk, every ahead/behind, every merge base and the whole lane pass are commit-graph traversals, and a written graph file makes all of them dramatically cheaper. It is the one verb whose benefit is to this program rather than to the repository in general.

Aggressive gc is offered and is not recommended, and the page says so. It recomputes every delta with a much larger window, takes minutes to hours on a large repository, and is worth running roughly once — after an import, a filter-repo, or a clone of something with a pathological history. Repack with an explicit depth and window is the same thing done deliberately and without the pruning, and the numbers are git's own documented recommendation for that case rather than a guess.

The two destructive verbs are offered because the alternative is worse. Expiring the reflogs and then pruning is how anybody actually reclaims space after deleting a large file from history, and a maintenance page that could not do it would send you to a terminal. Each asks first, and each confirmation names what stops being recoverable — the reflog being the one thing standing between you and a branch you deleted, which is why prune's own sentence says to press it after expiring and not before.

Background maintenance is two verbs rather than a toggle, whose label would claim a state. And the state is read from git's own global config, where git maintenance start writes it, rather than remembered here: somebody who ran the command in a terminal is told the truth rather than this app's opinion.

docs.title: What the panel says after a run
docs.text:
The size is measured before the run rather than read off the last walk, or pressing "Measure again" in between would show a difference against the wrong baseline.

The figure is signed, and that is not pedantry: writing a commit graph and running maintenance routinely make the directory larger — they write a file — and a figure clamped at zero would report "reclaimed nothing" for an operation that did exactly what it was asked to.

One at a time. A second run is refused while one is in flight, which is the refusal the transport lock makes one layer along and for the same reason: two gits writing one object database.

Every run gets a row in the operation log with the command you would have typed. None of them offers a way back, and that is stated rather than left to be discovered — what a gc reclaimed is gone.

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
A real git gc against a real repository is what proves the command reaches git, that the size is taken again and that the log gets a row. What is deliberately not asserted is that the repository got smaller: a three-commit fixture has almost nothing to pack, and a test demanding a number go down is one that fails on a repository that was already tidy.

The three destructive verbs are never run in the suite. Prune and reflog expire against a fixture would prove nothing the plan does not already say, and aggressive gc takes long enough that it has no business in a test run.

docs.title: Merging and conflicts
docs.text: Licensing — Free. Unconditionally, licence or no licence — a merge run at a command line can drop anybody onto the Conflicts surface, and every way out of a stopped operation is refused to the licence check before the table is even read. What a licence adds

docs.title: Merge
docs.text:
Entered from a commit that carries a local branch — the row is absent for a bare sha, because the dialog chooses from the branch lists and prints a verdict about a named ref, and a merge of a commit nothing points at records a merge with no name in it.

The analysis decides, and the controller only carries out the answer. git's merge analysis is asked first, every time, because the three answers it gives are three different operations and confusing them is how a client earns a reputation for doing something other than what it said:

Analysis What happens Up to date Nothing is written, and it is reported as the no-op it is — "merged" and "there was nothing to merge" reading the same is the whole complaint Fast-forward The ref moves and no commit is taken — unless --no-ff was asked for, or the repository's own merge.ff = false asked for it Normal The index is written, and it stops

Stopping is the design, not an unfinished path. A merge that has written the index and gone no further is a stopped operation: it is in the banner on every surface, the fleet card carries it, and it survives quitting the app.

MERGE_HEAD is the authority for that, not the app's own state file — a merge begun on the command line has to appear here and one finished there has to stop appearing. The file only carries what git records nowhere: the name that was typed and the commit HEAD was on.

It refuses over the files it is actually going to write, which is the intersection of what is dirty with what they changed since the histories parted. Not "the tree is dirty" — merging with work in progress is the ordinary case — and not libgit2's own refusal either, which knows how many paths are in the way but will not name one.

abortMerge() is never gated on anything: it works on a merge this app never started, with the state file deleted underneath it, and after a restart. HEAD does not move during a merge, so putting it back is a hard reset to the commit the merge began on, followed by the cleanup call that actually ends the state — without which MERGE_HEAD outlives the abort and every reader goes on believing a merge is running.

Committing refuses while anything is still conflicted, by path, because a commit taken there carries conflict markers into history — the single outcome this whole surface exists to prevent.

docs.title: The Conflicts surface
docs.text:
Opens by itself when something stops on one, and it does not care what stopped: a merge, a cherry-pick, a rebase and git am all leave their conflicts in the index's higher stages, which is what this reads.

Each conflicted file is re-merged in diff3 style and the marker output is parsed back into hunks, which is what yields each side's lines separately rather than one blob of marker text.

Three columns, equal thirds, and no splitter handle. Equal thirds are what makes three readings comparable; a handle would be an invitation to make one of them unreadable.

Choices live in memory until you write. Unresolved hunks keep their markers, so a partial resolution is still a readable file.

Stage all resolved is one operation rather than a loop — it used to re-merge every conflicted file per press, which is a quadratic number of three-way merges on exactly the repositories that have hundreds of conflicts because a big rebase just produced them.

The whole surface is free, unconditionally

A merge run at the command line can drop somebody onto it, and a licence that lapsed overnight must not leave anybody unable to finish. Continuing or aborting a rebase, a merge, a cherry-pick or a bisect, and every verb on this surface, are free and cannot be gated — enforced by a rule that refuses those ids ahead of the feature table, rather than by leaving them out of it.

docs.title: Your own merge tool
docs.text:
The built-in three-way resolution is and stays the default: it is on a surface of this app's own, it works with nothing installed, and every choice it makes is visible before anything is written. What it is not is kdiff3, and somebody with fifteen years of muscle memory in a merge tool is not helped by being told to learn a new one.

So there is a second verb beside it, and the surface draws both.

git's own configuration comes first. merge.tool and diff.tool name a tool; mergetool.<name>.cmd and difftool.<name>.cmd say how to run it. Those are already on the machine of everybody who uses a merge tool at all, and reading them is what stops this app disagreeing with git mergetool about what happens when the same button is pressed on the same repository. A setting of the app's own would be a second place for one answer to live.

The fallback is a template in the settings, and the row says which of the two answered — a field with something in it that is being ignored is the one state that row must not be silent about. A tool named with no .cmd beside it (merge.tool = vimdiff) is git's built-in table of known tools, which this app does not carry, so it falls through to the template rather than claiming git's answer for a command git never named.

It is not discovered, unlike the editor and terminal. Those take a path as an ordinary argument, so the first one present is a safe guess. A merge tool takes four paths in an order that differs per tool, and guessing at an argument order would open somebody else's changes as if they were your own.

A command needing a shell is refused rather than half-run. git runs a .cmd through sh -c; this does not, because the value is executed and here it comes out of a repository somebody may have cloned. The check removes the four placeholders first, which is not a detail — $ is a shell metacharacter and every valid .cmd is full of it, so against the raw string it rejected kdiff3 $BASE $LOCAL $REMOTE -o $MERGED, the example in git's own manual.

The three sides are files, because a merge tool takes files. Stages 1, 2 and 3 are written to a scratch directory outside the repository — or they would turn up in git status as three files nobody wrote — and $MERGED is the working tree's own file, markers and all. That is git mergetool's arrangement, and it is why nothing here reads the tool's output: what the tool writes lands where you can see it, and the existing Stage button takes it.

A conflict with no common ancestor — two files added independently on the two sides — has no stage 1, and $BASE is then an empty file rather than a missing path: every merge tool copes with an empty base and none of them copes with an argument that is not there.

The button is absent when nothing is configured, because there is genuinely no program to run.

docs.title: A suggested fourth side
docs.text:
Where a model is configured, a resolution can be asked for per hunk and is drawn as a fourth readable column beside ours, base and theirs. Choosing it is the same gesture that chooses one of the other three.

The controller knows nothing about where a side came from: making a suggestion available and choosing it are two different calls, and "suggested" is refused for a hunk that has none — a choice naming an absent side would write an empty region under a decision you believed you had made.

A model is allowed to refuse, and is told that refusing is a good answer: where the two sides make genuinely incompatible decisions there is no fourth side and the hunk says so. That is what keeps a confident wrong merge from being the only thing this can produce.

The whole-file verb offers a side per unresolved hunk and chooses none of them, so the file is still read hunk by hunk afterwards — the press that skips the reading cannot also skip the review. One file, never the set: a request per hunk across every conflicted file is a bill nobody agreed to.

See Asking a model for the gate, the providers and what is unverified.

Auto-resolving the mechanical cases is not in scope

GitKraken does it. Doing it requires trusting a classifier about which conflicts are mechanical, and the failure mode is silent by construction: a conflict resolved without being shown is one nobody reads, so a classifier that is wrong one time in fifty produces a commit nobody can tell from the other forty-nine.

Everything else in this app that writes says what it is about to do first, and this is the one verb where the whole point would be not saying.

docs.title: Repository metrics
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. This page is metrics. What a licence adds

What the history and the forge say about a repository, over a period you choose. No desktop client in the comparison has anything like it; this is normally a separate SaaS product.

docs.title: Four tabs, and the order is an argument
docs.text:
History, People, Flow, CI — and History is the tab that opens.

Every tool in this space that earned a bad reputation earned it by making a per-developer table its front page. Grouping this page into tabs was the chance to promote a leaderboard to a landing page, and it was not taken: everything that names a person is behind the second tab under the sentence about what a line count measures, and the ranked list is still last inside it. A test requires that the tab which opens draws no card naming a person.

The groups are cut by what a figure is about rather than by where it came from, which is why two of them mix the commit graph and the forge: "You, in this history" and "You, against the rest" are one question asked of two sources, and filing them apart to keep the sources tidy would be tidying the wrong thing.

The window control stays above the tabs, because the period bounds every group and a window that jumped between tabs would make four readings out of one.

docs.title: The window is two shapes, and they are not sugar for one another
docs.text:
A preset is "the last N days" and slides with the clock.

A custom period is two dates and does not. Somebody who picks 1 January to 31 March and comes back in June is asking about the first quarter, not about "the ninety days ending ninety days ago" — so the pair is stored as it was chosen and reopens meaning what it meant. Storing it as offsets would have kept one representation and moved the period every night, which is the sort of thing you discover by disbelieving a number you were right about last week.

The far end is inclusive of the whole day: a period naming its last day and then excluding it is the off-by-one nobody would think to check.

The period bounds both halves. The page used to carry a sentence saying its two halves covered different spans — a caption apologising for the one fault a single window control exists to prevent. Two things about the far end are load-bearing:

  • A commit newer than it is skipped and never a reason to stop. The walk is newest-first, so a period in the past is reached only by crossing everything above it, and treating those as "out of window" would end the walk on its first commit and report an empty repository.
  • Crossing thousands of commits to reach a period is the state a batched walk can look hung in, so the count of what was passed over is published and the reading state says it — and if the walk gives up at its limit before arriving, that count is the whole explanation rather than "no commits in this window", which would be reporting an absence of knowledge as a measurement.

Dates are typed or picked. The calendar's day cells register no keyboard entry — forty-two entries reading "17" would spend the alphabet twice over on a target that is not nameable without its month — and the keyboard route to a date is the field beside the grid.

docs.title: From the history
docs.text:
Commit size, cadence, where change lands, how thinly knowledge is spread, and who did it.

Counting lines means diffing every commit against its parent, which makes it the most expensive read in the app — so the walk is batched against a time budget, is cancellable, stops at a limit and says so, and is outside the general refresh.

Figures are published once, when the walk ends. A median over the first tenth of a walk is not "the median so far", it is a different number that moves under you.

Two things are counted the way they are because the alternative is how a line count usually lies:

  • A merge is counted and never diffed, so nobody is credited with the branch they merged.
  • Renames are exact-match-only, so a directory move is not two hundred lines of work.

The mean sits beside a median and a p90, which is also the honest answer to excluding generated files, since nothing in a repository reliably declares them.

docs.title: From the forge
docs.text:
Sizes and review timings cost one request per pull request, so they sit behind a button that prints its price before it is pressed. Time open, time to merge, throughput and the revert-based derivation are free off the list already fetched.

Time open is a distribution rather than a mean, because "12 open" and "12 open, oldest 40 days" are different situations.

First review to merge is labelled a wall clock — it holds waiting, further rounds and CI — because calling it "time to address comments" would claim to measure typing.

Opening the page is not a request, and the button means "spend again". A surface is loaded on demand, so nothing it held used to survive walking to History and back; both answers the free half stands on are keyed by the question now, and what is served from disk arrives labelled — "stored, read 14h ago" — because a page of medians is where a stored answer wearing a live one's face would cost the most: nobody re-derives a median in their head to check it.

The read time reported is the oldest of the answers in force, since a figure standing on a list read a minute ago and a run list read yesterday is as old as the older of them.

docs.title: DORA
docs.text:
No figure exists without the definition that produced it. The tile cannot render a number without the sentence, and the definition is computed beside the arithmetic rather than composed by the surface: "lead time: 3.2 days" with nothing saying what counted as a deployment is the number people take into a review meeting and get wrong.

The headline definition is a CI deploy run — a completed run whose name, file or job matches a pattern you set, on the shipping branch — read through a provider-neutral seam, with merges, tags and the forge's own deployments endpoint as fallbacks for a repository whose CI this app cannot see.

Nothing matching is a state rather than a zero: the page names the pattern it looked for and the runs that actually happened.

docs.title: CI health
docs.text:
Six tiles and a per-workflow table, moved here off the Checks surface whole. Those tiles answered a different question from the one that surface is opened with: "is anything broken right now" is a glance at a list, and a success rate over the last hundred runs is something to study — and studying figures is what this page is for. Checks carries a button here rather than a copy, because two drawings of one set of tiles is two chances for one of them to stop agreeing with the list beneath it.

Two things it publishes are worth knowing:

  • The success rate's denominator is the runs that reached a verdict, and the tile names it: a cancelled build is not a failure and a skipped one is not a pass, and dividing by all of them would report a repository that cancels a lot as one that fails a lot.
  • A rate over nothing decided is absent, not zero. "0% passed" and "nothing has finished" are opposite pieces of news, and drawing the second as the first is how a CI page first loses somebody's trust.

The span the figures cover comes back with them, because a rate over what this app fetched is not a rate over the repository and only the arithmetic knows which.

The figures are provider-neutral by construction: they read only the fields the provider seam documents, which is what keeps a tile from quietly disappearing the day a second provider arrives.

docs.title: You, against the rest
docs.text:
The four things asked for here were built, and nothing that argued against them was dropped.

The project's position — that a per-developer leaderboard is how tools in this space earn their reputations, and that per-author review latency beside a name reads as a judgement on the one participant with no influence over their queue — is still true, is still printed, and is now printed beside the figures rather than instead of them. The honest response to being asked for it anyway, with that understood, was to compute it correctly rather than badly or not at all.

Four decisions are the design:

  • Two latencies, never one. The time somebody took to give a review is about them; the time their own proposals waited is about the queue they were in. They are separate measures under separate names, and the table's last column says which of the two it is. Folding them together would name the wrong person for one of them.
  • An absent figure is absent. Every median travels with the count it was taken over, a row without the figure is not in the denominator, and a ranking drops what it cannot compute rather than ranking it last — last place is a claim about somebody and "this was never fetched for you" is not one. Counting a person the sample never reached as a zero would drag the team median towards a number nobody had, which is the most flattering mistake available here.
  • You are inside your own distribution. Excluding yourself would make "the team median" a different population for every reader, and two people comparing notes would disagree about a number they had both read off the same page.
  • Every measure carries the definition that produced it. "Reviews given: 4" is a number about a person; "four of somebody else's proposals had at least one submitted review from them, over the 30 sampled" is a number about the data.

"The team" is every login that authored a proposal or submitted a review in what this app fetched, inside the window — not the repository's collaborators, which nothing here asks for.

The three cards sit at the bottom in increasing order of how easily they are misread: the table of everybody, then you against the distribution, then the ranked list dead last, drawn plainly — no medals, no colour, no "1st" — under a control naming what it ranked by. rank 3 of 9 is a fact about a list; a badge would be a claim about a person.

It costs a request, so it is off by default. A page that spent a request because somebody opened a tab is a page people learn to avoid.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Authors are grouped by lowercased email with every name seen kept beside — one person with three addresses is three rows, and the page says so above the table rather than in a comment, because a half-built identity map merges some duplicates and leaves you believing the rest are real.

A forge login and a commit address are two identities and this app maps neither onto the other. Guessing would merge some people and leave you believing the rest were real — the same argument. So each half says who it is about, in its own vocabulary: the forge half is about a login, and the history half is about this checkout's own user.email, which is the address git will write on the next commit made here. An address with nothing in the window is a state and not a zero.

docs.title: Which figures are computed
docs.text:
The two halves of this page cost wildly different things, and the chooser behind the page's own Figures button is arranged around the costs rather than around the cards: a group is a price.

Group Costs Line counts A patch per changed file per commit Per-path tallies The tallies off the same diff — with both off, no tree-to-tree diff is taken at all, which is the whole saving DORA One request per read for the CI runs Proposal sizes Two per pull request, behind the button that already prints its cost CI health One request, under its own key Cadence, authors, flow, people Free, and the chooser says so in as many words

That honesty is load-bearing: switching the per-path tallies off on their own saves a hash entry per path and nothing else, because the paths come off the diff the line counts already paid for.

A group being off must not be a hidden card over figures that were computed anyway, so the walk really skips the work, the fetch really returns before its requests, and the Measure button really leaves the palette and the hint keys. The enabled set is part of the walk's own result key, because a walk that skipped the patches answered a different question — without that, switching the line counts back on would be served the cheap walk's answer, a page of zeros that "Read again" could not fix either.

The choice is stored as the off list, because an enabled-list cannot tell "nobody has chosen" from "everything is switched off" — and a group added by a later build would be hidden by an enabled-list written before it existed. Every group that already drew something defaults to on.

The ticks live where the price is legible, which is this page; the settings page carries only the reset and a sentence.

docs.title: Patches
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Writing one, the series, and applying somebody else's. What a licence adds

A file for a ticket, a chat message, or another machine — and one coming the other way. This and a permalink are the two things this app produces that leave it, and this is the one that carries the work itself.

docs.title: The shape is git diff, not format-patch
docs.text:
A diff patch is one file describing a state: what is different from something else. A format-patch series is one file per commit, carrying authorship and a message so git am can replay them as commits.

Which one you want follows from what you are sending, and that is why both exist rather than one being a mode of the other: "here is the change, look at it" is a diff, and "here are my four commits, put them on your branch" is a series. A flag would be a file whose shape depended on an argument.

docs.title: Six subjects
docs.text:
From What the patch holds The working tree Everything uncommitted, or only what is staged, or the files you picked A stash Its tree against the commit it was taken from — what git stash show -p prints A branch Against a base you choose, three dots by definition A comparison In the reading on screen, two dots or three A commit git show — the commit against its first parent Held hunks A patch you assembled out of several commits

They are subjects of one dialog rather than six dialogs, because what a patch is of changes and what it costs to write one does not: the plan, the counts, the empty refusal, the path field and the platform's chooser are the same questions whichever subject is in front of them.

docs.title: Everything uncommitted means everything
docs.text:
all is HEAD against the working tree — which is git diff HEAD and not index-to-workdir: the narrower diff omits everything already staged, and a patch of "what I have done" that silently leaves out half of it is the commonest way this would be wrong.

The scope is not remembered between openings: "everything uncommitted" is what the button's words mean, and a narrower scope left on from last time is a patch missing work nobody chose to leave out.

docs.title: Untracked files are a tick, and the count beside it is why
docs.text: git diff does not mention them — they are in no tree to be diffed against — so the honest default omits them, and a patch that quietly leaves out the three files you have just written is the failure this feature would be remembered for. The plan says how many are being left out, which is what makes the tick findable at the moment it matters.

docs.title: Two dots and three dots
docs.text:
A comparison is the one subject where you picked a notation, on a page that names it in git's own spelling — so the patch is taken under that reading and the dialog states it.

The failure this is arranged around

A file labelled A...B that holds A..B applies, backwards and quietly, undoing the base's own newer commits on whatever machine it was sent to.

So the branch route is a separate entry point rather than a flag: its doc comment forbids two dots and it is therefore not reachable with them. The diff itself is built in one private place, so the two routes cannot come to disagree about what a patch of two refs holds, and the plan publishes the notation it was taken under so the dialog reads that rather than keeping a second copy of the flag.

A branch's base defaults to the branch you are standing on. It was the trunk for a while, on the reading that a patch is a thing you send and so wants a base the reader at the other end certainly has — true of that errand, and not of the gesture: the verb is reached from a branch row, and what it is reached for is "what does that branch have that this one does not", asked from the branch it is being asked from. The trunk is one press away in the picker, and the branch's upstream is a third row, which is a trap either way: it is the forge's copy of that same branch, so a patch against it holds only what has not been pushed.

docs.title: A commit's patch drops the authorship, and says so
docs.text: The working tree and a stash have no authorship to drop; a commit does. The dialog says so outright, because that is the fact somebody finds out at the far end otherwise, when whoever applies it commits your work under their own name and words. Replaying a commit verbatim is format-patch and am — a different file format for a different errand.

docs.title: The refusal that matters
docs.text:
An empty patch is refused. git apply accepts a file with nothing in it and reports success, so a patch of no changes is a file that looks like it worked and does nothing wherever it is taken — the worst outcome available here. It is refused in the plan's own sentence, and the button is off before it is pressed.

Beside it: a folder that does not exist is refused rather than created, since a patch is one file you named. The write is atomic, so a failure half way leaves whatever was there rather than a truncated patch — which would be applied.

docs.title: A patch you assemble
docs.text:
The five subjects above are each one question with one answer, and the one thing none of them can say is "these two hunks out of the commit that added it, and the one out of the commit that fixed it".

Hold in a hunk header keeps a hunk back; the set survives walking between commits; and writing it out produces one file. Lazygit's custom patch is the same idea and stops at one commit at a time — the crossing is the whole reason this exists.

Six decisions in it:

  • What is held is the hunk's own patch text, not a coordinate. A (rev, path, index) triple would have to be read again to be written, and the reading depends on the context and whitespace preferences in force at the time — so "the second hunk", picked with three lines of context and written with ten, would be a different second hunk.
  • Only a hunk of a file the commit modified. An added file's patch opens with new file mode, a deleted one with the mirror, and a renamed one names two paths — every one of those a claim about the file rather than the hunk, and none true when only some of the file's hunks were picked. It refuses and points at the whole file's patch, which is what somebody asking about a new file wanted anyway.
  • A path held from more than one commit is a note and not a refusal. Two commits' hunks of one file are measured against two different versions of it, so they do not compose: git apply places the later ones by the lines around them and refuses the whole patch when it cannot, which is the safe failure. What must never happen is this app implying that they compose, so the plan names every such path.
  • The text is checked by git and written as it was assembled. git's own reader is asked first, because text built by hand is exactly the kind that is plausible and wrong — but the parse is a check and not a round trip: a diff parsed from a buffer carries no modes and no object ids, so serialising it back out omits the ---/+++ pair and produces a file that would not parse a second time.
  • The empty patch is refused here too.
  • Nothing is kept between runs. A held set is a scratch buffer somebody fills over a few minutes, and it holds patch text lifted out of commits — content this app has no business writing outside the repository that already holds it. It is dropped when the repository changes.

The Hold button is in the hunk header and asks the controller which diff it is over, so every surface that draws a commit's diff is covered by construction — including the three written before the question existed, and not one surface file changed. It is a toggle rather than Hold beside Drop, it takes the whole hunk and never the line selection the three verbs beside it act on, and it is away while a diff filter is on: what would be held is the text of a diff hiding a re-indent, sent to somebody as though it were the file.

A strip says a patch is half built, because assembling one takes several minutes in several places and something has to be on screen the whole time. It is on the diff panel rather than in the operation banner, which is the doctrinally tidier home and the wrong one: the banner is for an operation that is running or stopped, with a way out that has to be reachable, and nothing here is running.

docs.title: A series
docs.text:
One file per commit, oldest first — and that is not presentation: a series is applied in the order it is written, and every list in this app is newest-first, so a series written that way fails on its second file, asked to lay a commit on one that is not there yet.

A directory rather than a file, which is the one place this verb's shape differs from every other write here: a series is N files and naming one of them would be naming the first. The numbering and the names are git's own — 0001-fix-the-thing.patch — so somebody who has seen a series before knows what these are. There is no -- <version> trailer, which git puts at the foot of each file: it names the git that made it, this is not git, and a version this app is not is a claim rather than a courtesy.

Writing is all or nothing, since half a series applies half a branch. The empty series is refused for the empty patch's reason.

docs.title: Replaying one
docs.text:
The whole series or none of it, and that is where it deliberately differs from git am. That one stops on the file it could not apply and leaves a half-finished operation with its own state files, its own --skip, --continue and --abort, and its own way of being walked away from. This app already carries three such sequencers, each with a banner mode and a stop the Conflicts surface finishes — a fourth is a real feature and not a flag on this one.

So a file that will not apply rewinds to where HEAD was, names the file and why, and what you are left with is exactly what you started with.

That is only honest because it refuses a dirty working tree first, which is load-bearing rather than tidy: the rewind is a hard reset, and one taken over your uncommitted work would destroy the thing this verb was never asked to touch. An unborn HEAD is refused for the mirror reason.

The author is the file's and the committer is this machine's, which is what git am does and what the amend's own rule already argues: who wrote a change and when are facts about the change, and replaying it is not a new authorship. The [PATCH 2/7] marker is stripped from the subject, being the series' and not the message's, and a missing Date: falls back to your own clock rather than refusing. A missing Subject: or From: is refused by name: a directory of patches with one stray file in it is the ordinary way this goes wrong, and a plain diff among them is a patch to apply rather than one to replay.

It is the one entry in this class the log may honestly offer to reverse — the replay wrote commits and nothing else, so a mixed reset leaves the working tree exactly as it went in.

Reachable from no UI yet

The series verbs are implemented and tested and no control opens them. The patch dialog is built around a file field and a single-diff plan, and another subject there means a directory field, a different plan shape and a different set of counts — a restructure rather than a row. It is recorded here rather than left to be discovered, because a verb reachable from nothing reads as done.

docs.title: Applying one somebody else wrote
docs.text:
The other direction, and the only thing in the patch feature that writes to the repository. Apply patch… on Changes.

The plan is the dialog. It runs a real check pass, so what is drawn is a statement about this working tree as it stands rather than a reading of the patch text — the difference between "this patch touches four files" and "this patch will apply". Every file it names is listed, all of them, one elided line each, because a cap with "… and 12 more" hides exactly the paths you are deciding about while the count sits in the sentence above doing the counting. A refusal is drawn instead of the counts rather than beside them.

Nothing is committed, so nothing is confirmed. What it writes lands on Changes to be read and committed or discarded like any other edit, so the way back is the surface you are standing on. The dialog earns its place by describing rather than by asking. The apply is all-or-nothing for libgit2's own reason: it applies deltas one at a time, and a half-applied patch is a state nobody asked for.

The file is read when it is settled, not while it is typed. A missing file reports through the toast, so re-reading per keystroke would fire that toast for every prefix of a path you are halfway through typing. It is read on Enter, on Browse, and on opening with a path already in it.

docs.title: One tick, and two that are absent
docs.text:
--index is offered: apply to the index and the working tree, so what arrives is already staged. Off by default, because the honest reading of "apply this" is that edits arrive where edits arrive.

  • --cached — the index alone — is supported by the controller and not drawn. What it produces is a repository whose index and working tree disagree about every file in the patch, with nothing on Changes saying why: a thing to reach for deliberately at a prompt, not a tick beside a file chooser.
  • -3 is absent because libgit2 cannot do it. Its apply options carry exactly one flag, and there is no option meaning "merge this in where it does not apply cleanly". It could be built by hand — a patch carries index <old>..<new> lines, so where that blob is in this object database the pre-image can be reconstructed and merged — and that is a real feature rather than a flag to pass. A tick that quietly did an ordinary apply would be worse than the absence.

What stands in -3's place is that the refusal names the file whose pre-image did not match, which is what you need in order to go and do it at a prompt.

Its button is not governed by the change count, unlike the Patch button beside it, and that is the one place absent-not-greyed points the other way: a clean working tree is the state a patch is most often applied into, so keying the control to having changes would take it away at exactly the moment it is wanted.

docs.title: Remotes and transport
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Fetch, push, pull and clone, and the credential ladder behind them. What a licence adds

The four verbs that move objects — fetch, push, pull, clone — plus the remotes themselves, one credential ladder, and a background fetch that is off by default.

None of this is the forge integration. Reading pull requests and CI happens over HTTP with a different credential and moves no commits; see Pull requests and CI.

docs.title: One operation at a time, off the interface thread
docs.text:
Each of the four is a single blocking libgit2 call, and each runs on a thread of its own. Two at once is not a slower version of one: it is two remotes on one repository, two threads writing one object database, and two sets of progress figures arriving at one banner.

So there is a lock, and it is on the object that owns both halves of transport rather than on either controller — a lock owned by one of them is a lock the other consults by arrangement. The bar binds to one property rather than composing a fact out of two, which is what stops it going stale the day a fourth verb lands somewhere else.

A pull's own fetch is not a second operation: a pull is a fetch and then an integration, called through the sibling rather than reimplemented, so the lock lets a fetch through while a pull holds it. Without that one exception the feature deadlocks against itself on the first press of Pull.

Only the fetch half is threaded; the merge or rebase runs back on the interface's thread, because both write the index and the working tree and every controller that re-reads off them lives there.

A verb returns "accepted", and a refusal is still synchronous. Everything decidable without contacting anything — the lock, a build of libgit2 with no threads, a detached HEAD, a non-fast-forward against the tracking ref, a lease with nothing to lease against, a destination that is not empty — is decided before a job starts and reported in the same turn.

A libgit2 with no thread support is a refusal rather than a fallback: running inline instead would be a second code path nobody exercises, guarding against a state whose other symptom is a corrupt object database found weeks later with nothing to connect it to.

docs.title: Progress is in the banner
docs.text:
A row of its own rather than a fifth mode, because the four modes rank against each other (only one can be true at a time) and that argument does not reach a transfer — HEAD can be detached while a fetch runs, and a rebase can be stopped while somebody pushes another branch. Ranking a transfer into the same slot would let starting a fetch hide a stopped rebase.

A negative fraction — libgit2 has not been told the object count yet, and never is for a local clone — fills the track with a faint wash rather than leaving it empty, since an empty bar beside the word "Fetching" reads as a transfer stalled at zero.

Cancelling is never gated. Each controller's destructor sets the flag, waits and deletes the job, so quitting during a transport that will not answer is waited out — which is the honest price of it.

The transport buttons grey rather than disappear while one is running, which is a deliberate exception to the absent-not-greyed rule: "wait ten seconds" is not "this repository cannot do that", the verb is the one about to be pressed again, and taking the three off the bar moved every remaining control sideways at the moment somebody was aiming at one.

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
With progress, cancellable, and with prune as both a habit and a one-off.

Whether a fetch removes the tracking refs for branches the server no longer has is one setting with one home and one reader — three routes to a fetch and a flag at each of them would be three places for one choice to be spelled.

What that has no room for is the occasion: a forge full of merged branches cleaned up under somebody who does not prune by habit, or somebody who does and wants this one fetch to leave a colleague's refs alone until they have read them. So a caret beside Fetch offers the choice this once, and its rows say which of them the button would do — a menu offering "Fetch" beside a button reading "Fetch" has to say what the difference is, and the honest answer is "none, this time".

Cancelling happens inside the transfer callback and nowhere else: libgit2 is inside a blocking read, so a non-zero return from the callback is the only thing that makes it unwind. A cancelled fetch is not reported as a failure — the object database is consistent either way, git simply has fewer objects than it might have.

prune() on its own was removed rather than fixed

It could not have worked: libgit2's prune runs against the ref list a connection populates, so on a remote nothing has connected to it has nothing to compare against and prunes nothing. Nothing in the UI ever called it, which is exactly why that was never found out — and around it had grown a command-line spelling and a "run again" branch dispatching on an id no recorder ever writes. Three dead things propping each other up. git fetch --prune is the honest spelling.

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
Push always means push. The button used to replace itself with "Force push (with lease)" whenever the upstream had moved, which was wrong twice: the swap answered once and then went deaf while HEAD and the upstream moved under it, and it made the only push control on screen the forcing one at the moment forcing is dangerous.

There is one Push, it refuses in its own words, and both ways past that refusal are behind a caret beside it — a second, deliberate gesture.

Verb What it checks Push Refuses a non-fast-forward and stops. However many times it is asked Force with lease Against what the far end says it holds right now — a live ref listing compared with the remote-tracking ref Force Nothing

Three named entry points, no boolean: a caller has to type forcePush to get one, because a flag is what gets passed wrongly in silence.

The lease is the first row and is absent with no remote-tracking ref, saying why — a lease against nothing is a plain force under a safer name. It is checked against a live listing rather than the tracking ref, because a lease that trusted the tracking ref would be a plain force with extra steps: the tracking ref is precisely the thing that goes stale.

The plain force is the second row, drawn in the failure colour over a wash so the dangerous one reads as such before either label is — and it is still offered where the lease is not, having nothing to lease against in the first place.

The plain force needs a third gesture

Choosing it opens a dialog rather than pushing. It is the only confirmation in this app for a gesture inside a menu, because it is the only operation whose damage is on another machine: everything else that writes lands somewhere you can look at it, and the operation log files every push as remote with no way back precisely because nothing here can reach over the wire.

The dialog keeps two facts apart the way the reset dialog does: the commits that stop being reachable, and that nothing is checked. Its confirm button is deliberately not the primary — this is the one press in the app that should not be arrived at by following the highlight.

It is also not what a retry does: "Run again" in the operation log cannot re-issue a plain force. The lease stays repeatable, because a repeat of a lease is still a lease and declines on its own.

A push where one ref was rejected must say which. The refusal happens at two layers because they know different things: a plan compares the branch with its remote-tracking ref before anything is contacted (honest, and only as fresh as the last fetch), and the per-ref callback fires once per ref the server actually considered. Reporting overall success because the call returned zero is the single most common way a git GUI lies about what it did.

docs.title: Pull
docs.text:
--ff-only is the default, and it is a refusal rather than a mode: when the histories have diverged the pull declines and names both ways forward, having integrated nothing. The other two strategies each write a commit — a merge commit, or a whole branch replayed — and doing either because a button was pressed once is how a history acquires shapes nobody chose.

The fetch is kept when it refuses: the commits are in the object database and the tracking ref points at them, so the safe default costs a decision rather than a download.

A pull is a composition rather than a reimplementation — the existing fetch and then the existing merge, or the existing rebase. A second merge would be a second set of answers to conflicts, fast-forwards and merge.ff, and the two would disagree the first time one of them was fixed. A normal merge still stops, and a pull that stopped is reported as a success: the index is written and the Conflicts surface finishes it.

An unrecognised stored strategy reads as ff-only, so a hand-edited typo declines instead of picking the destructive one.

docs.title: Clone
docs.text:
With progress and cancellation, and on success it announces itself — the fleet registers it and the app opens it, rather than the transport reaching into a registry it does not own.

A cancelled clone leaves nothing behind, and a flag alone cannot promise that: libgit2's local transport never calls the transfer callback, so on a file:// clone only two callbacks fire and the flag may be set at a moment when nothing is left to read it. So a clone that was asked to stop and nonetheless finished has its directory removed and registers nothing — and only a directory this call created is ever removed, recorded before the clone starts, because deleting a folder you already had is far worse than a stray clone.

docs.title: Shallow, and why there is no partial
docs.text:
A depth dial, with shallowCost naming the four surfaces that go quiet — blame stops at the oldest commit fetched, a bisect has nothing older to search, a comparison against anything further back cannot resolve, and the graph starts where the fetch stopped — and naming git fetch --unshallow as the way back.

A depth against a repository on this machine is refused before anything is written, and libgit2 is the reason rather than a policy: git_clone bypasses the git-aware transport for a local path, and the local transport answers a depth with "shallow fetch is not supported" — after the destination has been created and removed again, seconds into an operation somebody committed to.

--single-branch is deliberately absent from both the call and the printed line. git implies it from --depth; libgit2 does not, so a shallow clone here fetches every branch to that depth — a larger clone than the same git clone --depth produces and a more useful one. Adding a refspec to imitate git would make the clone quieter than the command line beside it.

A partial clone is named and never offered

--filter=blob:none is reachable by shelling out, and doing it would produce a checkout this app cannot read: a partial clone records a promisor remote and leaves most blobs absent, expecting whoever opens the repository to fetch each one on demand — and libgit2 implements none of that. Every blob lookup would fail the moment a diff, a blame or a checkout asked for one.

A tick producing a repository the app then could not open is worse than no tick, so the sentence saying so is drawn on the dialog whatever is chosen.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
One ladder, in order:

  1. ssh-agent
  2. An explicit key path from the settings
  3. The platform keychain, where you asked for it
  4. A token typed into the app, kept in memory for the session

A credential is asked for through a C callback that libgit2 may call more than once per operation — once per method the server offers, and again after a refusal. Two things follow: the attempts must be counted and capped, because a callback that keeps returning the same rejected credential is an infinite loop inside libgit2 — the operation never returns, and nothing reaches the screen to say why; and which source answered has to survive the call, or the failure can say "authentication failed" but not "ssh-agent had no key for this host", which is the only version of that sentence anybody can act on.

docs.title: The keychain rung
docs.text:
Optional, and off by default. Qt ships no keychain API, so the two routes were a third-party library that would be required by a build that works perfectly well without it, or writing both platform halves by hand. Both halves are written and neither is required: Security.framework on macOS (part of the system, so always there) and libsecret through pkg-config on Linux. With neither found the app compiles unchanged and the token behaves exactly as it always did.

Three answers and never two, and the settings row says which:

No backend compiled in This build has neither half A backend named but unavailable The code is present and the service is not — no keyring daemon, a locked session, a headless machine A backend in force Only this one can keep anything

Collapsing the first two would make "install libsecret" and "start your keyring" read as one problem, and only one of them is yours to fix.

Off means not read. A switch that stopped saving new tokens while an old one went on answering would be off in name only. And resetting the transport section puts the choice back and touches nothing in the keyring — a settings reset quietly deleting from the platform's password store would be the one destructive thing on that page.

A stale entry costs a round trip and no more: a refused credential brings the callback straight back and whatever was typed this session is offered next. That is why this is a ladder rather than a choice.

Both arms are compiled by CI and neither is exercised

The Linux job installs libsecret-1-dev so that arm is compiled rather than merely written — an optional backend nothing ever builds is a guard that skips in silence. What no runner can do is exercise one: there is no keyring running and no unlocked login keychain, so the suite asserts the fallback.

The two credential ladders stay separate. A forge token buys a list of pull requests; this one can push. On GitHub the same personal access token can serve both, which is exactly the coincidence that would make one class look right and then be wrong the first time somebody pushes over ssh to a host their forge token knows nothing about. Nothing here can hand a secret to the interface layer, and a test walks the object's own metadata rather than trusting the declaration.

docs.title: Background fetch
docs.text: Periodic fetch of the open repository, off by default, interval a setting. It never touches the working tree, never runs during a stopped operation, and backs off on a credential failure instead of re-prompting every cycle.

docs.title: The working tree is watched
docs.text:
An editor saving, a build running or git in another window used to go unnoticed. The watcher supplies the missing signal and says which half moved: a file under the working directory means only the status lists can be wrong, while the index, HEAD or a ref moving invalidates the graph, the drift, the conflicts and the branch lists at once.

The watch set comes off the index rather than a walk of the disk: one file read instead of a stat per tree entry, and everything ignored is excluded for free, since an ignored file is not in the index. Directories are armed first because they are strictly fewer and answer a different question — a directory watch reports an entry appearing or vanishing, and only a file watch reports a rewrite in place, which is what an ordinary save is.

Three timings, and they are not the same thing: events are debounced so four hundred writes are one refresh (with a ceiling, so a running build cannot postpone it for ever); a short quiet window drops what the app caused itself, since staging already refreshes explicitly; and each automatic refresh is timed and the next held off by a multiple of it, which bounds what automatic refreshing can take from the interface whatever the repository costs to read.

That quiet window has to outlast the platform's own delivery latency, which is a number rather than an unknown: on Linux the engine is inotify and the delay is zero; on macOS Qt hard-codes a half-second stream latency it does not expose. For as long as the window was a flat 150 ms, every staging, discard and commit refreshed twice on macOS while the identical code was correct on Linux.

docs.title: Reviewing a proposal
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. forge-write, with the held-and-sent-later half offline-comments. What a licence adds

The one thing in this app that changes something on a machine that is not this one.

docs.title: The panel is two panes
docs.text:
A reader is only ever doing one of two things, and everything used to be one column — description, size, reviews, then a lower list with three chips over it — so a proposal of any substance was several screens of scrolling in a panel about 420px wide.

  • Proposal is deciding whether to pick this up: what it says it does, how big it is, and what its reviewers have said.
  • Content is reading what it changes.

The identity stays above the panes — number, state, title, author, branches, labels, and how long it has been waiting — for the tab bar's own reason: what you are looking at must not disappear when you change which part of it you are looking at.

Reviews sit with the proposal, because a review is a judgement about a change rather than part of it, and it is what the approval waits are computed from. Content is one pane and not two: commits and files are two readings of the same change, and they nest — a commit chosen out of the list is read inside the commits reading, so promoting the two would put "← Commits" at the same level as the tabs and make "Files" and "the files of the commit I opened" read as two lists that both exist.

Nothing is fetched by arriving at either pane, and Content rests on Files because the files came with the selection while the commits are still bought by their own chip.

docs.title: The diff of somebody else's proposal is a diff
docs.text:
A forge sends a unified patch per file, and it is turned into the same shape the local diff uses — so the same panel draws it, with the same highlighting, the same split and wrap preferences, and the same intra-line marks, none of it written twice.

Staging, reverting and discarding are all absent: there is no index behind somebody else's branch. And it is deliberately not re-readable, because re-reading matches on the path — so a proposal touching a file also open in Changes would otherwise have the local version silently swapped in the moment a context option changed.

Three honesty requirements sit on top of it:

  • A patch that did not arrive is not an empty diff. GitHub withholds one for three unrelated reasons — nothing to diff as text, a diff it has and will not send, and a pure rename — and they are told apart, because "no textual changes in this file" is true of all three and therefore says nothing about any.
  • A patch that will not parse yields nothing rather than half a diff, since half a hunk drawn as a whole one is a diff that is quietly wrong about which lines moved.
  • A commit's diff is the commit as it stands on its branch, which after a rebase, or for a merge, is not what the proposal would land. The pane says so, because both readings render as something plausible.

Whitespace is honoured, and the anchoring is what makes that safe. GitHub's REST API takes no whitespace parameter — the ?w=1 people know is its web UI's — so the filtering is applied to the patch that arrived. Nothing is ever renumbered: a reindented pair collapses to one context line carrying the removal's old number beside the addition's new one, and every surviving line keeps the numbers the forge gave it. That is the load-bearing property, because a comment is anchored to a line number on a side and a filter that closed the numbering up would put somebody's objection on a line nobody wrote. The context dial cannot be honoured at all — no filtering adds back lines that were never sent — and the pane says so.

docs.title: Three kinds of comment, and each says which
docs.text:
Who can see it Where it is Published Everybody The forge Pending Its author alone The forge, in an unsubmitted review — so a browser shows it Kept here Nobody outside this app This machine

The middle one is the kind worth being careful with, because it carries an author and a time exactly as a published one does — drawn without a word saying otherwise it reads as something the proposal's author has already seen, which is the single most consequential thing a reviewer can be wrong about here.

So the tag is a word and not only a tint, and the two unsent kinds get different words: collapsing them would hide the difference that decides whether closing the app loses anything.

The count on the band and the per-file comment count are over all three — a file carrying three of your own unsent objections and nothing else read as a file nobody had commented on.

docs.title: The review being written lives on the forge
docs.text:
It was the other way round for most of this feature's life, on the argument that a server-side draft makes every comment a round trip, puts a second copy of somebody's half-finished thinking on another machine, and leaves this app reconciling two of them whenever both have moved.

The last of those decided it, and it decided it the other way: there is one copy now and nothing to reconcile. A comment is appended to the pending review the moment it is written, and the same review is what a browser shows. What is given up is that writing a comment needs the network; what is bought is that a review begun here can be finished anywhere.

Nothing about the local half was deleted, because losing what somebody typed is the one outcome that is never acceptable: a provider that cannot append, no token, no commit to anchor to, or a request that failed all end with the comment kept here. That is not silent either — the state says failed, the toast says so, and the band says the comment is being kept here and why. A draft that quietly stopped syncing is worse than one that never tried.

docs.title: The second read nobody expected
docs.text:
A pending comment is on the forge and in no comment list: the published list is what everybody can see, and a review that has not been submitted is visible to its author alone — the forge keeps its comments under the review's own path and nowhere else.

While the draft was local there was nothing to miss. The moment it moved, every comment a reviewer wrote became something a browser drew and this app did not: the thread appeared once, in the session that wrote it, and was gone after a relaunch, after "read it again", and entirely for a review begun in a browser.

So there is a second read, under its own key — a third question rather than a share of the published list's, because the two are read from different endpoints and go stale for different reasons: that one changes when somebody else says something, and this one changes every time you write.

It costs a request only for the reader who has a review open: the id comes off the review list the app already bought, so a proposal with no pending review asks for nothing extra.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text:
Comment is in the hunk header rather than on every line, because a button per line would be a palette entry and a hint key per line — forty entries reading "Comment" and the alphabet spent on a list that runs to thousands. It acts on the panel's own selection, which is how staging has always worked here, and a forge takes a comment on a range, so two lines picked and one comment written is exactly the shape both ends already have.

The composer offers two verbs and they are not the same act:

  • Add to review is the primary — it goes into the pending review, and is reversible.
  • Comment now publishes immediately, is offered only where the forge takes one, and is the only write with a way back beside it.

Rewriting a comment reaches the third kind alone, and the button is absent on the other two. A published comment would need a PATCH, which is absent from the write list on purpose. A pending one is on the forge and rewriting it needs a second GraphQL mutation — the one allow-list row that names no operation, and widening it further to save retyping a sentence is not a trade worth making. A comment kept here is the fallback, so this app is its only holder and nothing leaves the machine — and that is not the marginal case it sounds like: a comment is kept here because sending it failed, which makes it the one most likely to want a word changed before the review is sent again.

The field opens in place of the rendered body rather than under it, since a box below the same sentence would show it twice and leave you working out which of the two the buttons act on.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
Sending a review that was already begun is a different request, and picking the wrong one was the bug. Creating a review out of whatever this app is holding is right when the draft never reached the forge and wrong the moment it did — and it did, in the ordinary case, because that is where comments go now. A forge allows one pending review per person per proposal, so creating a second is a 422: "Unprocessable entity", on every press of Approve after anything had been written.

The half that was worse than the error is that the request it refused carried none of the comments, which are in the pending review — so succeeding would have been wrong too.

So there are two verbs and the app picks between them on whether a pending review id answers. The submission sends the verdict and the covering note and nothing else: the comments are already in the review it names, each anchored to the commit it was written against.

A local draft that still holds comments is the fallback having fired for some of them — those are in no review, so the submission cannot carry them, and they are put straight back into the draft with a notice saying so. A notice rather than an error, because the review was sent and what is left is work still waiting, which is a different piece of news from a failure.

Only a success discards the draft, because what the forge then holds is the authority and a second copy would be sent twice by the next press. A failed submission keeps what it could not send and says why beside it — every reason a submission fails is one the same draft can be sent under a minute later.

docs.title: The band
docs.text:
The worst failure here is losing somebody's review; the second worst is their never noticing it was not sent. So the band is drawn from whether a pending review exists rather than from a tab or a hover, it counts the comments, it says when it was begun, and it says "not sent".

That predicate is not "is something being kept here": bound to the local draft alone, the band went dark the moment the comments started reaching the forge — which is to say it went dark in the ordinary case, for a review a browser was showing.

docs.title: Discarding discards, on both machines
docs.text:
Dropping this app's copy was never the whole of the verb once the review moved: what it left behind was a pending review sitting on somebody's proposal, shown in a browser as unsent work, with nothing here admitting it existed — "discard" meaning "forget", which is the one thing a destructive-sounding verb must not quietly mean.

The forge's copy goes first and the local one only if it went. Of the two half-failures one is recoverable and the other is not: dropping the local half and failing on the forge loses what somebody typed and leaves the review there; failing and keeping everything loses nothing and can be pressed again.

So a refusal throws nothing away and the sentence names that the forge still holds it — somebody told only "it failed" would reasonably conclude the review is gone. Where the forge is holding a review it will not take back at all, the local half is dropped and you are told plainly that its copy stands and its own page is where that one has to go: the alternative is a Discard button that cannot be pressed on a review this app itself opened. The confirmation says which of the two cases it is in before it is pressed.

That DELETE is a widening of the write list and not a crossing of it: what it deletes is a pending review, one this app opened, holding comments only its author can see. The list already takes one of those comments back, and allowing the first while refusing the second would mean a reviewer could take back three comments one at a time and never be rid of the review they were in. What keeps it off a submitted review — or anybody else's — is where the id comes from: the pending state and nothing else.

docs.title: Where the draft is kept
docs.text:
A file, and deliberately not the forge cache. That store is a cache: its schema carries a version and a bump throws every row away, which is right for rows whose entire replacement cost is a round trip and catastrophic for the only copy of something a person wrote. And signing out empties it outright — but a half-written review is not a private repository's data leaking onto disk after the account was forgotten, it is the reviewer's own words.

So signing out keeps the draft, and un-registering the repository is what discards one.

It is JSON beside the settings rather than in them, because a growing list of records in a settings file is an abuse of the shape, and it is written through on every keystroke: a save deferred to quit is a save that does not happen when the app is killed. Nothing recorded can carry a credential — it is paths, line numbers, a verdict and prose — and a test reads the file's bytes back.

Two launches used to erase each other's drafts

The file is one per machine and nothing stops the app being launched twice — a second window made that ordinary rather than unusual. Both copies read it once, held the rows in memory and rewrote the whole thing on every operation, so the second one to write erased everything the other had recorded since it loaded — including the only copy of unsent prose.

Every mutation re-reads the file immediately before writing now, which collapses the window from a whole session to a single write.

docs.title: A 403 is about the scope
docs.text: Rendering it as "the forge said no" would leave somebody re-typing a review that will be refused again. The sentence is composed from the provider's own scope reasons, so the sign-in panel and the review band cannot come to name different things — and on GitHub the repo scope covers reading and reviewing both, which is exactly why it is said out loud: granting it to read pull requests also grants the ability to approve one in your name.

docs.title: Mark as viewed
docs.text:
Unimplemented, which is a smaller and more honest thing to say than what used to stand here. GitHub has a viewed state and exposes it through GraphQL alone, and the reason this app did not reach it was that doing so would put that endpoint on the write allow-list. That row now exists, so the objection has expired rather than been answered.

The ticks are kept in the draft, and the panel says which: a viewed state that silently fails to sync is worse than none.

docs.title: What GitLab and Bitbucket cannot do
docs.text:
Each is a refusal with a sentence rather than an empty list — the rule the whole layer keeps.

GitLab has no server-side draft: a note posts the instant it is written and there is no container to accumulate comments in. So the local draft is the mechanism there, which is what this app did everywhere before the draft moved onto the forge — a working arrangement rather than a degraded one, and the band already says which of the three kinds you are looking at.

It also has no way to record an objection as a verdict: its model is approval and un-approval. So "changes requested" posts the covering note and approves nothing, and the entry names what actually happened (commented) rather than what was asked for — un-approving in its place would record a different act under your name.

Its approvals are read from the events rather than the direct endpoint, because that one answers who has approved right now and carries no timestamps — and the waits reading computes the merge wait from the earliest approval in force, so a wait measured from a missing timestamp is a wait of fifty years.

A comment there costs two requests and the first is a read: GitLab anchors a note with a position naming three commits, and the trio is read per comment rather than cached, because a merge request that gained a push between two comments has different refs and a stale trio would anchor the second comment to a diff nobody is looking at.

Bitbucket reads and writes nothing, and that is a decision rather than an unfinished path. Every write worth having there is a modification — leaving a review is a PUT on the proposal, and requesting reviewers or setting labels is a PUT that replaces the set somebody else chose — and a row nothing exercises is a row nobody audits, so shipping an approve row to have a write would be exactly the thing that keeps PUT off the table.

What it has instead of reviews is participants — a person with a role, an approved flag and a timestamp — which map onto the review fields honestly. A participant who has neither approved nor objected is dropped: being added to a proposal is not reviewing it, and a review list full of people who have said nothing makes "nobody has reviewed this" unanswerable in the one place it is asked.

docs.title: Rewriting history
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. The interactive rebase is free and is named in the table as such, as are amend, reword, edit, cherry-pick, revert and reset. What a licence adds

Six verbs, all entered from a commit in History rather than from a menu, and all arranged around the same two rules: refuse rather than clobber, and a stopped operation is always visible with a way out.

docs.title: Interactive rebase
docs.text: Two shapes, and which one you get depends on where you started.

docs.title: Entered from an object: it applies
docs.text:
"Rebase onto this", from a commit's menu, a branch row's ⋮, or a commit dropped on another commit. One call that plans as picks and replays at once.

This used to plan and then navigate to the Rebase surface, which was the wrong reading of the bargain: somebody who has picked a base out of the graph has taken the decision, and what they were handed was a page asking them to take it again on a plan whose every row was a pick.

Seven things about it are deliberate:

  • An empty plan is a fast-forward, not a refusal.
