A plan is the commits reachable from HEAD but not from the base, so an empty one means the branch is simply behind — and git rebase <upstream> fast-forwards there and reports success. Refusing was the app disagreeing with the very line it prints beside the control, under a sentence ("There is nothing to rebase") that was true about the plan and useless about the intention.
  • HEAD already being on the base is a no-op announced rather than refused, because git exits zero there and a correct no-op drawn in the failure colour is how a reader learns to distrust the toast.
  • Every commit is a pick, whatever the Rebase surface's mode chip says — that control is not on screen here, and a plan seeded by Autosquash would fold your fixup! commits because of a setting you cannot see.
  • Nothing is autostashed. A dirty working tree is refused in words that name what to do; stashing your working tree, untracked files included, because a row was pressed is not a default this route gets to take.
  • The plan is kept on that refusal, so the Rebase tab is one press away with the plan already loaded, and its Apply honours the autostash tick.
  • Nothing is navigated to, on either outcome. A replay that worked has rewritten the history the surface is drawing and the graph moving is the feedback; a replay that stopped is in the banner, on every surface.
  • There is no confirmation. It is entered from the object it acts on, the branch it rewrites is the one you are standing on, Abort is on the banner, and the reflog holds where HEAD was — which is also what the log row offers to put back. A dialog would buy a second reading of a decision already taken and cost the whole of what was asked for.

docs.title: The Rebase surface
docs.text:
Where a plan is edited: reorder, squash, fixup, reword, drop, edit, and the autosquash mode. Plan first, see the resulting branch, then apply — and nothing is written until you do.

Rows are dragged by a grip, and the gesture has two meanings because a row is dropped in two different ways: between two rows is a reorder, and onto one is a fold, which is what squash is. Thirds rather than halves — folding rewrites two commits into one, so it should take aim rather than be what a slightly-off drop does.

The index arithmetic is the whole of what those two verbs are for: dragging a row down, its target shifts up by one as the row is lifted out; dragging up, it has not moved. Got wrong either way the commit is folded into its neighbour — a rebase that reads correctly and replays something nobody asked for.

A fold is refused rather than quietly reordering for a commit dropped onto itself, an id that is not in the plan, and a target that is being dropped — folding into a commit that is not going to exist is not a thing to do quietly.

docs.title: How it actually runs
docs.text:
The replay is driven by cherry-pick, not libgit2's rebase driver: that one builds its operation list as all-picks and offers no public way to substitute a todo list, so squash, fixup, reword, drop and reorder would all be impossible through it.

Two consequences to know:

  • HEAD must end up attached. During the replay HEAD is detached and follows each new commit; finishing and aborting re-attach it.
  • The state is persisted, so quitting mid-rebase does not lose the operation, and the fleet card reports it.

Commits the replay creates are signed if commit.gpgsign says so — which is a departure from git, argued on the record.

docs.title: Rewording and editing one commit
docs.text:
Amending is HEAD's own verb and says so. These two are the rebase with the plan built for you instead of by you: plan onto the commit's own first parent, set that one row's action to reword or edit, and start — every other row a plain pick.

What the two verbs add is that somebody fixing a typo four commits back does not have to know any of that.

A reword finishes and an edit deliberately does not. A message is known before the operation starts, so the stop the replay makes for one is answered by the controller and you never see the rebase surface. Content is not known beforehand — the whole point of editing is to change it — so that one stops on the commit with its files on disk, and "Amend and continue" on the banner is what ends it. Which is why the reword has a dialog and the edit opens nothing.

The cost is a sentence and not a warning. "3 commits get new hashes" is a fact you can act on where "this rewrites history" is a noise everybody clicks through. The one thing that is a warning is a published commit, said once and done anyway.

Three refusals, each because the alternative is worse than a message:

  • A root commit has no parent to replay onto, and the refusal points at amending.
  • A commit not reachable from HEAD would produce a plan that does not contain it and a replay that silently rewrote the branch you are on, for nothing.
  • An empty message is refused rather than read as "keep what it has" — here the whole operation is the message, so an empty one replays the branch and rewrites every hash above the commit to change nothing.

Both rows are absent on HEAD: amending is what changes that commit, it is one press away in the commit box, and a whole rebase to reword the tip would be the wrong tool offered beside the right one.

docs.title: Cherry-pick
docs.text:
The same machinery, exposed as a verb of its own and entered from the commit.

Two modes, and -n is the one that matters. Committing behaves like git cherry-pick; not committing behaves like git cherry-pick -n, laying the change into the index and the working tree and recording nothing. The second is the primary, because the app already has a surface for reading a pending change and committing it — so the pick lands in Changes to be reviewed before it is permanent, and an unwanted one is discarded the way any other uncommitted edit is.

The two modes differ in exactly one argument and nowhere else, which is what keeps them from drifting apart.

HEAD is never detached, so it cannot end up detached — the rebase has to detach because it is rebuilding the branch it is standing on, and a pick has no such need. There is no window in which a crash leaves the repository detached.

A range is applied oldest first, stopping at the first conflict, and the order is resolved with a revwalk rather than trusting the caller — every list in this UI is newest-first, and a range applied that way conflicts with itself on the second commit.

It refuses a dirty working tree (which is what makes abort safe: there is no work of your own for the reset to take with it), and refuses while any other sequencer is running, because two of them writing one index is how a half-applied operation happens. A commit that comes out empty against HEAD is named rather than recorded as a commit that says nothing.

docs.title: Revert
docs.text:
Reverting means reverse-applying the change into the index and the working tree, committing nothing — git revert --no-commit for a whole commit, git apply --reverse --index for a file, a hunk or a set of lines. The undo is handed to Changes to be reviewed like any other edit, which also means an unwanted revert is discarded rather than needing a second commit.

Both sides are written rather than the working tree alone, because libgit2 validates the working tree against the index before applying, and the two disagreeing would make the next revert of the same file fail for a reason you could not see.

The mechanism is chosen per granularity rather than forced into one:

Granularity How A whole commit A real three-way merge, which is what copes with a merge commit and with a commit whose changes have since been rewritten One file The commit's own diff with the trees handed over in the other order, so add, delete and rename come out right with no patch text A hunk or lines A reverse patch built by hand, since libgit2 cannot be asked for a subset of a diff's hunks; an unpicked change is carried through as context rather than dropped

Every route refuses rather than clobbers. A conflicting whole-commit revert is rejected outright with the paths named, instead of writing markers into a working tree you may have unrelated work in — this operation is entered while reading history, not while looking at the files it writes. A file with unstaged edits is left alone, because the pre-image cannot be found.

Only the whole-commit case is confirmed: it can touch every file the commit touched, whereas a single line is a keystroke.

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
Three verbs, separated by how much of the repository each one moves: a reset moves the branch, a detached checkout moves only HEAD, and restoring a file moves neither. All three are entered from a commit, which is the rule rather than a convenience — a menu of verbs would let somebody reach --hard without having a commit in mind.

--hard is the most destructive thing this app does

Everything else that writes can be read back off some surface afterwards. A hard reset overwrites the working tree, and that half is in no reflog.

So the dialog states two things as deliberately separate sentences: the commits leaving the branch stay reachable through the reflog, and the working tree does not. Both halves are load-bearing. Without the first, a reset reads as permanent and nobody does one; without the second, it reads as reversible, which is the misunderstanding the dialog exists to prevent.

A working-tree backup is taken first, over exactly the files the dialog named, so there is usually a way back after all — and the log row says plainly when there is not.

The dialog composes none of that itself: the count, the commit subjects, the files about to be overwritten and the untracked ones that will be spared all come from the same plan the operation consults, and a test asserts the refused sentence and the emitted error are the same string.

An unknown count refuses, in every mode. A confirmation reading "this will discard some number of things" is not one, and a repository whose graph or status will not read is precisely where writing anyway is worst.

Untracked files are left alone, as git's own reset --hard leaves them — they are in no tree, so no tree can restore them.

Nothing resets while something else is half-finished, including the replay this app drives, which leaves git's own repository state at NONE and is therefore looked for separately.

docs.title: Detaching, and coming back
docs.text:
Checking out a commit detaches HEAD, the banner says so on every surface, and the way back is read out of HEAD's own reflog — the checkout: moving from <branch> to <commit> entry that git checkout - reads too. So a detach performed by git outside the app gets offered the same way back, and there is no second file to keep true. A branch deleted since the detach is not offered at all, because a way back that fails on being taken is worse than none.

A detach is not a ref move, which is the neatest way to get the undo wrong: no branch moved, and a mixed reset against a detached HEAD drags it back and leaves the repository detached — indistinguishable from having gone back, and the next commit made there is orphaned. That row points at re-attaching instead.

docs.title: Restoring one file
docs.text: Not a reset and not refused like one: nothing about HEAD moves and nothing is committed, so it lands on Changes to be read. Writing over an uncommitted edit to that path is the request rather than an accident, so it goes ahead. A path the commit does not hold is refused — a checkout whose pathspec matches nothing succeeds having written nothing, and "restored" with the file untouched is the worst outcome available.

docs.title: Dragging one commit onto another
docs.text:
The gesture every other client has, and the one this project's rules make most dangerous: a drag is ambiguous — merge, rebase and cherry-pick are three different operations over the same pair — and a slip of the hand must never replay a branch.

So the drop names the operation, and choosing the row is the second gesture. A menu opens at the point the drop landed, spells the pair out at the top, and every row does exactly what the commit menu's row of that name does. The drop itself decides nothing, which is the whole safeguard.

One end has to be the current branch's commit, because every verb here is relative to HEAD: dragged from it is "move where I am onto there", dropped onto it is "bring that here". Anything else draws a sentence, because a popup that opens with nothing in it reads as broken rather than as a refusal — and the drop wash says, before you let go, whether dropping there would offer anything.

The row is dragged by a grip and clicked by its body, because the body is already spoken for twice, by the click that selects and the right-click that opens the menu.

docs.title: Undo, backups and the log
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. The reflog is free, and so are the backups a destructive verb takes before it writes. The operation log and the way back it offers are operation-log. What a licence adds

Manage → Operations. One row per operation, newest first, with the git command beside it — and a way back where one exists, and a sentence where one does not.

This is the feature the comparison calls effectively unique in the field, and what makes it so is not that it exists but that most of it is refusals.

docs.title: Why "Undo everything" is not offered
docs.text:
A log makes that button look even more plausible than a reflog does — every row names an operation, so surely every row reverses. It is the same falsehood: git records refs, not files. A commit that left a branch is still in the object database; an uncommitted edit that reset --hard wrote over was never in an object at all.

So a row does not carry "undoable". It carries what kind of thing it did, and what is offered follows:

Kind Meaning What is offered ref-move A ref moved and nothing on disk was destroyed A mixed reset back to where it was inverse Additive, with a real inverse that has its own name That inverse, named for what it does destructive It overwrote files Nothing, and a sentence — unless a backup was taken remote It left this machine Nothing, and a sentence none Nothing to take back Nothing

The inverse button never reads "Undo". It reads "Delete the tag again": deleting a tag is not the undoing of having made one, and the shorter word hides which of the two is about to run.

Mixed is not a parameter. Soft would leave the index holding a tree nobody staged; hard would overwrite the working tree, which belongs behind the reset dialog that counts and names what it is about to destroy.

A ref-move recorded without the commit it moved from degrades to none rather than reaching you as a reset to nowhere. The fast-forward merge is the real case: it never enters the in-progress state, so nothing ever published the commit it came from, and that row honestly points at the reflog instead.

docs.title: Two arguments decide a kind, and only the call site holds them
docs.text:
reset --hard is destructive where soft and mixed are ref-move; a forced worktree removal is destructive where an unforced one is none, because unforced refuses anything uncommitted.

A commit is the case worth arguing out. It moves a ref, so a mixed reset genuinely undoes it — and it is honest precisely because that reset writes no file, so the working tree comes out byte for byte as it went in and the change lands back on Changes. Undoing a hard reset the same way would restore the commits and quietly not the files, which is the same button making two different promises.

A detach is not a ref move, and calling it one is the neatest way to get this wrong: no branch moved, and a mixed reset against a detached HEAD drags it back and leaves the repository detached — indistinguishable from having gone back, and the next commit made there is orphaned. That row points at re-attaching.

docs.title: There is no redo; there is "Run again"
docs.text:
Re-applying is not the inverse of having reversed, because the repository has moved — the commit is not where it was, the remote holds different refs. So it re-issues the operation through the controller that owns it, with every precondition re-checked against the repository as it stands.

The list is short and excludes everything destructive (running a reset twice is running it once more), the plain force push, and the clone, which the second time round is a clone into a directory that now exists.

docs.title: An undo says so
docs.text: Pressing "Put the files back" changed something on disk and the log itself drew nothing, which is indistinguishable from a button that does not work. Both verbs have one exit for that, so the sentence is said once rather than at a dozen call sites — and the channel is deliberately narrow: a verb whose result is visible where it was pressed says enough by changing what is drawn.

docs.title: What is recorded, and where the row is written
docs.text:
Everything whose completion signal says which verb ran is recorded centrally: rebase, cherry-pick, merge, push, pull, clone, fetch, an ignore rule.

Everything else records at the call site, and the reason is stated rather than hidden. One signal is emitted identically by a soft reset, a mixed reset, a hard reset, a detach and a re-attach — and the difference between the second and the third is the entire difference between an operation this app may offer to reverse and one whose consequences are in no journal at all. Another says a list moved and not what moved it; another cannot tell a stash push from a duplicate or a pop from a drop.

Guessing there would put an Undo on precisely the row where pressing it proves the button was a lie.

A call site records once, at the point the operation is over — the call has been made and its result is known, or a plan function has refused. Both are the operation: the plan's refusal is the sentence you were already shown before pressing, and "I confirmed it and nothing happened" is a question a log owes an answer to. An early return on "no repository is open" is deliberately not recorded, because nothing was attempted — a log filling up with rows for half-typed forms is one nobody reads to the bottom of.

docs.title: The command is never stored
docs.text:
An entry holds the id and the arguments, and the row resolves the command on every read — so correcting a spelling in the registry corrects the log with it. A rendered string on disk would be a second copy of every command in the app, going stale in the one place whose output is meant to be run somewhere the app cannot see.

An id the registry does not know renders nothing, here as everywhere.

That is also why two rebase routes are two ids rather than one with an argument: rebase -i prints a line that stops and opens an editor when pasted, which is honest for a plan you read and edited and misleading for one nobody was shown.

docs.title: It is kept, in JSON, and per repository
docs.text:
A log that vanished on quit answers "what did I just do" and not "what did I do on Friday". The settings file is for choices and a growing list of records in it is an abuse of the shape; a database earns itself by answering differently-shaped questions and by being a cache, which this is not.

Entries carry the checkout they were recorded in, the surface reads only the open one, and a repository leaving the fleet takes its rows with it. Nothing recorded can carry a credential: the arguments are refs, paths, branch names and messages, and the one remaining route — a clone url with userinfo in it — is redacted before the entry is built, with a test reading the file's bytes back.

Two launches used to erase each other's log

The file is one per machine, and both copies read it once, held the rows in memory and rewrote the whole thing on every operation — so the second one to write erased everything the other had recorded since it loaded. What went with those rows was not only the history: the backup tokens hang off them, so every way back they offered went too, silently, in the one part of the app whose whole subject is saying what it did.

Recording re-reads the file immediately before appending now. That does not make it safe against two writers landing in the same instant, but it collapses the window from a whole session to a single write. The token a row is identified by had to be re-seeded with it — two readers continuing from the same number would share an identity, and "Put the files back" on one would reverse the other.

docs.title: What the log keeps, and what it costs
docs.text:
Three bounds, because they bound three different things and you reach for whichever matches the reason you came: days, entries per repository, and megabytes of snapshots.

Zero is no bound in all three, which is a real answer rather than an off-by-one: somebody who wants every operation they have ever run should not have to type a large number and hope. It is also why the age default is not infinite — a row whose copies the store's own cap dropped long ago offers a way back that is not there.

Clearing the log and clearing the snapshots are separate verbs. Tidying a log and reclaiming a few hundred megabytes are different acts, and only one of them destroys something with no other copy — so it asks first, names what is about to go, and its confirm is not the primary.

The figure lives on the Operations tab and the bounds live in the settings, which is the split this project draws everywhere: a number is read at the moment somebody is deciding whether to press the button beside it. It is measured when asked for rather than kept, because a stale figure in front of somebody about to destroy something is worse than none.

docs.title: And where a copy makes one of the refusals untrue
docs.text:
Everything above stands. What a working-tree backup changes is not the argument but the facts for the operations that go through it: it copies what they are about to write over, before they write, and then there is something to put back.

The promise is narrow and is stated in those terms: these files, as they were a moment before this operation ran. Not "the repository as it was" — a hard reset moved a ref as well, and putting the files back leaves the branch where the reset put it. So the sentence names that half and points at the reflog, and the verb is "Put the files back" rather than "Undo".

Four call sites take one, and they are the ones that destroy content held in no git object: a hard reset (over the plan's own list, so exactly the files the dialog named — and never the untracked ones git leaves alone), a file's discard, a hunk's or a line's discard, and a hook being edited or deleted.

Switching a hook's executable bit takes none, because nothing is destroyed and the way back is the same control pressed again; creating anything takes none either.

It is a file copy, deliberately, and not a git object. A stash is a commit with a tree, so it needs the index and HEAD in a fit state — which is what they are not, half way through a reset — and it would show up in the stash list where somebody would reasonably drop it. A dangling blob is what git gc exists to delete. A plain copy outside the repository survives every git operation and can be dropped by a size cap without a ref anywhere going stale.

Best effort, and the row says which. A copy that could not be taken — nothing there, a path that climbs out of the base, a file or a snapshot past the caps — answers with nothing, and the caller does not abort: an operation somebody confirmed is not cancelled because a convenience could not be arranged. A row with no token offers nothing and says why, which is where every destructive row was before this existed.

What must never happen is a row offering a restore with nothing behind it, so the token is recorded only once the copy has landed, and it is refused whole rather than taken in part — half a snapshot restores one file and leaves its neighbour, a state the repository was never in.

A path that was not there is part of the state too. A tracked file deleted in the working tree, or a hook that did not exist yet, is recorded as absent, and restoring it deletes what the operation created. And the permission bits travel with the copy, which is the whole of what makes a restored hook a hook: one that came back without the executable bit would sit there being skipped, which reads as the restore not having worked.

The copies go when the row goes — pruned out of the log, dropped with a repository leaving the fleet, or cleared — so the two cannot disagree about which rows are backed. An old row's answer is "the copies are no longer kept" rather than a failure.

docs.title: The log this app keeps about itself
docs.text:
Separate from the operation log, and for a different reader: when something has gone wrong and you want to see what actually left the machine, there is a rolling file.

Six categories rather than a level, and all of them are on: transport, the forge's HTTP, the replay engines, the working-tree watcher, timing spans, and the app itself. There is no verbosity dial, because the question a log answers is always asked after the thing happened.

One file a day, with two bounds you can set — how many days to keep, and how many megabytes the directory may hold. Zero is "no bound" in both, retention is read off the file's name rather than its modification time, and today's file is never deleted to make room.

Every line is redacted as it is written, in the one place every line passes through, so a call site added later cannot forget: userinfo in a URL, an Authorization header (Basic included), a bare bearer token, a JSON-encoded secret, a parameter named for what it holds, and the token shapes the forges use. The host survives, which is what makes the log worth reading, and a test asserts it by reading a written file back.

Paths are kept, deliberately. That is what makes a transport failure diagnosable, and it is also why Reveal log sits beside the path on the About page: a log that records where your work lives is one you should be able to read before deciding to send it to anybody. Clearing it is a press on the same page.

docs.title: What you would have typed
docs.text:
The app is a way of driving git without knowing git, and that is exactly how somebody ends up never learning it. One registry answers "what is the command for this", and both routes into it read it: a hint beside the operation, and the palette printing the line for the entry it has highlighted.

One registry rather than a string beside each button, because the moment two surfaces offer one verb the literals are two copies that drift.

A path or a ref comes out safe to paste, and only quoted where it must be. POSIX single quotes — the only form with no interior escapes — and quoting everything was the other candidate and is worse than useless: nobody learns git add src/main.cpp from git add 'src/main.cpp', and somebody who sees quotes on every argument stops being able to tell which of them needed them.

The safe set holds braces, on the strength of stash@{2}, and ~ when it is not the first character, which keeps HEAD~3 plain while a path beginning with one is quoted rather than silently expanded to somebody else's home directory.

An id nobody registered answers empty, and the UI then draws nothing. There is no fallback and no guessing. This is the one thing in the app whose output is meant to be run somewhere the app cannot see, so a guess is not a degraded answer — it is a command somebody pastes.

The command says what the app does, or it is not offered. Every revert carries --no-commit; a file's discard names both sides and a hunk's is git restore --patch, because one goes back to the last commit and the other to the index; the autostashing checkout is three commands with apply && drop rather than pop, since pop discards the entry even when it has just written conflict markers.

git checkout - is deliberately not offered for re-attaching HEAD: it means "wherever HEAD was", which is only this branch while nothing else has moved HEAD in between, and a command that is equivalent most of the time is the worst kind to teach.

Two things it does not try to be:

  • Not a record of how this app is implemented. The interactive rebase is registered as git rebase -i <upstream> with the plan printed beneath as the todo file's own comment lines, even though the replay here is driven by cherry-pick.
  • Not complete where git is not. There is no entry for reverting a single hunk, because git has no verb that reverse-applies a chosen subset of one commit's hunks — the nearest spelling offers a different set of hunks, so "the third one" would mean two different things in the two places — and none for renaming a stash, which is a reflog rewrite git has no command for at all. An absent line is the absent-not-greyed rule applied to prose.

Where it appears is the argument, not whether. Beside the place an operation is decided — the confirmations, the stash detail, the operation banner — and in the palette. A hint on every button would put a monospace line beside forty controls, which is noise rather than a lesson.

It can be switched off, default on: a line somebody has to switch on is a line for the people who already know what it says.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Every preference on both pages. Running the interface in another language is localization. What a licence adds

⌘, / Ctrl+,, or the button at the end of the workspace bar — and either of those again to leave, because the page has no tab and the key that opens a destination nobody can see a seat for is the key anyone presses again to be rid of it. The button renames itself with what the next press will do, since a toggle whose name never changes is one nobody can find the way out of.

Everything the app remembers is still a chip, a tick or a dial where it applies, because a control beside the thing it changes is the right way to change it. What this page adds is an answer to "what does this app remember?", and a home for the handful of choices that had none.

docs.title: Two pages, chosen by chip
docs.text:
They were one and could not honestly stay one:

Kept in Applies What the app remembers The app's own settings Wherever you are What this checkout says One repository's .git/config To everybody who works on it, and gone the moment you open something else

You could not tell which of the two a row was without reading its sentence to the end, and the answer decides whether what you type follows you to the next repository.

The second holds the ticket links, the ticket id rules, the expected subject shape, what may be sent to a hosted model, and what signs a commit here.

It writes this app's own keys and not git's. Overruling gpg.format from a settings page would be this app taking a second view on something every other git tool reads; the keys it does write are ones nothing else has ever heard of. What it draws beside git's own values is the half you cannot see from your own config file — which rules are in force, which came from the forge, and which were dropped and why, since a rule with half of itself missing or a pattern that will not compile is silent everywhere else.

docs.title: Eighteen sections in six bands, and a search
docs.text:
Eighteen sections down one column is a list rather than a page: every one names a place, and nothing said which of them somebody with a question about how a commit is written should be looking in.

And there is a search, because the bands answer "where would that be filed" and never answer "where is the one about whitespace" — the question you arrive with, already knowing the word. It matches the sentence as well as the name, deliberately: the sentences here are as much the deliverable as the switches, and every word worth searching for is far more likely to be in one of them. A section head whose own label matches keeps all of its rows, and a heading with nothing left under it goes.

The page leads with Appearance and then Type size, which are the two sections that name what every other section is drawn in rather than a place — and the two somebody arriving for the first time has most likely come for, since "this reads small" and "this is too dark" are complaints about the app rather than about a surface.

Three rows that could only be read are gone: the folder the last repository was created in, how many repositories are registered, and the OAuth client id. Each stated a fact and offered nothing, and a row you can only read is one you scroll past on the way to the ones you came for. The rows that state a count under a section head carrying a Reset stay — those are what the reset puts back.

docs.title: Type size
docs.text:
Two dials: the interface and the monospace.

They are not seven choices but one scale — what a caller means by "tiny" is "two steps below the body" rather than "eleven pixels" — so the offsets stay fixed and the body size is what you set. Nothing on any surface had to be touched to make the whole app resize.

The defaults moved up a step each, because a size somebody has to go and find in a settings page is a size for the people who already know it is there. One step and not two: every fixed row height in the app was measured against the old numbers, and larger sizes are reachable anyway because the control height is a floor rather than a formula — nothing moves at the sizes the app was designed at, and a button, a chip, a row and the bar all follow past that.

The monospace is a size of its own and is deliberately not derived from the other, for three reasons in increasing order of cost:

  1. They are read differently — chrome is scanned, a diff is read line after line, and every editor that ships both settings ships them apart.
  2. The mono size is a layout input where the interface size is not: it decides a diff's horizontal scroll range and the row height that makes the diff virtualise at all.
  3. The side-by-side threshold is 55 columns of it, so one dial over both would silently change when a panel is wide enough for two columns as a side effect of a change to the tab bar.

docs.title: Three palettes
docs.text:
Nocturne is the default and is untouched — the migration is the absence of a settings key, which is what makes an upgrade look exactly like the app you closed. Slate is the plain dark: neutral greys with no violet cast, for somebody who wants Nocturne's darkness without its colour. Daylight is the light one.

"Follow the system" is a rule rather than a fourth palette, and it chooses between Daylight and Nocturne — not Slate, because Slate is a deliberate departure from what this app looks like in the dark and having the operating system pick it would be the OS choosing the app's identity. It is live where the platform reports a change.

docs.title: What a light theme actually costs
docs.text:
A palette is not fifty colours but a set of seeds and weights: an ink, an accent, five grounds, and then the weights, which is what makes the difference between the three palettes data rather than fifty numbers each.

The weights are per palette, and that is the whole reason a light theme is work. Ink at 0.55 over Nocturne's ground is 5.2:1 and comfortable; the same weight over Daylight's is 3.5:1 and fails AA for body text. Every rung of Daylight's ladder was measured against its own ground and set so it matches or beats Nocturne's — and the figures are asserted by a test rather than left in a comment, with each floor being Nocturne's own measured value rounded down, so a floor is an observation about the shipped app rather than an aspiration and a new palette has to be at least as readable as the one this app has always had.

Four things needed real answers rather than an inversion, and each is where a light theme built by swapping two colours fails first:

  • The diff washes. The intra-line word marks are a step weaker on Daylight rather than stronger — they sit behind the syntax colours, and on a light ground a wash moves the paper away from the ink rather than towards it. The gap wash drops from 0.16 to 0.055: "a shade deeper than the ground" is the rule, and a sixth of black is a bruise on white.
  • The four verdicts. Nocturne's are pastels tuned not to vibrate on its ground; the same four on white are unreadable. Every one of the twelve verdict-on-ground pairs clears AA outright — a lower bar than the ink ladder's on purpose, because "is anything broken" is the only question the Checks tab is opened with.
  • Syntax highlighting, with the hue assignments kept — keyword takes the accent, strings green, numbers red — so you read the same code in the same colours at the value that ground needs.
  • The graph's lanes, declared per palette rather than derived, because the ramp positions that give six distinguishable lanes on a dark ground give Daylight one duplicate and one invisible.

The lane guard measured the wrong thing for a while

Its floor was a contrast ratio, which compares lightness — so two weights of one ink differ in exactly that and pass, while two real hues at one lightness score 1.00 and are unmistakable. The test licensed the ramp it existed to guard, and rendered, four of the six "lane colours" were duplicates of another. It is a perceptual colour distance now, and run against the old ramp it names four pairs as the same colour.

docs.title: Which figures are computed
docs.text: A reset and a sentence; the ticks live on the metrics page where the price of each group is legible. It is its own reset entry rather than a line in "metrics" — that one is the window the figures cover, and one reset over both would put your period back while you were turning a card on.

docs.title: Moving between places
docs.text:
Its own section, because there is no other it belongs in: everything else on that page is about how something is drawn or read, and this is about how the app is driven.

It holds the two-finger swipe, whose row is absent where the platform has no such gesture — and the preference is stored and reported as a changed section on every platform all the same, because a choice made on a laptop should not be forgotten because the app was last opened on a desktop.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
The interface in something other than English. French, partly filled, so far.

The choice is applied at the next launch, and the row says so — which is the decision worth arguing, because the other answer is reachable. Re-evaluating every binding that holds a translated string would change the ~1900 strings in the interface for one call and no edit to any of them.

What is not cheap is the other half: forty-nine sentences are produced during a walk rather than computed on read — why a file history is empty, why a comparison stopped, what a rebase plan summarises. Each is produced during a walk that is batched against a time budget precisely because it cannot be run again casually, so recomputing them means re-running those walks, and not recomputing them means a window half in each language — with the untranslated half being exactly the sentences that say why a list is empty, which is the state you are in front of when you have most reason to read carefully.

What makes waiting acceptable is that the row is honest about it, and while the chosen language is not the one on screen it names the one that is — "…until then the words on screen are French". A drop-down showing one language over a window drawn in another, with nothing said, is a control that reads as broken.

Each language is drawn by its own native name, because somebody looking for their language in an app they cannot currently read needs the one string they are certain to recognise.

Two things are never translated

A printed git command, because its output is meant to be pasted into a shell and a translated word in it is not a degraded answer but a command that does not run. And a control's git verb, which is the palette's search index — a translated stash push silently stops the palette finding it for anyone who searches the vocabulary, while its title is prose and is translated.

Both are asserted by tests, the second read off the source, because it is a fault in a declaration and is invisible at runtime until a catalogue happens to translate that verb.

docs.title: Where it all lives
docs.text:
The app's own settings are QSettings — one key per choice, including one key per panel size and one per figure group, so the file stays readable and migration is an absence per key: a build that adds a group finds no key for it and uses that group's own default, where a single stored list would have had to be read as complete.

Three things are JSON beside it rather than in it, because a growing list of records in a settings file is an abuse of the shape: the operation log, the action sequences, and the review draft. All three are written through on every edit — a save deferred to quit is a save that does not happen when the app is killed — and all three re-read immediately before writing, because two launches of the app used to erase each other.

The forge's answers are a database, which earns itself by answering three differently-shaped questions and by being a cache: its schema carries a version and a bump throws every row away, which is right for rows whose entire replacement cost is a round trip.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Signing and verifying, in all three formats. What a licence adds

Three questions that look like one: what this repository would sign with, how a buffer actually gets signed, and whether a signature somebody else made is good.

docs.title: libgit2 cannot sign, and that decides everything else
docs.text:
There is no signing call in the library. What it offers is the three-step dance its own header documents — build the commit's text without writing an object, have something else sign those bytes, then write the object with the signature in its header.

The "something else" is a program, because that is what git does too: git has never held a signing implementation either, and gpg.program exists precisely so a user can name theirs.

So this is the second thing in the app that shells out, and it keeps the subtree rules verbatim: arguments go as an argument list, never a command line and never a shell; no terminal prompt is allowed; and the program is asked rather than merely found, since one on the PATH that will not run leaves every control live and every press failing.

docs.title: Three formats, because gpg.format has three values
docs.text:
gpg.format Program Note openpgp gpg -bsau <key> The default ssh ssh-keygen -Y sign -n git -f <key> - Needs no keyring at all, which is why the format exists x509 smimesign -bsau <key> Presents gpg's interface over S/MIME, so it takes the same arguments

Shipping two and refusing the third would leave somebody whose employer mandates S/MIME with a client that reads their config, understands it, and declines — worse than one that never looked.

x509 is implemented and unexercised

No test here has run smimesign. What is pinned is that the format resolves to that program with those arguments.

gpg's exit code is not the test, and that is git's own finding: gpg exits 0 having warned instead of signed — an expired key, a subkey with no signing capability — so success is asserted from SIG_CREATED on the status channel.

docs.title: A refusal, never an unsigned commit
docs.text:
The one outcome this whole feature exists to prevent is a commit that was asked to be signed, was not, and said nothing.

No program, a program that will not start, a key that will not load, a passphrase with no agent to supply it, a wait that expired — each is a named sentence and a write that did not happen. There is no fall-through, because a repository whose policy is "everything is signed" is one where an unsigned commit is worse than no commit.

The plan and the write refuse in the same string, asserted by a test.

docs.title: Three different answers to "is this ready"
docs.text:
Not an inconsistency:

  • Probing — "would this work at all", for the settings page — is asynchronous and lazy, because a blocking gpg --version at startup is a wait every session pays for a feature most never use.
  • Signing is synchronous and deliberately does not consult the probe: a commit cannot be half-made, the signature has to be in hand between two libgit2 calls, and the alternative is making every write path in the app asynchronous to buy a responsive window during an operation that normally takes milliseconds. What that costs is stated: while a passphrase prompt is up the window does not repaint, and if the two-minute wait expires nothing is written.
  • Verification is asynchronous, because nothing waits on it.

docs.title: The per-commit override, in one direction only
docs.text:
A tick on Changes reading "commit without a signature, this once", absent unless commit.gpgsign is on.

Skipping a signature is a decision about this commit — the key is not to hand, the machine is somebody else's — and it is the case people actually hit. Signing one commit in a repository that signs none is a decision about the repository, there being no key configured for the app to name, and the honest way to make it is commit.gpgsign, which every other git tool then reads too.

It is keyed to config rather than to whether the program was found, for one reason: the probe answers a moment later, so a tick gated on it would appear under the pointer at the instant you were aiming at the commit button.

docs.title: A tag's signature is in its body
docs.text:
Unlike a commit's, which goes in a header. libgit2 has no signing variant of its tag call, so a signed tag is the object's own header lines assembled by hand with the armour after the message.

The printed command is -s rather than -S, which is git's own asymmetry: git tag -s is the signing verb and it replaces -a, a signed tag being annotated by construction.

docs.title: The replays sign, and git does not
docs.text:
git cherry-pick and git rebase do not re-sign what they replay unless they are given -S. So a signed history quietly loses its signatures the moment anything is rebased onto a new base — every commit comes out unsigned, and nothing says so.

This app follows commit.gpgsign in both replays instead. That is a departure from git, and the argument for it is that the replayed commit is a new object with a new committer: the signature on the original could not travel with it even in principle, since it signs bytes that include the parent and the committer. So the choice is not "keep the old signature or make a new one" — it is "make a new one or leave a gap", and a repository whose policy is that everything is signed wants the former.

It covers all six sites, including the four folds and rewords, which had no signing variant and would otherwise have come out unsigned while the picks beside them were signed — the worst of the two outcomes, because a history that is mostly signed is one nobody audits.

A signature that cannot be made stops the replay, in the signing layer's own sentence rather than a generic "could not commit <sha>": the cause is a key or a program, and naming the commit would hide it.

docs.title: Reading somebody else's signature
docs.text:
Four verdicts, drawn as a mark on the commit row with a tooltip naming it:

good Verified bad Cryptographically unsound unknown Sound, and the signer is not on any list this machine has unsigned There is no signature

Plus four states about the reading rather than the signature: known, asking, spent (the per-list ceiling was reached), failed.

unsigned is drawn rather than left blank, and that is the whole reason the column is legible. Drawing nothing for it is the obvious economy and exactly the mistake: a blank would mean both "there is no signature" and "nothing has looked yet", and the second is the ordinary state of every row that has just scrolled into view. So it is a faint hollow dot, and a genuinely blank square means only that this row has not been answered.

docs.title: It is asked per visible row
docs.text:
Verifying is a subprocess per commit and a history is thousands of rows, so a row asks as it is drawn — the cost follows what you are looking at rather than how long the history is. Presence is free and settles most rows without a process starting, and an unsigned commit is deliberately not charged to the ceiling: spending it on the free answer would make a long unsigned history stop answering half way down for no reason you could see.

Only one process runs at a time: a process per row all at once is a fork bomb with a scroll bar.

docs.title: Two answers that must not be wrong
docs.text:
A missing allowed-signers file is unknown and never bad. The ssh verify verb answers "is this from somebody on the list", and with no list the answer is no — for every ssh signature, including every good one. Reported as bad that would be this app accusing a colleague of forgery because a file is missing. So the verdict is taken in two steps: is the signature cryptographically sound at all (which needs no list), and only then, is its signer allowed.

The format is read from the signature and never from gpg.format. A repository that has moved from gpg to ssh holds both kinds, and asking gpg about an SSH signature produces "no valid OpenPGP data" — which drawn as bad would accuse somebody of forgery for having signed the older way. Config decides what is written; the armour on the object decides what is read.

docs.title: Searching for signed commits
docs.text:
The history's signature filter — any, signed, not signed, signed with a key — matches presence and never validity, and the field says so where it is offered.

Validity is a subprocess per commit inside a walk that is batched against a ten-millisecond budget precisely because it cannot be run again casually, so a filter that quietly meant "validly signed" would answer a question nobody asked at a price nobody agreed to.

Signed with matches a key, and the field says that too. A person's name is not in a signature — gpg keeps it in the keyring and ssh in allowed_signers — so producing one means running the signing program per commit. What is in the bytes is the identity that can be read without one: an SHA256:… fingerprint for SSH, computed as ssh-keygen -lf computes it, and the 16-hex issuer key id for OpenPGP. An X.509 signature has a signer this cannot name and drops out rather than being guessed at.

docs.title: The settings page reads and never writes
docs.text:
The four values are git's own, read by every other git tool on the machine, and a second set of fields here would be a quieter route to writing them with none of git's own per-repository / per-user / system-wide semantics around them.

What the page does carry is the half you cannot see from your own config file: the program that was found, said to be found rather than chosen, and whether it would run. The allowed-signers row is absent off gpg.format = ssh, and says plainly when there is no file — because without it every ssh signature verifies as an unknown key, which is a different piece of news from a bad one and must never be drawn as one.

docs.title: Splitting a branch
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. This page is stacked-branches. What a licence adds

A proposal nobody will review because it is too big is the commonest complaint anybody makes about anybody else's work, and the answer everywhere else is "split it up" — which until now meant leaving the app for a terminal and an afternoon of rebase -i and checkout -p. This is that errand as one operation, at four granularities: a commit, a file, a hunk, or the lines picked out of one.

What comes out is a stack of branches, each based on the one before it, each proposable on its own. What is not touched is the branch you split: it keeps its commits, its hashes, its upstream and its pull request.

docs.title: How to split one
docs.text:
1. On Manage → Branches, open a branch's ⋮ — or right-click the row — and choose Split into a stack.
  2. Check the On field at the top. That is the branch the first part will sit on; it arrives filled in with the branch's recorded base, or the trunk as this checkout has it, and it has to be a branch you actually have (see below).
  3. Press Fill this one on the part you are loading. Everything you take goes there until you choose another part. Any part can be filled, the last one included.

  4. Take change, at whatever size suits it:

    You want Where to press A whole file Take on the file's row in the middle pane A whole commit the Commits chip, then click the commit's row One hunk click the file to read it, then Take hunk in the hunk's header Some lines click each line in the diff, then Take 3 lines

  5. Give each part a branch name and a commit message. The sentence under the header says what is still missing, and once it is clear it says how many changes will land in the last part instead.

  6. Press Split. You land back on Branches with the new branches there, and you propose each one from its own row.

Cancel costs nothing. Nothing on that page writes: an assignment is a note the app keeps until you press Split, so walking away drops the arrangement and leaves the repository exactly as it was.

docs.title: The last part is whatever is left over
docs.text:
Parts partition the branch's diff, and the last one takes everything you did not assign. That is what makes the parts add up to the branch: nothing can be dropped by an arithmetic mistake, because the last part's tree is the branch's tree.

You can still fill it like any other part, and its row says so — "2 pieces, and everything left over". Doing that is a convenience rather than a mechanism: what you put there was already going there. But "these files in part 1 and those in part 2" is what splitting something in two means, and with two parts the second one is the remainder, so the page would otherwise refuse the most obvious arrangement there is. A change still belongs to one part only, wherever you put it.

Where nothing is left for the last part, the split is refused by name — give it something, or make one part fewer.

docs.title: Nothing is rewritten, and that is why it is safe
docs.text:
Each part's tree is synthesised from the branch's diff rather than replayed: part n's tree is the base tree with the pieces of parts 1…n applied, worked out by walking the diff and emitting each line or not. Three things follow, and each is a state this operation cannot reach:

  • A conflict is not possible. Not unlikely — impossible. The selections are disjoint subsets of one diff, so composing them is concatenation rather than a merge. There is no stop point and nothing for the Conflicts surface to finish.
  • The working tree and the index are never written. It is the only write in the app that does not care whether your working tree is dirty, and it runs perfectly well while a rebase, merge or cherry-pick is half-finished, because nothing it touches is in their way.
  • HEAD does not move and your branch is not touched. The parts are new branches beside it. That is what makes the whole thing reversible.

Everything is checked before one object is written — every name, every piece, every message — because a split that made two branches and then found the third name taken would leave a stack that is neither what you asked for nor what was there.

docs.title: A commit is a shortcut, and it says when it is a coarse one
docs.text:
Pressing a commit takes every file it touched. Where its files are its own — the ordinary shape of a branch somebody wants split, "the API change and the docs change" — that is exactly its work.

Where another commit in the range touched one of the same files, the row is tagged shares files and what you get is the whole file rather than that commit's lines. This is not a shortcoming to be fixed: a commit's contribution to a file a later commit rewrote is not in the branch's diff at all, because the lines it wrote are gone. The tag is there so a coarse selection is one you chose rather than one you were not told about.

docs.title: Files that can only be taken whole
docs.text:
Some files are tagged whole only, and the row says which of four reasons it is: it is binary, so it has no lines to pick from; the branch deletes it, and taking some of its lines would leave a shorter file rather than remove one; it moves, and a hunk of one name is a claim about the other; or only its mode changed, so there is no hunk to take.

Two parts may hold different hunks of the same file — that is the point of hunk granularity. What is refused is the same piece in two parts.

docs.title: The base has to be a branch you have
docs.text:
The On field takes a local branch, and only local branches are offered. A stack is recorded per branch in this checkout, so there is nowhere to record one against origin/main — the server's copy of the trunk is not something the first part can sit on. Pointed at one anyway, the page says so and names the branch to use instead.

The diff itself is measured from the merge base, which is what a pull request shows and the only reading that stays right when the base branch has moved on since you cut yours. Measured from the base's tip instead, a part would carry the base's own newer commits backwards — a plausible-looking diff that undoes somebody else's work.

docs.title: Undoing one
docs.text:
Manage → Operations carries one row: Delete the N branches it made. There is nothing about your branch to put back, because it was never modified.

It works while the parts are untouched. Commit onto one of them and it is refused by name rather than forcing over your work — a part's commit is not reachable from HEAD, so the delete has to be forced, and what earns forcing it is that the tip is still exactly where the split left it. Unmoved, that commit is a synthesis whose every line is still in the branch it came from, so dropping it loses nothing. A branch you have already deleted by hand is not a failure, so a split half tidied up can still be finished from the log.

docs.title: What it deliberately does not do
docs.text:
• A part lands as one commit. Assign three of the branch's commits to a part and their changes arrive as a single commit, not three: a part is a synthesis, so there is no original commit for it to preserve. Where keeping the commits matters, reorder them with the interactive rebase first and split the result.
  • The parts are authored by you, now. A synthesis is a mixture with no single author, so there is no original authorship to carry. They are signed where your repository signs commits — see Signing.
  • Your existing pull request is untouched by a split. Splitting writes only names that were free, so closing or re-pointing the original is your decision on the forge. Where the errand is "take this out of that proposal", the other verb crosses that line on purpose and says so — see Taking pieces out of a proposal.
  • A part need not compile. Take half a hunk and you can leave a file that does not build. That is true of every tool offering this granularity, and it is your judgement rather than something the app will refuse.

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
The synthesis is checked byte for byte at all four granularities against a repository built to order, including the two shapes where an off-by-one would hide: taking an addition without the removal it replaced, and taking one line out of a block of three. The guarantee the whole design rests on — that the parts add up to the branch — is asserted as a tree equality, and the plan and the operation are required to refuse in the same sentence, so what the page promises cannot drift from what the button does.

The page's own arrangement logic is covered separately. What no test here covers is a repository with more than one local branch drawn in the QML suite: the shared fixture has one, and adding another would move counts other suites assert — so the git behaviour is pinned in C++ and the page's behaviour is pinned against a branch that is deliberately not there.

docs.title: Stash, worktrees, submodules, subtrees
docs.text:
Licensing — Free, with paid parts. Create, apply, pop and drop a stash, and everything about worktrees, submodules and sparse checkout, are free. Rewriting a stash is stash-rewrite and subtrees are subtree. What a licence adds

Four tabs on Manage, plus sparse checkout. Everything here is about something the repository holds beside its history.

docs.title: Stash
docs.text: Push, pop, apply, drop and branch, plus four verbs that are rare or unique.

docs.title: Stashing only what is staged
docs.text:
git stash push --staged has no libgit2 equivalent — the library's stash always takes the whole working tree, and its keep-index flag only puts the staged changes back afterwards. So the entry is assembled by hand, in a shape git stash list, git stash show and apply --index all read as their own.

The harder half is taking the staged change back out of the working tree, because a reverse patch takes its pre-image from the index and so cannot be laid over a file that also has unstaged edits — the ordinary case in an app that stages hunks and lines. A file with none is checked out of HEAD again, or deleted where the stash is what created it; a file with both is rebuilt by a three-way merge with the index as the common ancestor, the working tree as ours and HEAD as theirs, which leaves the never-staged edits sitting in the file.

A merge that will not resolve refuses the whole operation, by path, before anything is written: half a stash is worse than none.

docs.title: Editing a stash
docs.text:
A stash is an immutable commit reached only through refs/stash's reflog, and libgit2 offers no store or replace — so editing one means building a new stash commit and putting it back in the same stack slot. Three things make that work:

  • Un-recording a change is not deleting an entry. Removing a path from the stash's tree makes the stash say "this file was deleted", so applying it would delete the file. The path is instead reset to the base commit's version, leaving the stash recording no change for it. A path the stash itself created has no base version, and there the entry really is dropped.
  • Every tree the stash owns is rewritten, the index parent included — or apply --index would resurrect a file that was just removed. The base parent is left alone; it is real history.
  • The reflog has no "replace entry N". The entries above the target are read out, dropped, and re-appended around the new one — and refs/stash is updated before the rebuilt log is written, because updating a ref appends a reflog entry of its own that would otherwise leave a duplicate at the top of the stack.

Renaming rewrites both the commit's message and the reflog entry's, because what git stash list prints comes from the reflog and changing only the commit would look right in the app and wrong in git. The On <branch>: prefix is preserved, since the branch is recorded nowhere else.

Duplicating is additive — a second reflog entry pointing at the same commit. Nothing is rewritten, dropping one leaves the other, and editing one rewrites only that entry, at which point they stop sharing.

Restoring individual files is the non-destructive counterpart to removal: paths are checked out of the stash's tree into the working tree and the stash is untouched.

Stashing is free forever

Create, apply, pop and drop are never gated: stashing is where work goes to be safe. Editing a stash is what a licence adds.

docs.title: Worktrees
docs.text:
List, add, remove, and switch — and switching is just opening the other path, so every controller re-reads from the new working tree. Removal therefore refuses to delete the one that is currently open.

git's own list reports only linked worktrees, so the main one is synthesised from the repository's common directory and always listed first. Opening a linked worktree resolves the same set, because every lookup goes through the common directory rather than the worktree's own gitdir.

docs.title: Submodules
docs.text:
The full lifecycle: add, init, update, sync, set-url, deinit, and "open this as a repository" — the last being the cheapest useful thing here.

Two files, and only one of them is history. .gitmodules is tracked: it is what the project says about its submodules, and a comment somebody wrote in it is as much a part of the tree as any other line. .git/config is this checkout's private copy, written by init and sync and taken back by deinit. Every write edits the one entry it was asked about and leaves every other line where it found it — nothing here reads a file into a model and writes the model back.

That is also why set-url does not sync and sync does not set a url: they write different files, one of them is a commit and the other is not, and doing both at once would hide which half the rest of the team is going to receive.

Adding is three steps and stopping after the first is the hazard: the entry and the gitlink are prepared, the clone fetches, and the pair is staged. Skip the last and the entry and the clone exist while the index records no gitlink — a submodule registered, present and untracked all at once. The middle step is the only one that can fail for a reason outside this repository, so a clone that fails is rolled back: .gitmodules restored byte for byte, the directory and the modules entry removed.

Init and clone are two buttons because they are two different promises. Init copies the url into .git/config and touches nothing else: instant, offline, and the one step that always works where the clone has no credential to offer a private remote. Update needs a remote to answer. Folding them into one control would make the cheap certain thing inherit the expensive uncertain one's failure mode.

Not initialised is a state, not a fault — it is what every fresh clone looks like.

docs.title: Deinit refuses rather than clobbers, and there is no force
docs.text:
It is the only thing in this app that deletes a repository's working tree, and it is only allowed at all because the objects live in the superproject's .git/modules rather than under the working copy — so Init brings the same clone back.

That reasoning fails in exactly three cases and each is refused by name:

  1. Uncommitted changes, untracked files included — those are in no tree, so no tree can restore them.
  2. Commits no remote-tracking ref can reach. Computed as a revwalk with every local tip pushed and every remote ref hidden, which is exact where comparing a branch against its upstream is not: a submodule normally sits on a detached HEAD with no branch and no upstream, and a commit made there is the case most worth catching.
  3. The old layout where the git directory sits inside the working copy, and removing it would take the history along.

No force exists. Every refusal names something to go and settle in the submodule, and the row already opens it as a repository. A flag that skipped the check would be the only route in this app to losing work that is nowhere else.

docs.title: Subtrees
docs.text:
Somebody else's repository vendored into a folder of this one — and the only feature here that runs the git command line.

git subtree is a shell script that ships with git. There is no subtree API in libgit2 and there never has been: its four verbs are a subtree merge with a rewritten path prefix, a synthesised squash commit, a push of a split history, and the split itself, which rewrites history. Reimplementing them would be a feature the size of the rebase engine, built from a shell script's semantics, with every subtle case this app's own to be wrong about.

So it runs the script and reads what it says. The cost is stated rather than assumed: with no git, the tab draws a sentence naming that libgit2 has no subtree support at all, rather than controls that cannot work. git is asked rather than merely found — a git on the PATH that will not run would otherwise leave every button live and every press failing — and asked asynchronously and lazily, because a blocking probe in a constructor is a wait every session pays for a feature most never open.

Two rules apply here that do not to a read-only probe, because these calls write: every argument goes as an argument in a list, never a command line and never a shell; and a prefix is refused if it is absolute, contains .., or is a bare ., since a prefix reaches a path and is the one thing you type that could name a write outside the checkout.

There is no list, so the list is inferred. git keeps no registry — no config section, no file — but git subtree writes a git-subtree-dir: trailer into the commits it makes, so the list is a walk of the history looking for it. That finds subtrees added at the command line years before this app existed, which a record of the app's own would not; and a prefix somebody deleted by hand goes on being listed, saying "folder gone" rather than dropping out.

The walk is O(history), so it is asked for rather than refreshed — one commit message per commit is cheap per commit and not cheap in total, and this was in the general refresh for a while under a comment calling it "the same order of work as the tag list". A tag list is O(refs).

What is remembered is what git does not keep. git subtree pull takes the url and the branch as arguments every time and keeps neither, so without a note every pull is a retyping. They live in .git/config, not .gitmodules, because git records nothing here for a teammate to receive.

Squashing is on by default, which is the opposite of git's own default and deliberate: without it every commit of the other project is replayed into this history, which is what makes subtrees unpopular.

Removing one is git rm -r and a commit, because git subtree has no remove — refused while anything under the prefix is uncommitted, that content being in no commit and no reflog.

docs.title: Sparse checkout
docs.text:
Which of a repository's directories are on disk at all.

Reading needs no git; writing does. What is in force, whether cone mode is on and how many entries the index is skipping are answered through libgit2. The verbs shell out — and the reason is stronger than the subtree's: writing the pattern file and setting the config is four lines, and doing it would produce a repository that is configured and inert. libgit2 has no sparse support of any kind: it knows what the skip-worktree bit is and sets it nowhere. The file would be there, the config would be true, every file would still be on disk, and nothing on screen could tell that from a sparse checkout that happens to include everything.

Cone mode only, with the caveat on the tab rather than in a comment. git has two pattern languages: cone takes directories and non-cone takes full gitignore-style patterns. A directory picker is a control somebody can use, where a field accepting a negated recursive glob is one where a mistyped pattern silently removes a thousand files — and, the half that decides it, the refusal has to be exact: deciding whether a path survives a proposed set is a line of arithmetic in cone mode and a reimplementation of git's matcher in the other, and a refusal computed by a matcher that disagreed with git's would be a promise this app cannot keep, in the one direction where being wrong deletes uncommitted work.

A repository already using non-cone patterns is read and reported, never converted.

It refuses over the files, by name, before anything is written. Narrowing deletes from the working tree, and anything uncommitted in a directory that is leaving is in no commit and no reflog. git's own sparse-checkout set warns and carries on; that is a state to be in deliberately rather than one to arrive in from a directory picker.

The picker is HEAD's tree and not the working directory, which is the whole point: a directory that is already skipped is not on disk, and a filesystem listing would leave it out of the one control that could bring it back. Ticks assemble a proposed set and Apply spends it, because a checkout per tick would be a dozen working-tree rewrites for one decision — and an empty set is refused rather than read as "everything", since in cone mode it means the root's own files and nothing else.

Implemented and unexercised

The sparse verbs run git sparse-checkout, which no test here does: a suite that ran one would be asserting git's behaviour rather than this app's, and would fail on any machine whose git predates cone mode. What is pinned is the reading, the cone matcher, and that the plan and the verb refuse in the same words.

docs.title: Tags and notes
docs.text:
Licensing — Free. Both, entirely. What a licence adds

Two ways of saying something about a commit without changing it: a tag, which gives it a name, and a note, which gives it text. Both are refs, and neither rewrites anything.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Manage → Tags lists every tag, newest first by the commit it resolves to, and creates and deletes them.

The two kinds are genuinely different objects rather than a display detail, and the row says which leads. An annotated tag is an object of its own with an author, a message and a date — and is the only kind that can be signed. A lightweight tag is a ref and nothing else, so its second line falls back to the subject of the commit it names. Borrowing the commit's author and date to fill the empty fields would make the two kinds look alike, which is the one distinction the row exists to draw.

The age column is the target commit's for both kinds, so a figure read down the list compares like with like.

A duplicate is refused, and there is no force. Moving a tag that has been pushed is how two people end up with the same name pointing at two commits; deleting it and making it again is the same act with the loss visible.

An annotated tag with no message is refused, as git refuses it: the message is the whole content of the object, and an empty one would read in the list exactly like a lightweight tag that cost less.

An annotated tag is signed where this repository signs, through the same signer commits go through — see Signing.

A tag's two verbs are Show in history, which narrows the history to what the tag can reach, and Delete. Making one is recorded in the operation log as an operation with a named opposite: a tag is a ref, so creating one destroyed nothing and deleting it again restores exactly the state before.

Pushing a tag is not offered

Transport moves branches. A tag made here is local until you push the ref yourself, and the app does not pretend otherwise by listing a verb it does not have.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
A note is text attached to a commit and kept outside it, on a ref of its own — refs/notes/commits unless core.notesRef says otherwise. It is written from a commit's own menu in History, and it is what to reach for when something has to be said about a commit after the fact: a review verdict, a ticket that turned up later, why this one was reverted. The alternative is rewriting history to add a sentence.

The dialog states three facts before you write anything, because each is something you would otherwise find out afterwards:

  • The commit's hash does not change. Writing a note is not a rewrite, so nothing above it is replayed and nothing anybody has pulled goes stale. That is what separates this from rewording, which is a rebase.
  • It is not pushed with the commit. Notes refs are not in a default refspec, so a note stays on this machine until somebody pushes that ref by name. Silence about that would be the worst of it — a reviewer writing three notes and expecting the author to read them.
  • It is a ref, so it can be moved. Which one is in force is read from the repository rather than assumed, and the dialog names it: "this commit has no note" and "this commit has no note on the ref this repository is pointed at" are different things to be told.

An empty note is refused rather than read as a removal. Removing one is its own row on the dialog, and deliberately not the primary press.

Nothing is confirmed twice. Writing over a note destroys nothing held in no object: the previous text goes into the operation log's entry and the row there offers to put it back by name, which is also what happens when one is removed.

Notes are read for one commit when that commit is selected, never on a refresh: History is thousands of rows and none of this is worth knowing until a row is chosen.

docs.title: The tracker
docs.text:
Licensing — Paid. The tracker is tickets. The link rules that turn an id into something to press are free, permanently. What a licence adds

What the work is for is on a page this app is not: a ticket in GitHub Issues, Jira or Linear. Tickets is a destination of its own that reads that board and writes back to it — what is assigned to you, what a commit's PROJ-88 actually says, and moving one when the work lands.

The link rules are not replaced and never will be. Turning #412 into something to press needs no key, no network and no configuration, works on a tracker this app has never heard of, and is free — see A ticket id, and the page it names. Everything on this page is what you get in addition, once you have said which tracker and handed over a key.

docs.title: Its own destination, not a tab of Manage
docs.text:
Manage's tabs are things a repository holds — its stashes, its worktrees, its hooks. A tracker is somebody else's service and the tickets on it outlive this checkout, which is the argument that moved Branches out of Manage and gave Pull requests and Checks seats of their own.

There are three states before there is a list, because an empty list is the one answer this must never give by default: no tracker configured, no key, and the tracker said no are facts about everything except the board. Drawing all four as an empty frame is how an integration earns its reputation for lying.

docs.title: Setting one up
docs.text:
Four keys go in .git/config under sourcemanager.tickets — provider, host, scope, account — which is the link rules' rule and its reason: a statement about this repository's tickets cannot arrive with somebody else's branch, and two checkouts of two projects do not share a board.

No key is written there. It goes in the platform password store, keyed by host, and a test asserts that nothing credential-shaped reaches a file you might share.

Where the tracker is the forge your remote is on, there is nothing to paste at all — being signed in for the proposals is being signed in for the issues. The host has to match: a remote on github.com with a tracker on an enterprise host is two accounts, and handing one's token to the other would send a credential somewhere it was not issued for.

GitHub Issues Scope is owner/repo. No key needed where you are already signed in for proposals Jira Scope is a project key. An API token and your account email — Jira's tokens are HTTP Basic, which is why this provider alone draws a second field Linear Scope is a team key. A personal API key

A tracker with no scope is refused rather than written. Half-configured is the worst state to be in: every request 404s and that reads as a broken key.

Changing a setting is not a one-way door. The fields are drawn filled in from what is configured, and pressing the same button writes whatever is in them — so moving to a second Linear team, or pasting a token that was rotated, is one field. Use a different tracker means "start from the picker", and clearing everything is its own row, named for what it does, last on the page because it is the destructive one.

docs.title: Two fields for a state, and why you see both
