docs.text:
Tracker What it actually has GitHub Two states, plus a reason on a closed one since 2022 Jira A workflow per project, named by an administrator Linear Five fixed types, any number of named statuses under each

A shared vocabulary holding all three would be Jira's, and the other two would be pretending. So a ticket carries both: status is the tracker's own word, drawn verbatim, and state is one of four categories — open, started, done, cancelled — which is what a colour, a filter and a count are built on.

Jira maps onto three of the four, having no notion of cancelled apart from done, so a ticket resolved "Won't Do" is done here. That is a real loss and it is the honest mapping — inventing cancelled out of a resolution name would be guessing at words an administrator chose — and what stops the loss being invisible is that their word survives beside it.

docs.title: What a tracker tracks is declared, never assumed
docs.text:
A table written against the union of three trackers draws six empty columns on GitHub Issues, which is how a reader learns to stop reading a list. One written against the intersection throws away most of what Linear knows. So each provider declares its fields, and a field it does not declare is absent from the table, the ticket page and the menu.

GitHub Issues Jira Linear Status read/write read/write (a transition) read/write Assignee read/write, several read/write, one read/write Labels read/write read/write read/write Cycle milestone, write sprint, read cycle, write Priority — read/write read/write Estimate — story points, read read/write Due — read/write read/write Parent / sub-issues — read parent, write Blocking / blocked by — read read Project / team — project, read read/write

Present and writable are two questions, and the asymmetry is real rather than an oversight: Jira reports story points and will not take them from here, the field's id being per site and a control that wrote it blind putting a number in some other field entirely. A field a tracker will not take is refused by name and without a request — the alternative is what makes a write look like it worked, Jira accepting a PUT naming a field it does not have, answering 204 and changing nothing.

docs.title: The columns default to five, not to everything
docs.text:
Status, assignee, priority, due, last moved. Linear declares nineteen fields and a table opening with all of them is the "too cluttered to read" report the branch table already earned once.

The title is never a column — it is the one elastic thing on the row — nor is the body, which is a document rather than a cell, nor the key, which is the row's own leading slot so it lines up down the list.

docs.title: Filters, not three hard-coded readings
docs.text:
The chips are the same vocabulary the proposals and the CI runs use, and a chip narrows what has already been read — it costs no request. What replaced was three readings (Mine, Open, and a search box) that each sent a different request: exactly three questions, no way to ask a fourth, and a round trip between them.

The search box stays, because it is not a filter — it asks the tracker to look through tickets this app has never read.

The built-in readings are Unfinished, In progress, Finished and All, plus three that earn their place:

  • Unfinished is the resting reading and what an unmarked tab counts. Deliberately not open, which is one of the four categories and would drop everything anybody has started.
  • Ready to start — unfinished, unstarted and unblocked. This is the reading that makes the blocking fields worth filling: a board where everything is blocked by something looks busy and is stopped.
  • Overdue, which is a due date further in the past than nothing at all.
  • Mine, absent where no login is known rather than drawn as a chip that could only ever be empty.

The vocabulary is the shared one rather than the configured tracker's, and that is the opposite of what the columns do, deliberately: a saved filter is yours and travels with you, so a reader with a Linear repository and a GitHub one would otherwise find their filters silently changing meaning as they walked between the two. A clause naming a field this tracker does not fill matches nothing rather than everything — the safe way round, because a filter that found nothing is visibly wrong where one that found everything looks like it worked.

A saved question earns three routes: counted on the tab's badge, kept as a chip on the strip along the foot of the window, and watched. A watched one announces a ticket that matches, once, and never off the first list read — everything on a board when you open it has already happened, and a hundred notifications on arrival is how a notification is taught to be ignored.

docs.title: Reading and writing one ticket
docs.text:
The description, the comments and every declared field are on the ticket's own page, with an editor where the tracker will take one and absent entirely where it declares nothing — a panel of eight empty rows on GitHub Issues being what the catalogue exists to avoid. The title, the description and your own comments can all be rewritten, which is the ordinary reason somebody opens a ticket they already know about.

The status is one drop-down, opening onto where the ticket can go from where it stands. The choices are asked for when the control opens, never per row, and on Jira they are the transitions — what a ticket can move to depends on where it is, so they are replaced rather than accumulated. A tracker that cannot be written to draws a tag instead.

Whether a comment is yours is the provider's answer, not a comparison of two display names: GitHub answers a login, Jira a display name beside an account id whose email is hidden by default, and Linear a bit. Comparing strings would offer Edit on somebody else's comment about half the time.

A write is re-read rather than claimed. A Jira workflow can have a post-function that changes the assignee, a field or a resolution, and a claim would be confidently wrong about every one of them — which is why Jira's transition endpoint answers 204 with an empty body. Jira also hands a comment back changed, its descriptions being a JSON document tree rather than markdown.

Creating one takes a title and a body and nothing else, deliberately, and the dialog says so: a tracker's create form is a project's own — issue types, components, required custom fields — and a form drawing half of it would fail on submission with a message about a field it never showed.

docs.title: Nothing costs a request that was not asked for
docs.text:
refresh() is a config read and no request at all, which is what lets it sit on the general refresh path while the list does not. The list is asked for, by Reload or by a query being pressed; typing in the query box fetches nothing per keystroke. The ticket hover on a commit subject in History answers out of the list already read, and says nothing where that list has never been read.

Arriving on a list read longer ago than your page-refresh setting asks again. Zero minutes is never, and a board never read at all is not stale — that is a first fetch, and this destination does not make one on arrival, or every ⌃Tab would carry a request.

docs.title: Both lists are paged, and say when a bound stopped them
docs.text:
A GraphQL connection answers a page, and publishing that page as the answer is how a board of two hundred reads as a board of fifty with a count on screen to prove it. On GitHub it is worse than a truncation: /issues answers pull requests too and they are dropped afterwards, so a repository that proposes more than it files gets a first page that is entirely pull requests and a tab that is empty for a reason nothing explains.

So both page, both are bounded — a board of ten thousand is a hundred requests behind one press, which is a rate limit rather than a feature — and the count line says when the bound stopped the read.

A read reports two things. As well as "it failed and here is why", there is "it worked and here is what you cannot see from the rows": how many were read, how many were dropped and why, and whether a bound stopped it. The page has three empties with three sentences — a filter matching none of what was read, a board with nothing on it, and a read that fetched rows and showed none of them — because an empty list is only the thing empty means if everything else says which it is.

docs.title: Licensing and what is proven
docs.text:
The tracker is a paid feature (tickets). The link rules are free, permanently.

Fixture-proved, not live-proved

Nothing here has been run against a live Jira or Linear. Their tests pin the requests built and the JSON mapped onto the documented fields, from recorded replies; a green suite says the mapping is right about the JSON that was recorded and says nothing about the API having that shape today. GitHub Issues is the one that could be live-proved, its token being the one this project has.

No fixture carries a credential, asserted by a test that reads its own bytes back.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
There is no installer yet, on any platform. What the release pipeline produces is a runnable build rather than a distributable one, so getting the app is either downloading a release artifact or building it — both are documented in Installing.

Once it is running, three pages cover finding your way:

  • :material-download: Installing

    Dependencies, cmake -B build ., and the install rules per platform.

  • :material-view-dashboard-outline: A tour of the window

    The breadcrumb, the tab bar, the operation banner, and the nine destinations.

  • :material-keyboard: Keyboard and the palette

    ⌘K, the two-press hint overlay, ⌃Tab, and moving back and forward.

docs.title: The first five minutes
docs.text:
1. Register a repository. The app opens on the fleet page. Press Add ▾ and pick one of the four ways in: Import repository for a checkout already on disk, Clone, New repository, or Scan a folder to find every checkout beneath one directory at once. See The fleet.
  2. Open it. Press the card. The whole tile is the target, not the small button in the corner.
  3. Read the history. The History tab opens on your own branch's tip rather than at the top of the list, with that commit's files and diff already on screen.
  4. Stage something. On Changes, tick a file, or select lines in the diff and stage those. Space stages or unstages whatever is picked.
  5. Learn one keyboard route. Tap ⌘ (or Ctrl) once and let go — every primary control on screen grows a letter. Press the letter. Tab reveals the long tail; Esc puts them away.

docs.title: Two things that surprise people
docs.text:
The branch crumb does not check out. Choosing a branch in the breadcrumb's picker narrows the history to it. That is what clicking a branch has always meant here, the picker says so in as many words, and people rely on it. Checking out lives on Manage → Branches, where the row also tells you what the checkout would overwrite before you press it.

A control that cannot apply is not drawn. Not greyed — absent. So a repository with no remote has no Push button rather than a dead one, and the first reading of a thinner-looking window is usually that a verb does not apply here rather than that it is missing. The exceptions are deliberate and few: the transport buttons grey while a transfer is running (the verb applies, it is just busy), and an AI control with no provider configured stays live so that pressing it can explain itself.

docs.title: From a release
docs.text:
Tagged releases carry four artifacts:

Platform Artifact Self-contained? macOS SourceManager-<version>-macOS.dmg yes Windows SourceManager-<version>-Windows-x64.zip yes Debian, Ubuntu source-manager_<version>-1_amd64.deb no — needs system Qt and libgit2 Linux SourceManager-<version>-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz no — needs system Qt and libgit2

Releases are published to source-manager/dist.

docs.title: macOS: Homebrew, or the disk image
docs.text:
brew tap source-manager/tap
brew install --cask source-manager
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/SourceManager.app

macOS runs its first-launch check on the com.apple.quarantine attribute, which is set by whatever downloaded a file; Homebrew sets it on what it installs, and the second line takes it off. Without that the app installs and then refuses to launch, because these builds carry an ad-hoc signature rather than a Developer ID one. Open Anyway in System Settings > Privacy & Security does the same thing.

It is arm64 only — built on an Apple Silicon runner against a non-universal Qt — and the cask declares it, so brew refuses on an Intel Mac instead of installing something that cannot run.

The disk image is the other way: open it and drag the app onto the Applications folder beside it. Being unsigned, it is refused on first launch — and on macOS 15 and later the Control-click > Open bypass no longer exists. Open it, let it be refused, then go to System Settings > Privacy & Security and press Open Anyway.

docs.title: Debian and Ubuntu: the apt repository
docs.text:
Add it once and the app upgrades with the rest of the system:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/source-manager.asc \
  https://source-manager-apt.pages.dev/source-manager.asc
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/sources.list.d/source-manager.sources \
  https://source-manager-apt.pages.dev/source-manager.sources
sudo apt update && sudo apt install source-manager

Check it landed, and see where it came from:

apt policy source-manager

Then it is an ordinary package:

sudo apt upgrade                             # with everything else
sudo apt install source-manager=<version>-1  # a particular release
sudo apt remove source-manager               # or `purge` to take the config too

Every release stays in the repository, so a pin and a downgrade work as well — which matters on the day a release is the thing you need to get away from.

The second file names the key in its Signed-By:, so this project's key is trusted for this source rather than for every source on your machine, which is what the old apt-key route did.

There is no Homebrew route on Linux: brew has no casks there, and a formula cannot install a .deb — no dpkg, no root, and a package whose dependencies come from apt landing in a brew prefix.

apt update says NO_PUBKEY

The signing key was rotated and your copy predates it. Re-download the key file over the first curl above and run apt update again; nothing else needs to change, and the packages you have already installed are unaffected.

apt says the package has unmet dependencies

It is built against Ubuntu 26.04's Qt 6.10 and declares that, so apt refuses it on anything older rather than installing something that will not start. On an older release take the tarball and its system Qt, or build from source — both are below.

Or take the .deb off the release and install it by hand with apt rather than dpkg — apt pulls the dependencies in, where dpkg only reports that they are missing:

sudo apt install ./source-manager_<version>-1_amd64.deb

Either way it is built against Ubuntu 26.04's Qt 6.10, so apt refuses it on anything older — which is the good version of that failure. The tarball is the same tree without the metadata, for distributions that are not dpkg ones.

docs.title: A test build somebody sent you
docs.text:
A .deb handed over directly, rather than taken from the repository above. It is the same package; it is just not signed for, indexed by, or upgraded through apt, so everything here is manual and deliberate.

sudo apt install ./source-manager_<version>-1_amd64.deb

apt, not dpkg -i: apt resolves the Qt and libgit2 the package declares, where dpkg only reports that they are missing. If apt refuses it over dependencies, the build does not match your distribution — and it can be built for a newer or an older one, since libgit2 is depended on by SONAME and the package name differs per release. Say which distribution you are on and ask for a matching build, rather than forcing it: a forced install produces an app that starts and then fails somewhere else entirely.

Run it from the applications menu, as Source Manager, or in a terminal:

SourceManager

It needs a graphical session. Over plain ssh with no X or Wayland forwarding it exits on the platform plugin, which reads as a broken package and is not one.

When something goes wrong, what makes a report answerable is:

  • what you did and what happened instead;
  • lsb_release -ds and apt policy source-manager;
  • the log, at ~/.local/share/pasdam/SourceManager/logs/sourcemanager-<date>.log.

The log records the paths of repositories you opened — deliberately, since most questions about this app are about a particular checkout — so read it before sending it on if any of those names are private.

Removing it is ordinary:

sudo apt remove source-manager     # --purge to drop the settings as well

Signing is optional, and the release says which

The pipeline builds and packages whether or not signing certificates are configured, and says what is unsigned in the step log, the job summary and the release notes. An unsigned macOS build is refused by Gatekeeper on a machine that did not build it; an unsigned Windows zip raises SmartScreen.

There is no AppImage, no Flatpak, no .rpm and no Windows installer — both Linux artifacts need Qt and libgit2 from the distribution, and the Windows one is a zip of the deployed tree. Each is its own piece of work rather than a step to bolt on untested.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
cmake -B build .
cmake --build build

That is the whole of it on every platform. Nothing platform-specific is needed to build; only the install rules differ.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• Qt 6.2 or later. There is no Qt 5 arm — it was removed rather than kept as a set of conditionals nothing exercised. The app builds against 6.2; the test suite needs 6.5, because eleven QML suites call waitForPolish.
  • libgit2, through pkg-config.
  • OpenSSL's libcrypto, which arrives with libgit2 (which requires it) and is what verifies a licence key.
  • Qt's Linguist tools — lupdate and lrelease. Translations are compiled on every build, and a configure without them stops with the package to install rather than quietly producing a build that speaks one language.
Debian / UbuntumacOSWindows 
sudo apt install ninja-build pkg-config libgit2-dev \
     qt6-base-dev qt6-declarative-dev libqt6sql6-sqlite \
     qt6-tools-dev qt6-l10n-tools \
     qml6-module-qtquick qml6-module-qtquick-controls \
     qml6-module-qtquick-layouts qml6-module-qtquick-window \
     qml6-module-qtquick-dialogs qml6-module-qtquick-templates \
     qml6-module-qtqml-workerscript qml6-module-qttest \
     qml6-module-qt-labs-platform qml6-module-qt-labs-folderlistmodel

The -dev packages carry the CMake config files and the qml6-module-* ones carry what the engine loads at run time. They are separate packages, and a machine with only the first builds everything and then fails every QML test with "module not installed".

Optionally libsecret-1-dev, which enables the keychain rung for an https token. Without it the app compiles unchanged and the token stays in memory for the session.

brew install qt libgit2 pkg-config

Homebrew's qt already carries the Linguist tools.

Qt through aqtinstall, libgit2 through vcpkg — whose pkg-config file is what keeps the root CMakeLists.txt from needing a third dependency arm. MSVC 2022 x64; there is no MinGW arm.

Nothing Windows has been executed

Every line of the Windows support was written on Linux. CI is the only evidence it works, and a green Windows job means the tree configures, compiles, links and passes the suite headless. It says nothing about window chrome, the native file choosers, high-DPI scaling, or a path typed with a drive letter.

docs.title: The build output
docs.text:
build/SourceManager.app on macOS, build/src/SourceManager on Linux, build/src/SourceManager.exe on Windows.

-Wall -Wextra (/W4 on MSVC) are on and -Werror deliberately is not: turning warnings on is one decision, and failing the build on them is a second one with a different cost — a toolchain upgrade adds diagnostics, and a build that stops on those is a build that gets the flag removed rather than the code fixed.

docs.title: The build with no paid tier on screen
docs.text:
cmake -B build -DSOURCEMANAGER_FREE_ONLY=ON .

Hides the paid features, the switch that would show them, and the licence window — for handing a copy to somebody who should not be offered something they cannot buy. It is not a second product: the gate, the feature table and the licence check compile in exactly as they do otherwise, and only what is drawn changes. The suite passes in both configurations.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
cmake --install build

On none of the three platforms is the result self-contained: the app goes on loading Qt and libgit2 from wherever this machine keeps them. Re-run it after every build — the old copy is replaced outright, not merged over.

LinuxmacOSWindows

Installs bin/SourceManager, a desktop entry under share/applications/ and six icon sizes under share/icons/hicolor/, through CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX as any other program does.

The default prefix is ~/.local rather than CMake's /usr/local, so installing needs no sudo and the desktop finds the entry with no configuration — ~/.local/share is $XDG_DATA_HOME. Pass -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr for a package; --prefix and DESTDIR both work normally.

Puts SourceManager.app in ~/Applications, where Finder, Spotlight and Launchpad all find it. Reconfigure with -DSOURCEMANAGER_INSTALL_DIR=/Applications for a machine-wide install.

That variable, not --prefix, is what moves the bundle — Qt Creator forces CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX to /tmp from a deferred call that runs after everything in CMakeLists.txt, so the destination deliberately does not go through it.

Installing ad-hoc signs the bundle, which is not optional on Apple Silicon: copying the app rewrites its rpath, invalidating the signature the linker applied, and the kernel then refuses to execute it — the app dies on launch with no dialog and nothing in the log.

bin/SourceManager.exe under CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX, and nothing beside it. There is no icon to install (it is compiled into the binary) and no desktop entry.

This is the platform where the "not self-contained" caveat bites hardest: Windows has no system place for a library, so an executable finds its DLLs beside itself or on PATH and the install rule arranges neither. What makes a Windows build runnable elsewhere is windeployqt over the staged tree, which the pipeline runs and the install rules do not.

docs.title: Redistributing a macOS bundle
docs.text:
Shipping to anyone else needs macdeployqt to copy the Qt frameworks in, then a Developer ID signature and notarisation to get past Gatekeeper. Between those two steps run:

tools/verify-macos-bundle.sh <bundle>

It reports any load command naming an absolute path outside the bundle — a Homebrew libgit2 that macdeployqt did not copy in works on the machine that built it and on no other. The script is macOS-only and was written on Linux, so it has never been executed.

See Third-party notices for what a redistributed build owes the libraries it carries.

docs.title: From Qt Creator
docs.text:
CMakePresets.json is committed, so Qt Creator offers each preset as a build configuration — pick Debug, then install to ~/Applications and ⌘B builds and installs in one go.

Qt Creator only imports presets when it has no configuration of its own, so on a project it has already opened, delete .qtcreator/CMakeLists.txt.user and reopen. That also discards which kit the project was using, so check the kit's Qt is still valid afterwards — a Homebrew upgrade moves the Cellar path, the kit is left with no Qt, and Qt Creator then passes an empty -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH= and nothing is findable.

The robust answer is a gitignored CMakeUserPresets.json that inherits from the committed ones and pins Qt itself, because it does not depend on the kit being right:

{
  "version": 3,
  "configurePresets": [
    {
      "name": "local-debug",
      "inherits": "debug",
      "cacheVariables": {
        "CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH": "/path/to/Qt/6.10.1/macos",
        "Qt6_DIR": "/path/to/Qt/6.10.1/macos/lib/cmake/Qt6"
      }
    }
  ],
  "buildPresets": [
    { "name": "local-debug-install", "configurePreset": "local-debug",
      "targets": ["all", "install"] }
  ]
}

Qt6_DIR is set as well as CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH because Qt Creator puts its own (possibly empty) prefix path on the command line too; Qt6_DIR is something it never sets, so it cannot be overridden.

A configure that fails this way leaves a cache with the empty path in it, so fix the path and delete the build directory — reconfiguring in place keeps failing.

docs.title: Keyboard and the palette
docs.text: Every interaction is reachable two ways — by name from the command palette, and by key from the hint overlay — and both read from one registry that the design system's components register themselves with. A build in which a control is reachable by neither route fails its own audit test.

docs.title: The palette
docs.text:
⌘K / Ctrl+K.

Type part of a title, or part of the git verb. The design rule is that the CLI vocabulary is the search index, so stash push finds the button that stashes, restore --staged finds unstage, and rebase -i finds the plan. With nothing typed the list is ordered by how often you have run each thing.

Highlighting a row prints the git command it corresponds to, which is the second half of the same idea — see the command line.

docs.title: The hint overlay
docs.text:
Tap ⌘ (Ctrl elsewhere) and let go. Every primary control on screen grows a letter; press the letter.

  • Tab adds the long tail — list rows, tick boxes, filter chips.
  • Esc, a second tap, a click, or running one puts them away. So does six seconds passing: a tap on the way to something else is not an instruction.

A tap rather than a hold, because held the operating system wins — ⌘Q quits, ⌘W closes, ⌘H hides, ⌘Tab switches application — so three of the label keys would have been dangerous and the second press would never have arrived at all.

Two presses rather than one, because labelling everything at once put 37 badges on History, past the 26-key alphabet, and every label then grew to two characters including the ones you actually use. The first press labels 14–19 things, so every key is a single character.

What gets promoted is measured. Every run is counted, from either route, and a secondary command run often enough takes a first-press key — somebody who lives in the stash list gets those rows without the second press. The room for promotions is whatever the alphabet has left after the declared primaries, so favouring something never costs the labels their single character.

The badges sit inside the top-right corner of what they name. A label drawn outside an element lands on whatever is beside it, and four placements meant four ways for a key to appear where the eye had no reason to look. The legend along the bottom names every key, because a badge beside a button you can read explains itself and one beside a tick box does not.

One accepted limitation

⌘C over a focused text field can raise the labels. The latch that prevents this clears on any key coming up that is not the modifier, and on the caret having moved — and a copy does neither. Catching it would mean watching the clipboard (a global the app does not own) or timing two key releases (guessing at fingers), and both would run on every chord anybody types. The labels appear over a field nothing was typed into, and Esc or a click dismisses them.

docs.title: Moving between places
docs.text:
Key What it does ← / → Back and forward through where you have been Two-finger swipe The same two verbs, on macOS only ⌃Tab Repository switcher: hold to show, Tab to step, release to commit ⌘, Settings — and again to leave Space On Changes, stage or unstage what is picked Esc The switcher, then the hint labels, then the settings page

A place is the surface, the repository, the sub-tab of whichever surface draws one, and the one object opened inside it. Not the active file — the line between what is in a place and what is not is whether you would say you went there, which is why a proposal's number is in it and scrolling a file list is not.

The repository is in a place because leaving it out would make the feature lie: Fleet → open A → History → open B → Changes, and a Back carrying only a surface id would draw B's History under A's name.

Nothing is consumed unless it moved. A ← at the beginning of the history falls through rather than being eaten, because a key that is swallowed and does nothing is indistinguishable from a key that is broken. Only the bare spelling is read: ⌥← is a word and ⇧← a selection.

docs.title: The swipe
docs.text:
On macOS a two-finger horizontal swipe is the platform's own idiom, and it adds no verb — it calls the same back and forward, declares no palette entry and takes no hint key. It cannot eat a sideways scroll: a diff wide enough to scroll keeps its sweep, and only a gesture nothing under the pointer wanted navigates.

It can be switched off (Settings → Moving between places), on by default, because a page that jumps back while somebody is reading it is worth being able to stop rather than learn to live with. The row is absent on Linux and Windows, where a horizontal two-finger scroll means "scroll sideways" in the rest of the desktop.

docs.title: What has no key, on purpose
docs.text:
Splitter handles, calendar day cells, the diff's per-line Comment button, a commit's drag grip, a ticket link in a commit message, and an elided label's reveal. Each is either a continuous drag with nothing to name, or one per row in a list of thousands — and a key per row spends the alphabet several times over on one list.

The reveal on a truncated label is the one genuine gap: it is reachable by pointer alone. Where that mattered most the answer was a real keyboard route rather than a second tooltip — the path above a diff has a Copy path button beside it, and the metrics rows were given the width they were actually short of.

docs.title: A tour of the window
docs.text:
The window is one shell with a set of destinations, and the frame around them is two strips where each strip is one kind of thing.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ⌂ › my-project › main ↑2 ↓3            Fetch ▾  Pull  Push ▾  Actions ▾  ⚙ │  the workspace bar
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Changes 3   History   Rebase   Conflicts   Blame   Manage   …       │  the tab bar
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Rebasing — stopped on conflicts in 2 files    Conflicts  Abort      │  the operation banner
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│                          one surface                                 │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  9 repositories · 2 with work in progress                            │  the status bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The workspace bar
docs.text:
Says which repository, which branch, and what can be done to that pair.

Home › my-project › main is a breadcrumb rather than a sidebar, and each crumb is the way to change what it states:

  • Home goes to the fleet.
  • The repository crumb opens the fleet as a filtered list, with the marker dot, the drift counts and the group as a tag.
  • The branch crumb opens the branches with a filter, carries ↑ahead ↓behind, and is the only place that says which branch those counts are about. Choosing one narrows the history to it and moves nothing.

Then Fetch (with a caret for fetch-and-prune), Pull, Push (with a caret for the two forcing verbs), the actions menu, and the way into the settings.

Push always means push. It refuses a non-fast-forward in its own words rather than replacing itself with a forcing verb at the moment forcing is dangerous; both ways past that refusal are behind the caret, and the plain force needs a third gesture. See Remotes and transport.

On the fleet page the transport verbs and the crumbs are hidden — the fleet is not one repository and stopped pretending to be — and the foot says how many repositories are registered and how many have work in progress.

docs.title: The tab bar
docs.text:
The tab bar is the list of destinations. Nine of them have a tab:

Tab What it holds Changes The working tree, staged and unstaged, with a diff History The graph, the search, and a commit's contents Rebase Plan a rebase, edit the plan, then apply it Conflicts Three-way resolution, per hunk Blame Per-line blame with a revision list Manage Stashes, worktrees, submodules, subtrees, branches, remotes, hooks, LFS, sparse, actions, the operations log Pull requests The forge's proposals, and a review Checks CI: this commit's checks, and the forge's own runs Metrics What the history and the forge say, over a period

Changes and Conflicts carry a count of what they hold. Zero renders as nothing at all — "Conflicts 0" is what the tab would read on all but a handful of days, and a number that is almost always the same stops being read, while a badge appearing where there was none is the whole signal.

Five more destinations have no tab and are reached by name from the palette or from an object: Fleet (the Home crumb), Compare, Settings, File history and Reflog. A tenth tab would cost every other tab some of its width on every surface.

Exactly one surface exists at a time

Surfaces are loaded on demand rather than stacked. History and Blame each hold thousands of rows, and there is no reason for the ones you are not looking at to exist. The consequence you can see: a filter typed into a search box is gone when you come back, while a reading habit — split diff, wrapped lines, tree view — is remembered, because those live in the settings rather than on the surface.

docs.title: The operation banner
docs.text:
The design rule the whole app is arranged around is that operations are modal in time, not in space. A running or stopped operation shows in a banner under the header on every surface, so walking away from a half-finished rebase is safe and it cannot be lost track of.

It reports five kinds of state — a stopped rebase, merge or cherry-pick, a bisect, a detached HEAD — plus two rows of its own for a transfer in flight and a long write over many paths. The way out is always on it, and never gated: a lapsed licence cannot leave anybody in a detached HEAD with no button.

docs.title: Operations are entered from the object
docs.text:
There is no menu of verbs anywhere. Rebase is entered from a commit in History; revert from a commit; bisect from the commit where the thing still worked; ignore from the file in Changes; a proposal from a branch row or from the comparison page. Conflicts opens by itself when something stops on one.

That is why a few features have no obvious front door, and why Bisect, stacked branches and workflow recipes each get a walkthrough of their own.

docs.title: Panels are dragged, and stay where you put them
docs.text:
Every two-panel division goes through one restyled splitter: the handle is in the app's hairline idiom, and the size survives a relaunch and being restored into a window smaller than the one it was chosen in. Sizes are in pixels rather than fractions, because a quarter of a wide window is not readable as a quarter of a small one.

Three divisions deliberately have no handle: the three conflict columns (equal thirds are what makes three readings comparable), the blame gutter (a per-row column is not a division), and the two Rebase steps (a form has a right width rather than a preferred one — dragging prose narrow is the same words in more lines).

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The backlog this project was built from is closed — 115 of 115. What follows is what genuinely remains, and it is short.

Eleven of those 115 closed as recorded decisions rather than code, and each says what it would cost and what would unblock it — because a decision is a deliverable here, and what is not acceptable is an entry left implying work nobody has thought about.

  • :material-clipboard-check-outline: Closed as decisions

    Five things that look like gaps and are not: what each would cost, and what would change the answer.

  • :material-hand-back-left-outline: Deliberate non-goals

    Positions this project has taken. These are not backlog and should not be read as one.

docs.title: Outstanding, and real
docs.text: Missing Who has it Note Azure DevOps as a forge Tower, SmartGit, GitKraken 💰 The seam now carries three providers and a per-host base URL, so this is a class and a registration line — the claim the seam was built on, and now actually tested twice A plugin / scripting API Sublime Merge, Git Extensions, Magit, GitLens Custom commands landed as a template; letting somebody extend the app rather than run a program beside it did not Semantic / language-aware diff SmartGit (SemanticMerge) Never scoped. A genuine gap rather than a decision Non-git VCS (SVN, Mercurial) SmartGit Out of scope and argued — but it is still a reason somebody picks SmartGit Live verification of Windows, GitLab and Bitbucket Everyone who ships them Not a feature. The most valuable thing on this list

docs.title: The most valuable item is not a feature
docs.text:
Everything about the capability gap is closed. What is left is evidence, and it is worth stating as the top of the roadmap rather than a footnote to it:

  • Nothing Windows has ever been executed. CI proves the tree configures, compiles, links and passes the suite headless under MSVC. It says nothing about window chrome, the native choosers, high-DPI on a real display, or paths typed with a drive letter. Do not read a green Windows job as "Windows works."
  • GitLab and Bitbucket have never had an answer from a live instance. Their tests pin the URLs built, the JSON mapped onto the documented fields, the errors told apart and what the transport will let through — a real guarantee, and not the one a user cares about.
  • X.509 signing, both keychain backends, the sparse verbs and every AI provider are implemented and unexercised.

What would close each is somebody using the app on that platform, against that instance, with that key. There is no test that substitutes for it, and pretending otherwise is the failure this project's whole documentation style exists to avoid.

docs.title: Two items that are unfinished rather than declined
docs.text:
These are recorded here because a verb reachable from nothing reads as done, which is a defect this project has been caught by five times and now has a test for:

  • The format-patch series verbs are implemented, tested, and opened by no control. The patch dialog is built around a file field and a single-diff plan, and another subject there means a directory field, a different plan shape and a different set of counts — a restructure rather than a row. See Patches.
  • The Rebase surface's first step is a dead end for a branch that is only behind. Typing a base that yields no plan leaves the reader on that step with the same faint sentence it opened with and a "Continue to plan" that does nothing. The surface has no third state for "the branch is only behind, and fast-forwarding is what you want" — the controller already has the verb, and this is interface work on that page.

docs.title: How the backlog is worth reading now
docs.text:
The value of BACKLOG.md is no longer the list — it is the reasoning. Every closed entry says what landed, what was given up, and what is still unproven, and four things it records are worth carrying into any future work:

Four defects nobody had reported were found while implementing features, and each was invisible to a green test suite:

  • Two launches of the app erased each other's operation log and review drafts. Three whole-file writers each held an in-memory copy; the second to write erased everything the other had recorded. For the log that took the working-tree backup tokens with it; for the drafts it was the only copy of unsent prose.
  • A quit-time crash: killing a process in a destructor with its handlers still attached delivers two signals synchronously, so the first clears a pointer and the second dereferences it.
  • Eight things reachable from nothing. That class is now closed by a test with no allow-list, reporting zero dead across 484 declarations.
  • Labels readable by pointer and by nothing else, in three places.

And two operational findings. A merge lock has to be held through rebase → build → test → merge or nothing converges, which serialises the expensive part — correctness over throughput, deliberately. And an incremental test run hides warnings that only a clean build reveals; the clean build is the one to believe.

docs.title: Closed as decisions
docs.text: Five things that look like gaps in the comparison and are not. Each says what it would cost and what would unblock it, because a decision is a deliverable here and an entry left implying work nobody has thought about is not.

docs.title: An embedded terminal
docs.text:
GitKraken, Sublime Merge (its git console) and Lazygit have one.

The argument the external merge tool is offered on applies here with more force: the reader already has a terminal, and it is theirs — their shell, their prompt, their profile, their multiplexer, their keybindings, fifteen years of muscle memory. A pane here would be a second, worse terminal that has to be configured separately.

What it would cost is three problems rather than a widget:

  1. A pty, which is forkpty() on Linux and macOS and CreatePseudoConsole on Windows — two unrelated APIs, and the Windows half would be unrunnable code in a port whose own record says nothing about it has ever been executed.
  2. A terminal emulator. A pty hands over a byte stream of escape sequences: cursor addressing, scroll regions, the alternate screen, SGR, character sets, mouse reporting, bracketed paste. That is what libvterm and QTermWidget exist for, so it is a new hard dependency — and the rule the keychain was settled under is that a dependency is settled before anything is written and a platform-only implementation is worse than none. QTermWidget is a widgets library besides, so it does not compose with this window even if the dependency were taken.
  3. The suite could not say whether it worked. Every assertion that matters — does a prompt render, does resizing reflow, does ⌃C reach the child — is a question about the emulator, offscreen, in a headless runner.

That last one decides it. A pane that draws something terminal-shaped and is not a terminal is the one outcome worse than the absence, and it is the outcome a feature nothing can test converges on.

What exists instead: an external terminal template that opens yours, in this repository's directory.

docs.title: A Windows Explorer shell extension
docs.text:
TortoiseGit's whole point, and Git Extensions has one.

Status overlays in the file manager are the headline Windows integration every competitor ships, and it is refused on four grounds rather than deferred:

  1. It cannot share a line of this codebase. An overlay handler is an in-process COM server loaded into explorer.exe, so it must not link Qt — wrong process, wrong threading model, and a crash takes the shell down with it. It would need its own libgit2, or its own IPC to a service, which is a second application with a second answer to "what is this file's status".
  2. The overlay slots are capped at fifteen, system-wide, handed out alphabetically by registry key. That is why every product that ships one prefixes its key with spaces to win the race, and why a new entrant on a machine that already has a cloud drive realistically gets none. A feature whose visibility depends on beating other vendors in a sort is not one to build on the strength of it compiling.
  3. CI could prove it compiles, and that is the wrong bar. The SDK headers are on the runner, so a job could build and link a COM DLL — and nothing on a runner can register one (elevation), load one (no Explorer, no session) or exercise a single thing it does. A component that compiles and has never run is precisely the silent-skip guard this project has a position on, and committing one blind would read as done.
  4. The port it is meant to follow has not landed in any verified sense. What is known about Windows is that the tree builds and the suite passes headless, and an integration with the shell is the furthest thing from that from being answerable.

What would unblock it: a Windows machine somebody actually uses this app on — not to write the COM, which is well-documented, but to answer whether the overlays appear at all on a real desktop, and whether a status-per-directory cache can answer inside Explorer's own budget.

What exists instead: "Show in File Explorer", which needs no DLL, no registry and no elevation.

docs.title: Partial clone
docs.text:
SmartGit and Git Extensions offer it.

libgit2 has no promisor support, so a --filter=blob:none clone — reachable by shelling out — would produce a checkout this app cannot read: a partial clone records a promisor remote and leaves most blobs absent, expecting whoever opens the repository to fetch each one on demand. Every blob lookup would fail with a not-found the moment a diff, a blame or a checkout asked for one.

A tick producing a repository the app then could not open is worse than no tick, which is the absent-not-greyed rule applied to a capability rather than to a control.

It is named on the clone dialog rather than silently absent, whatever else is chosen, because it is a fact about this build and not about anything on the form.

Shallow clone is offered, with what it gives up named beside it. See Remotes and transport.

docs.title: LFS state on the fleet
docs.text:
The answer asked for — "this checkout has objects it never fetched" — costs a file read per managed path, per repository, across every repository in the fleet. That is exactly the cost the fleet page is designed to refuse, and it is why the fleet is outside the app's general refresh in the first place.

The tempting substitute is worse than the absence: a root .gitattributes naming filter=lfs is cheap, and it answers "this project uses LFS" — which is not the question. Drawn as a badge on a card it would be read as "something here needs fetching", which is true of a checkout that has never fetched and false of every properly checked-out one, with no way to tell from the card which kind you are looking at. A badge that is right by coincidence on some cards is worse than no badge.

What exists instead: the figure on Manage's LFS tab, where one repository has been asked about and the walk is affordable.

docs.title: Auto-resolving "mechanical" conflicts
docs.text:
GitKraken does it.

It requires trusting a classifier about which conflicts are mechanical, and the failure mode is silent by construction: a conflict resolved without being shown is one nobody reads, so a classifier that is wrong one time in fifty produces a commit nobody can tell from the other forty-nine.

Everything else in this app that writes says what it is about to do first, and this is the one verb where the whole point would be not saying.

What would change it: a mechanism for showing afterwards what was decided without asking — an operation-log row per hunk with the two sides in it. At which point the reader is reading the hunks anyway, which the whole-file suggestion verb already offers.

docs.title: Virtual branches
docs.text:
GitButler's whole thesis.

Stacked branches landed. GitButler's virtual-branch model — several branches applied to one working directory, each change assigned to a lane, committed independently — is a different thesis about what a working tree is, not a missing verb.

It is worth noting that this app's line-level staging would be an unusually good substrate for one: it already assigns individual lines to an outcome and reconstructs patches to apply them. The hard parts are conflicting lanes and unapplying one, and both need answering on paper first.

docs.title: Repository tabs
docs.text:
Recorded as the shape that could not have delivered what was asked for.

One set of controllers holds one repository path, so a tab strip over one of them is a visible drawing of the ⌃Tab list: pressing a tab swaps the repository underneath every surface, which is what the switcher already does with no chrome at all.

Two repositories side by side needs two sets of controllers, which is a second window — and that is what shipped.

docs.title: Deliberate non-goals
docs.text:
Positions this project has taken and written down. These are not backlog, and an agent or a contributor working through the outstanding list should leave them alone.

Each is here because the absence would otherwise read as an oversight — which is the same reason the decisions are recorded rather than left silent.

docs.title: No "Undo everything" button
docs.text:
The reflog records refs, not files. A commit that left a branch is still in the object database; an uncommitted edit that reset --hard wrote over was never in an object at all.

A button that cannot tell those apart is at its most confident exactly when it is most wrong, because it is pressed at the moment the work was destroyed.

What ships instead is a typed operations log that offers a way back only where one can be kept, and working-tree backups before the four writes that destroy content held in no git object — which makes some of those rows recoverable and says plainly when a row is not.

docs.title: No agentic AI
docs.text:
Nothing edits files, runs commands, or takes more than one turn. Generation produces a draft a reader reviews before it is used.

Every argument for that arrangement is an argument against the other one: an agent producing work nobody read is the failure the original refusal to generate anything was protecting against, restored at a larger scale.

What would change it is not a better model. It is a way for a reader to review a sequence of edits as cheaply as they review a sentence — and this app's answer to that is Changes, which is where a patch applied by hand already lands.

docs.title: No streaming generated text
docs.text: A second shape on the transport, on the replay and on every surface that draws a partial answer, to save a moment on answers that are short and reviewed anyway.

docs.title: Non-git version control
docs.text:
Subversion, Mercurial and the rest are not on a list of things to get to.

Every controller here is written against libgit2's object model — a commit graph, an index with stages, a reflog, refs — and none of those is a shape the others share. Supporting one would not be a backend behind an existing seam but a second application in the same window, with its own answers for staging, for what a branch is, and for what an "undo" can honestly promise.

The two things this project spends most of its care on — refusing rather than clobbering, and saying exactly what an operation did — are where that would go wrong first: a Subversion "revert" and this app's are not the same act, and a client that used one word for both would be doing the thing the whole documentation exists to prevent.

git subtree is the one place a non-libgit2 mechanism is used at all, and it is shelled out to with its cost stated.

docs.title: In-repository distributed code review
docs.text:
SmartGit ships this, as a separately licensed add-on: review state kept as objects or refs inside the repository, so a review travels with a clone and needs no server.

It is a genuinely good idea and it is not this app's. Reviewing here goes through the forge's own API, because the review a team actually argues in is the one on their forge — and a second review store, visible only to people using this client, would be a place for comments to be written that nobody else can see or answer. That is worse than not offering it.

What this app does instead is make the forge's own review readable and writable from here, with the band saying which of the three kinds of comment you are looking at.

docs.title: A branch picker that checks out
docs.text:
The breadcrumb's picker narrows the history to a branch and moves nothing, and it says so in as many words. That is what clicking a branch has always meant here and people rely on it.

Checking out lives on the Branches tab, where the row also tells you what the checkout would overwrite before you press it.

docs.title: Greying a control that cannot apply
docs.text:
Absent, not greyed. A verb that does not apply to this repository is not drawn at all, which also takes it out of the palette and off the hint keys, since a control registers those on being enabled and visible.

The cost is stated rather than hidden: it makes coverage read as thinner than it is on a repository where a verb does not apply, which is why several pages here say "the button is absent because…" rather than leaving you to wonder.

There are four deliberate exceptions, each argued where it lives: the transport buttons grey while a transfer runs (the verb applies, it is busy); the fleet's Add control greys when the free cap is reached (a control that vanished would take the sentence explaining it with it); an AI control with no provider configured stays live so that pressing it can explain itself; and the confirm button inside a dialog is what disappears when the plan says no, rather than the button that opens the dialog.

docs.title: Arbitrary shell steps inside action sequences
docs.text:
A step is one of this app's own verbs, so every refusal a sequence meets is a controller's own, in the words you would have seen pressing the button.

Custom commands exist as a separate template rather than a widening of that rule: an argument list, never a shell.

docs.title: No --force on a tag, and no force for submodule deinit
docs.text:
Both refusals name something to go and settle instead.

A tag name pointed at a different commit is a different tag wearing an old one's clothes and nothing on disk records what it displaced — plain git tag declines for the same reason. And a forced submodule deinit would be the only route in this app to losing work that is nowhere else.

docs.title: No confirmation on per-hunk and per-line verbs
docs.text:
A dialog per keystroke is a habit rather than a safeguard, and both land somewhere you can look at them and change your mind. The same trade revert already makes.

What replaces it is refusing: a conflicted path, a selection with nothing undoable in it, and — through the apply itself — a file whose content has moved on since the diff was read. An empty patch applies cleanly and reports success for having done nothing, which is exactly how a destructive verb comes to be trusted.

docs.title: No PUT on the forge write list, and no mark-as-viewed row
docs.text:
The three things a PUT would carry are the three ways of changing something somebody else made: rewriting the body of a review, dismissing one, and replacing the label set. The audit asserts each is refused.

Mark-as-viewed would have been a fourth and is GraphQL-only. The argument that used to keep it out — that no GraphQL URL may be on the list — has expired rather than been answered, since the review being written needed that row. So it is now simply unimplemented, which is a smaller and more honest thing to say.

docs.title: No fully-merged claim the commit graph cannot support
docs.text: Nothing here is called "fully merged", because a reachability test cannot catch a squash or a rebase merge. The wording says what was checked, and the forge's answer is drawn beside it where there is one.
